en: (B1) Śrīḥ! The Bhāṭṭadīpikā, accompanied by the commentary Prabhāvalī.
In this regard, the first quarter of the second chapter:
(Section 1) (A.2 Pāda 1 Adhi.1) "Words denoting action have the sense of being; from them the ritual act is to be understood, for it is this meaning that is enjoined. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.1)
Thus, having defined dharma, adharma, and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their essential nature (*svarūpa*) is now being defined.
Although that [nature] is indeed already understood insofar as it is the object to be established by these many means of valid cognition,
nevertheless, because it has not yet been understood in terms of its unity, plurality, and so forth, it is defined here according to those aspects.

And here, the subject matter of the chapter is precisely the distinction between the various forms of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) based on the six means of proof, beginning with "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*).
The distinction between the meanings of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) is investigated only occasionally as a means to establish that [distinction],
and the distinction between the unseen potency (*apūrva*) is also not a primary subject of the chapter, as it serves merely as its result.

Since even the distinction between the various types of *apūrva* that have become the results depends upon the distinction between the means (*sādhana*) to that *apūrva*, when there arises an inquiry into those means, it is considered whether— given that the *apūrva* as an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) is indeed the means for achieving heaven and so forth— the status of the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) is that of the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the result such as heaven, or whether it belongs to the meaning of the subordinate word (*upapadārtha*),
such as *soma* and the like. Thus, in this deliberation:

Since even the Siddhāntin accepts that the connection with the initial meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) belongs to all [the factors], it follows that the subsequent connection with the result also belongs to all of them.

However, since this would entail the postulation of multiple unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa*) if all were considered instruments (*karaṇa*), the status of being an instrument as defined by the result belongs to only one,
while for the others, their status as instruments exists only through visible means.

Therefore, in this case, since the meaning of the verbal root itself serves as the instrument (karaṇa), and the purpose of the root-meaning is achieved precisely through its status as the substratum (āśraya), there is no assumption of multiple unseen effects (adṛṣṭa).
Thus ends the first section concerning the Pratipad.
(B2) (Invocation) I bow to the beautiful and glorious Light, which destroys the darkness of ignorance, illuminates the knowledge of reality, and bestows all desired objects. 1.

I bow to my father Bālakṛṣṇa, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of the Vedas and Śāstras, who is exceedingly skillful in the performance of rituals such as sacrifices, and whose mind is purified by the constant worship of Sadāśiva. // 2 //

Having prostrated before the venerable Śrī Khaṇḍadeva, my true guru, who is the sun to the lotus-heart of the Mīmāṃsakas, I compose this commentary titled *Prabhāvalī* upon his work, which treats the categories of existence in an extremely concise manner. (3)
Even though some inconsistency has been pointed out here by me regarding the work of the Guru, this is not an act of malice on my part, for I am skilled in promoting [the teachings].

Rather, my intention is this: may those ornaments of the earth, whose intellects are as sharp as kusha-grass and who are devoted to the established tenets, set aside my words and instead grace the work composed by him.

(An exposition of the necessity of investigating the nature of Dharma within the first chapter itself, followed by an exposition of the contextual connection (*avasara-saṅgati*) with the preceding chapter, and finally the formal declaration of the subject matter of the second chapter:

Although the inquiry into the very nature of Dharma was declared first in the opening sūtra, and since that same inquiry into the nature of Dharma—prior even to the inquiry into its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—was declared in the Bhāṣya commentary on that sūtra in the passage "What is Dharma? What is its definition?", it would indeed be appropriate to undertake the determination of its nature at the outset.

There is no formal definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); nevertheless, since the establishment of the object of knowledge (*meyasiddhi*) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition, and because its essential nature was already stated in the *Codanāsūtra* by way of its inclusion among the means of valid cognition, the investigation into the means of valid cognition was carried out in its entirety in the first chapter, while setting aside the investigation into that essential nature even though it was capable of being performed.

According to the maxim that when something is undertaken for a certain purpose, upon its completion, that which was present in the mind arises, so too, when the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is concluded, the nature [of dharma]—which has been present in the mind—finds its opportunity; intending this, the determination of that nature is now undertaken as a "contextual connection" (*avasara-saṅgati*).

Alternatively, since injunctions (*vidhi*) concern the origination of ritual acts through indicators such as "different words" (*śabdāntara*), and since a re-injunction of what has already originated would be purposeless, the establishment of difference [between rituals] depends upon the removal of such purposelessness.

Showing now, by means of the word "thus" (evam), the logical connection of cause and effect—that [the subsequent arguments] can only be stated once the validity [of cognition] has been established—he sets forth the subject matter of the entire chapter: "Thus... (Na0).
(On the connection with the treatise in the second chapter:

By this [statement], it is indicated that the determination of the subject matter of this chapter—since it falls under the portion [of the inquiry] "What is dharma?"—is connected to the treatise as being the object of the proposition in the first sūtra.

(The justification for the determination of difference [bheda] prior to the determination of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal [śeṣa-śeṣibhāva], and after the determination of the means of valid cognition [pramāṇa]): Although even the eleventh book (*adhyāya*), which proceeds after the definition of the means of valid cognition, is dependent upon that definition of the means of valid cognition, nevertheless, the fact that the determination of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal is established in dependence upon the determination of difference is evident from the very opening of the section on the definition of the subordinate: "Now, therefore, follows the definition of the subordinate" (*athātaḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam*).
Since this has been demonstrated by the author of the Sūtras himself, this is precisely the occasion for defining the divisions [of Dharma] which must be established for its sake.

Thus, the intention is that there is no lack of coherence in first discussing the divisions and so forth—following the definition of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—and only afterwards performing the determination of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), thereby overriding the order of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) regarding "What is Dharma? What are its characteristics? with the order of the actual subject matter (*arthakrama*).

(The meaning of the chapter is precisely the distinction between meditative realizations (*bhāvanā*), and not their unity or the distinction between the meanings of the verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) and so forth; however, the determination of those [distinctions] is for the purpose of being relied upon as an exception (*apavāda*) or as a result, and so on.

Now, he dispels the doubt that if the nature of those [realizations] were determined by means of their unity or plurality, it would follow that there is a division in the subject matter of the chapter—this is addressed by the words "In this regard" (*atra ca*).

The meaning is as follows: although the difference in *bhāvanā* has been established as the subject matter of the chapter by means of various proofs such as "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*), even when non-difference is established in certain cases as an exception (*apavāda*) to that, it does not constitute the subject matter of the chapter.

Now, one might object: "Even if non-difference is not the subject matter of the chapter, since the difference among all three—the *bhāvanā*, the *apūrva*, and the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*)—will be established hereafter, why is it not the case that difference [as a whole] is the subject matter of the chapter?
To this, he says: "But the difference of the root-meanings... (*dhātvarthabhedastu*).

Although in this context the promise is to define the divisions of *dharma* alone, and since that *dharma*—being the meaning of verbal roots such as "sacrifice" (*yāga*)—is *dharma* precisely because it is the means to the highest good (*śreyas*), it might follow that the subject matter of the chapter is the division of that [root-meaning] itself, rather than the division of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).

Nevertheless, since a sacrifice and the like, which have not yet been accomplished, acquire their very existence only by being the object of an effort (*kṛti*), they possess primacy as the means to the highest good; therefore, it is not improper that the subject matter of the chapter is the division of that very effort.

Precisely for this reason, since the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is not the direct meaning of the word, it is impossible to determine its distinctions by way of its own nature; therefore, its distinction is co-produced with the distinction of the *bhāvanā* (the efficient force).

This is because there is an invariable rule that a distinction in activity is pervaded by a distinction in result, and because the status of being a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatva*) is impossible without the *apūrva*. Since all *bhāvanās* cease only upon the production of the *apūrva*, and because [the *apūrva*] is regarded as the result itself, its distinction is also co-produced insofar as it has become the result.
This is not at all contradictory;
rather, the determination of the difference between the meanings of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) is for the purpose of establishing the difference between the productive operations (*bhāvanā*).

Although it is observed that a difference in effects arises precisely from a difference in the activity of the causes, it is the difference in the *bhāvanā* itself that serves to establish the difference in the meanings of the verbal roots.

Nevertheless, since the distinctness (vaijātya) residing in the cause is established in dependence upon the distinctness residing in the effect, one should understand that the statement regarding the difference in the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) as the proof for the difference in productive energy (*bhāvanā*)— made with reference to all [roots]— is intended to mean that those roots such as *yajati* (he sacrifices), which are presented with differences in their own forms, serve to manifest a difference in the productive energy.

(An analysis of the statement that [the distinction of *bhāvanā*] is "occasional" because the distinction of *bhāvanā* is established from a quality (*guṇa*) even when there is no difference in the meaning of the verbal root):

Since it will be explained in the section on qualities and results (*guṇaphalādhikāra*) that a distinction of *bhāvanā* arises from a quality—even when there is no difference in the meaning of the verbal root—which would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the author intends to convey that a difference in the meaning of the verbal root is not the means for establishing a distinction of *bhāvanā* in all cases; thus, he stated that it is "occasional."
(An exposition on how the *pratipadādhikaraṇa* proceeds as an introduction to the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, which itself serves as an introduction to the entire chapter.

Since the investigation into the differentiation of *bhāvanā* will be discussed starting from the second pāda, one might raise the objection: "If that [differentiation] is not being investigated here, how is there a logical connection (*saṅgati*) for the subsequent discussion? This objection is addressed by means of the introductory connection (*upodghātasaṅgati*) to the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* which is about to be treated as an introduction to the entire chapter.
He avoids [the objection] by stating: "having become the fruit."

Since the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is not produced directly by the *bhāvanā*, but is understood to be produced by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and so forth which serve as its medium, and since that which is the means to the fruit (*phala-sādhana*) alone generates the *apūrva* as an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), it follows that when there is a difference in the means to the fruit there is a difference in the *apūrva*, and when there is unity [of the means] there is unity [of the *apūrva*].

It is for this purpose—namely, as an introductory discussion (*upoddhāta*) to the investigation into whether the status of being a means to the fruit resides solely in the meaning of the verbal root that is yet to be performed—that this section concerning the individual words (*pratipadādhikaraṇa*) is commenced. This is the meaning.
(An explanation of how sentences such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" fall within the scope of the aforementioned section, rather than the scope of sentences concerning Soma, etc.

In cases such as "he threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) and "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), since the status of the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth as the object (*karman*) is established by the accusative case-ending itself, it follows by elimination that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) alone functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Similarly, in cases such as "he offers oblation with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), because the act of offering (*homasya*) is already established and thus not something to be enjoined, it lacks the status of an instrument; therefore, [the curd] is construed only as the object (*karman*).

Intending to show that this is not an example here because there is no doubt that the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) belongs exclusively to the meaning of the secondary derivative (upapadārtha), the phrase "of soma and so forth" (somāder api) was stated in order to indicate that the sentences concerning soma and so forth are indeed the examples.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of the term *caru* found in the sentences concerning the Saurya sacrifice and others is intended.

Therefore, in the section concerning the exception to this [rule], namely "those [actions] are twofold," the meaning is that those [examples] are cited because the meaning of the verbal root itself functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

(The establishment of Soma's connection with the efficient force [bhāvanā], either by means of not engaging in the locus of the action [bhāvādhikaraṇa] or by the position that does not accept the indication of possessive meaning [matvarthalakṣaṇā]):
"it is subsequent" (auttarakālika).
The meaning is "belonging to the subsequent [section].

This should be understood with the intention that this point is not yet established, since the fact that the verbal root-meaning alone is the instrument (*karaṇa*) will be proven in the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*).

Otherwise, since the production of the effect (*bhāvanā*) would already be occupied by that instrument, it would be impossible for Soma and the other factors to be connected with it at the outset, and thus it would be impossible for this to be accepted by the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*).

Alternatively, the text should be construed as follows: "Or else, because [the view] is accepted even by the proponent of the final conclusion (siddhāntin) under the position that does not admit the indication of possessive meaning (matvarthalakṣaṇā)."

(Since they are more highly esteemed due to their connection with the principal [act], and since it is possible for them to be independent means even when there is an option, all are determined to be connected as instruments for the result:
"Of all indeed."

Since the connection with the principal [element] is more highly esteemed when possible, and because if one element were connected to the fruit while the other were connected to a subordinate quality of the fruit,

there would result both a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) and the necessity of resorting to possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), it is proper to accept that all [elements] are connected directly to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) itself, and thus they possess the status of being instruments for the fruit.

Although it will be stated in the twelfth [book] that when there is independence in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the fact of having a single purpose (*aikārthya*) alone is the determinant [of syntactic connection],

for otherwise, if mere having a visible purpose were said to be its determinant, there would result the undesirable consequence of optional alternatives (*vikalpa*) among optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) that have a single purpose; and in the present case, since both the nominal suffix (*sup*) and the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) require semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) just as much as a compound does, there is the cognition of an independent instrumentality.

It would result in nothing but conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); nevertheless, because they are presented in a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) through mutual expectancy— just as in the case of the *aruṇā* (red) and the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow)— even though the instruments are understood to be independent of one another within a single productive activity (*bhāvanā*) by the force of the instrumental case endings, their mutual dependence remains, thereby subverting the independence established by the instrumental case.
Because it is accepted that the object [of the injunction] is distinct from the instrument (karaṇa) expressed by its own word, and because— just as in the case of the *darśa* and other sacrifices—

the conjunction (*sāhitya*) perceived through being contained within a single sentence is intended to reside in the things to be employed (*upādeya*), even though there is no lack of combined efficacy when the means (*sādhana*) themselves are combined; with this intention, the word "all" (*sarveṣām*) was stated.

(The commencement of the final conclusion [siddhānta], without direct connection of all [subsidiaries] to the efficient force [bhāvanā], by means of possessive indication [matvarthalakṣaṇā], due to the contingency of postulating numerous unseen potencies [adṛṣṭa] in order to justify the status of being independent instruments [nirapekṣakaraṇatva] as understood in the third [section]:

Although there is unity of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and therein the connection of all [subsidiaries] as instruments through conjunction by way of a single fruit, nevertheless—even though the supreme transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*) and the fruit are one—there is necessarily a distinction among the "origination-transcendental-results" (*utpattyapūrva*) produced by each respective instrument. Having thus brought about the postulation of multiple unseen potencies in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the final conclusion: *Note: The term *utpattyapūrva* refers to the intermediate transcendental result produced by each individual ritual act before it contributes to the final *paramāpūrva*. The *pūrvapakṣa* argues that because these intermediates are distinct, one must assume many unseen potencies for each, which is inefficient. The *siddhānta* resolves this by positing that all subsidiaries connect directly to the *bhāvanā*, thereby avoiding the multiplication of unseen potencies.*
"Of all"—this means:

Nor should it be argued that— because the instruments (karaṇas) are dependent [on one another] and thus lack simultaneity— one should postulate only a single *utpattyapūrva* (origination-apūrva); for,
since the instrumentality understood through the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth must necessarily be defined in relation to some effect,

and since that [instrumentality] is impossible in relation to the fruit or the fruit-apūrva, it is understood as being defined in relation to the *utpattyapūrva* of the curd-offering and the milk-offering.
The meaning is that even in the absence of sequential order, just as the distinction between those [actions] is unavoidable here as well, so too is the distinction between them.

Therefore, having no other recourse, one must abandon the primary connection for all [elements], and even by accepting a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), the status of being the instrument for the fruit belongs either to the verbal root-meaning qualified by Soma and so forth, or else to Soma and so forth qualified by the verbal root-meaning, in the subsequent cognition (*pārṣṭhikabodha*). As for anything else...
He states that it is logical [to hold] that this is for its sake: "of the one alone."
(The conclusion of the established doctrine: "The utility [of the Veda] is through the mode of direct perception, by means of providing the substratum through subsequent cognition.
That is, "only by way of providing the substratum."
Although a contextual substratum (*āśraya*) is not obtained,

nevertheless, because this is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there is no defect whatsoever, as it is possible to enjoin *soma* as the substratum for the sacrifice within the subsequent cognition (*pārṣṭhikabodha*).

Thus, the sense is that since a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) is achieved by effecting the instrumentality residing in the accessory (*guṇa*), there is no definitive conclusion [regarding the primary status].
Thus ends the first section concerning the Pratipad.
This being established, when there arises a desire to know the specific details, it follows that Soma and the like alone possess the status of being the instrument for the result.
Because that [desire] is established as having the form of a logical mark (*liṅga*) consisting of fitness (*yogyatā*);

because the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is stronger than the word-hearing (*pada-śruti*)—which consists in being contained within a single word—due to its power to denote instrumentality as a *kāraka*; and because, in the connection with the fruit, even the word-hearing is absent.

Therefore, the meaning of the verbal root in sacrifices and the like is simply the purpose of the *soma* and other materials. Nor does this imply the postulation of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*); for, just as the status of being an instrument residing in the curd is accomplished by the *agnihotra* oblation, the status of being an instrument residing in the *soma* is accomplished by the sacrifice without any unseen potency, thereby establishing that the sacrifice is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *soma*. This being the position reached:
By virtue of direct verbal expression (*padaśruti*), the sacrifice alone possesses the status of being the instrument for the result.
Although this [direct expression] does not apply to the connection with the result, nevertheless,

while the relative strength of whichever means of proof applies to the initial connection with the *bhāvanā* may be irrelevant at that stage, it remains the decisive factor for the subsequent connection with the result.

Therefore, the direct hearing of the word (*padaśruti*) existing in its connection with the primary productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is more authoritative than its connection with the result; nor is it weaker than the direct hearing of the factor (*kārakaśruti*), because even though it is secondary (metaphorical), the instrumentality of the sacrifice is connected to the productive operation prior to its connection with the instrumentality of the *soma*, and thus that connection occurs first.

Otherwise, because the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) would lack completeness, it would be impossible for *soma* to be construed with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) presented by that verb, according to the maxim that "a complete word is construed with another word.
Nor can there be a sublation of what was first understood— even if it is merely hypothetical— by something occurring at a later time.
Because it is that upon which the sacrifice depends, it is established that the sacrifice is the means to the fruit and Soma is for the sake of the sacrifice.
The practical application is that, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is no taking of a substitute in the event of the loss of Soma;
however, according to the final conclusion (siddhānta), there is.

Now, one might object: this [inference] would hold if there were a *bhāvanā* distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), but there is no proof for its existence. For the verbal roots themselves possess the capacity to denote not only results such as "being cooked" (*viklitti*) but also the mere activity that prompts it—such as blowing, effort, and so forth.

If it is argued that because effort and the like, which constitute *bhāvanā*, are also denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*), all the factors of action (*kāraka*) must therefore be construed with the meaning of the root itself— which is of the nature of an action— and thus the sacrifice cannot be the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the fruit due to the direct word-hearing (*padaśruti*) [of the verb],

[we reply: this is not so, because effort and the like, when analyzed as distinct from the cooking in such expressions as "he cooks," "he performs cooking," or "he exerts himself toward cooking," cannot logically be the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook).

Nor is it tenable to provide a separate analysis [of the root] on the grounds that the word *pāka* ending in the suffix *-ghañ* has its denotative power (*śakti*) restricted solely to the result (*phala*); for since the usage "cooking exists" would still apply even when the operation (*vyāpāra*) has ceased—provided the state of the result remains—it necessarily follows that this suffix also must denote the operation.
Therefore, that which appears [as the meaning], such as effort (*yatna*), is indeed denoted by the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*).

Therefore, even that which is denoted by the verbal root (dhātu) is precisely the "coushingness" (pākatva) and so forth, which reside in operations such as blowing [on coals] that directly produce the result;
and whether that is a universal (jāti) or a segment-qualifier (khaṇḍopādhi) is another matter.
However, the effort and so forth that produce that [operation] are denotable only by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta).

In that context, the delimiting factor of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is either the *tiptva* (the property of being the suffix *tiP*) and so forth as explained by the root *kṛ*, or simply *tiptva* and so forth due to parsimony (*lāghava*), but not the status of being a substituendum (*sthānitva*).

If the specific locations that bring about those [meanings] were included within the scope of the causal determinant (kāraṇatāvacchedaka) residing in the knowledge of words, there would result the necessity of postulating an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations composed of cumbersome causal determinants; if they were not included, there would result the undesirable consequence that the productive operation (bhāvanā) could be brought to mind even from a *lakāra* (verbal suffix) that has been presented in some arbitrary manner.
The delimitor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), however, is the state of being an operation distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which has a result as its objective.
And the result is, according to the speaker's intention, sometimes the meaning of the verbal root itself and sometimes heaven (*svarga*) and so forth.
Thus, in cases such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), there is no metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Pārthasārathi [Miśra] maintains that the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is exclusively the operation conducive to motion.
In reality, however, the property of effort (*yatnatva*) alone is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), due to parsimony (*lāghava*);
but when that is sublated, there is always a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the locus (*āśrayatva*).

It should be understood that effort (yatna), which is conveyed by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), is always expectant of an object; because it is a synonym for "to do" (karoti), it possesses a single object;
and because it is conducive to the arising of a result, it should be regarded as having the nature of objective efficient force (arthabhāvanā).
And this *bhāvanā* (productive operation), which is conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), is the primary semantic focus (*mukhyaviśeṣya*);
for, apart from it, there would be no completion of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meanings of the other words.

And precisely within that *bhāvanā*—whether conveyed by a verbal suffix or by an affix such as *ktvā*—there occurs, in accordance with semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) and other factors, that which is understood through words other than particles (*nipāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

Every meaning that is distinct from the gender and number denoted by the nominal suffix (*sub*) is construed as a qualifier (*prakāra*). However, in the case of particles (*nipāta*) and prefixes (*upasarga*), when they are used in conjunction with a verb, they are construed with it; but when used in conjunction with something else, they may also be construed with that other thing.
Furthermore, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is also construed with the meaning of the nominal suffix, such as its being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) and so forth.

However, in cases where the meaning of the parts of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)— such as those in secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) or compounds— is related through the relation of being a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) to the function of the derivative or compound, as in "āgneya" and similar forms,

there the fire (*agni*) is construed with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) itself because it possesses the status of a deity (*devatātva*), and not with the substance (*dravya*) denoted by the secondary derivative;
that [connection with the substance], however, occurs only subsequently (*pārṣṭhika*).
But where it [the action] is connected by a relation other than that of being a *kāraka*, there is also mutual coreferentiality (*parasparānvaya*),
as in the case of "the horse's halter" (*aśvābhidhānīm*) and so forth.

Likewise, gender and number conveyed by a nominal suffix (*sub*) are construed with the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and other such factors within the meaning of the suffix itself, due to the direct statement of co-utterance (*samānābhidhānaśruti*).

However, all other categories of meaning—namely, the meanings of case-terminations such as instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), as well as the entire meaning of the verbal root—connect only with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) presented by a word expressing *bhāvanā* that does not itself correlate with gender (*liṅga*).
For this very reason, there is no connection [of these meanings] with that *bhāvanā* when it is presented by words such as *bhāvanā* itself.
But when it is presented by a verb ending (*ākhyāta*) or by an affix such as *ktvā*, there certainly is a connection with it as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*).

Furthermore, all the relations that constitute the mode of presentation (*prakāratā*) are to be understood as they apply at the time of the subsequent inferential cognition (*pārṣṭhikānvayabodha*), as explained in the *Kaustubha*.
Therefore, it is established that the efficient force (*ārthībhāvanā*) is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and its end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) is heaven and so forth.
The meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is the instrument (karaṇa), while the soma and so forth are the procedure (itikartavyatā) because they assist the instrument. // 2 //
Thus ends the second section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*).

(B2) [The presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the status of the subordinate term’s referent as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) is established even by overriding the proximity inherent in the word itself through the superior force of the direct scriptural statement of the *kāraka*:
When such an uncertainty has arisen, the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root proceeds with the words "In this way" (*evam*).

Since the sacrifice, which is the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*), lacks any further requirement for another thing to be accomplished, a connection [with such a thing] would be impossible; therefore, that which is required—namely, something already established—is alone capable of being construed. Thus, by means of the logical mark (*liṅga*) consisting in "fitness" (*yogyatā*), it establishes that Soma and the like alone possess the status of the instrument (*karaṇatva*).
This is what is meant by "of Soma and the like alone."

Nor can it be argued that, by means of a proximity inherent in the word itself, the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) might somehow be rendered complete by providing the substance and deity that serve as its own factors (kāraka), and thus be connected [to the result] as an instrument; to this, he says: "Of the third case-ending" (tṛtīyāyāḥ).

To begin with, the connection with the primary efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) first accrues to the *soma* and so forth alone by virtue of a more powerful direct-statement of agency (*kāraka-śruti*). Thus, because the sacrifice is understood through the weaker word-statement (*pada-śruti*), it cannot be construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

However, at the time of subsequent syntactic connection, although there is no difference between the two (the sacrifice and the *soma*) in that both are presented by other words relative to the word for the fruit, there is no evidence to sublate the [instrumental] gender [of the sacrifice].

Therefore, just as the sacrifice is displaced from the status of being the end (*bhāvya*) according to the logic of the *svargakāmādhikaraṇa*, so too is it displaced from the status of being the instrument; thus, falling into the portion of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) by virtue of the word-statement, it is connected with the efficient-force.
It is connected [to the result].
And he states that, upon the subsequent cognition, the sacrifice has Soma as its purpose, saying: "For this very reason."
(Conclusion of the prima facie view by refuting the assumption of an unseen result [adṛṣṭa] if the sacrifice were for the sake of the Soma):

Now, one might object—since no visible benefit can be produced in the Soma by means of the sacrifice, this would entail the assumption of an unseen result—and in response to this, he refutes it with the words "And not... (na ca).
The meaning is this: the sacrifice does not have the Soma as its purpose by way of being a preparatory rite (saṃskāraka) for the Soma;

rather, since the Soma and so forth exist at all times, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of the fruit arising [without effort], which would render the injunction (vidhi) useless. Therefore, in order to avoid that, it is postulated that the sacrifice has the Soma as its purpose by way of being its substrate (āśraya). Consequently, its status as having a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatva) is established through its function of sustaining the instrumentality (karaṇatā) residing in the accessory (guṇa).

(An analysis of how, because that which is to be postulated [on the basis of syntactic expectancy] must depend upon what is directly heard and cannot sublate it, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) alone possesses the status of the instrument (*karaṇatva*);

and thus, since items such as *soma* are employed solely as subordinate members (*aṅga*) of that [root-meaning], they connect directly with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), whereby the purpose of procuring a substitute in the event of the loss of the *soma* is accomplished, and so forth.
First of all, there is no direct connection of *soma* and other such items with the fruit independently of their connection with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).

Because it is impossible for the various factors of action (*kāraka*) to be mutually connected, and because it is more appropriate for the other factors of action— as well as for the result— to be connected directly with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) due to parsimony; therefore, when a connection must be stated through the medium of the *bhāvanā* alone, the connection occurs immediately with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which serves as the limiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

Intending that, since the requirement for an instrument (karaṇa) is paramount, it is not logical for Soma and other elements conveyed by other words to be construed as the instrument, the author states the final position (siddhānta):
"By the direct statement of the word" (pada-śruti), even though [the connection] is figurative (lākṣaṇika).

For in this case, unlike the relation between other word-meanings, a relation such as that of objecthood (*karmatva*) or instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) does not appear between the root-meaning and the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) by virtue of the "relation-boundary" (*saṃsargamaryādā*).
If that were the case, the grammatical rule stating "they express [the meaning] together" (*saha brūtaḥ*) would become meaningless.

Therefore, since it is necessary for these two to appear either as word-meanings (*padārthavidhayā*)—whether through primary denotation (*śakti*) or through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*)—the meaning is that even though they are metaphorically indicated (*lākṣaṇikatve*), [they are still related].
Because it is that upon which others depend for their livelihood.
Because it serves as the means for the moon through the accomplishment of its fullness, it possesses the status of being that upon which others depend (*upajīvyatva*).

Therefore, just as in the case of the sentences concerning the *āgneya* sacrifice and others, although the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth is figurative, it is accepted—via the mediation of the postulation of a sacrifice—as being instrumental in a mediated sense because it occurs prior by virtue of being that which is depended upon; even though the instrumentality expressed directly in the subsequent Vedic text is [figurative].

Likewise here too, it is proper to accept that even the status of *soma* and other materials as instruments (*karaṇa*) occurs through the sacrifice within the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). Since the verbal root-meaning itself, by way of being the instrument, connects with the productive activity through the medium of the fruit, there is the possibility of its fitness at the time prior to the fruit—even though it was unestablished—once it has been rendered established by means of the *soma* and so forth. Therefore, because that [verbal root-meaning] alone serves as the instrument for the fruit, it functions as the instrument toward the *apūrva*.
The meaning is that because the means of accomplishing the fruit (*phalasādhana*) is one, there is oneness of both the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the unseen potency (*apūrva*). And thus,

since it is established here that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) possesses the nature of *dharma*— consisting in being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) by virtue of being the instrument for the fruit—

the present section is established as an introductory (*upoddhāta*) discussion for the inquiry regarding the unity or plurality of that [meaning], which will be undertaken throughout the entire subsequent book (*adhyāya*).

Even though, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), Soma and other materials serve as means for the sake of the fruit, since the sacrifice is accomplished by Soma alone, [the author] says "the purpose" (*prayojanam*) in order to refute the charge— shared by both the prima facie and final views (*siddhānta*)— that the investigation of this section is devoid of utility.

In the case of all [rites], when there is a connection with a fruit, in the case of a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), [the substitute is taken] after the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*); in the case of an obligatory rite (*nitya*), even before that. However, if the prescribed substance or action is unavailable, no substitute is to be employed because it would serve only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Since, like the *prayāja* offerings and other such actions, it lacks the status of a substitute, the rite is nevertheless completed by employing some indeterminate substance or action in order to avoid the fault incurred by failing to finish a commenced performance.
However, it does not become a substitute on that account alone;
for since only that which is similar can serve as a substitute, there is no authority for accepting something dissimilar.
Thus, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) of the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha-adhikaraṇa), there is no substitute for the Soma and other such substances.
The completion of what has already begun may be performed with any material whatsoever;
however, according to the final doctrine (siddhānta), the purpose is that its completion must be done by means of a substitute (pratinidhi). This is the meaning.

(Refuting that the property of being the delimitor of the capacity for [denoting] the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) belongs to the *la* suffix, it is established that either the *karoti* [root] as explained, or simply the *tip* suffix and so forth, is the delimitor of the capacity for denoting the efficient force; therefore, it is also denoted by the verbal root.
Thus: "Therefore, it is also expressed by the verbal root."
In the *Vivaraṇa*, the meaning is that the sense of the root *pac* (to cook) is understood in the form of "cooking" (*pāka*). Regarding the phrase "that which is explained by the root *kṛ*":

since effort (*yatna*) is not perceived in [verbs] such as *jānāti* (he knows), whereas it is perceived in [verbs] such as *pacati* (he cooks), it follows from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the suffixes *tiP* and so forth, as explained by the root *kṛ*, are the delimiters of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).

Alternatively, [the meaning is as follows]: that very thing, such as *tip* and so forth, is [the denotative power]; the point is that in cases such as *janāti*, when that [specific form] is sublated, one resorts to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

As for what was stated by the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra* and others—accepting that the nature of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) consists simply in the property of *l*-ness (*latva*), and that *latva* alone is the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*)—[that is not our view].
He refutes that [position] with the words "But not so," and this has been established by me in detail in the section concerning the Arthavādas; it should be consulted there.
(The determination of Pārthasārathi’s view that the delimitor of the denotatum is "the state of being a favorable operation" rather than "the state of being an effort"):

In this regard, because [the verb] *pacati* is explained by the causative form of the root *bhū* (*bhāvayati*)— meaning "he brings about the cooking"— which denotes a favorable operation, and because of the parsimony of the inclusive [definition], the meaning of the *tiṅ* suffix is indeed the favorable operation, and not merely the result.
Nor does the root *kṛ* have "effort" (*yatna*) as its meaning,
such that, by virtue of being explained by it, the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) could also be said to have that as its expressed meaning;
for even that [root *kṛ*] is not established as having "effort" as its meaning, since it is a synonym for *bhāvayati*.

Just as in expressions such as "the pot comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), the pot—which has attained the status of an agent—is likewise the object in expressions such as "another causes it to come into being" (*tam aparo bhāvayati*), so too is it the object in expressions such as "another makes it" (*evam aparaḥ karoti*). Since there is no distinction between its being the agent and the object of the meaning of the root *bhū*, it is logically established that [the roots *bhū* and *kṛ*] are synonyms of *bhāvayati*. As for the analysis of the word *pacati* ("he cooks") by means of a term expressing effort, namely *pāke yatate* ("he exerts effort toward cooking"), [this is merely a semantic clarification].

That too should be understood as being figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), because it is appropriate for a word whose primary meaning is "activity in general" to indicate a specific [instance] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

However, it is not proper to resort to the view that in cases such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), a word denoting a specific [action] such as effort (*yatna*) indicates a specific property residing in the chariot and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is simply a collection of activities, whether aimed at the result (*phala*) or aimed at the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

Intending to show that even when there is understanding through the statement of [the action] in its essential form (*tattva-rūpa*), there is still a presentation of it in its specific form (*viśeṣa-rūpa*) by means of sentences beginning with the placing of fuel on the fire (*agnyanvādhāna*) and ending with the satiation of the Brahmins (*brāhmaṇatarpaṇa*), he sets forth the opinion of Pārthasārathi: "The delimitor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), however... and so forth.

(And because, due to the non-occurrence of the expectancy for the *itikartavyatā* [the "how-to"], it is impossible to postulate a potency (*śakti*) in a favorable operation either in a general or specific sense, one must follow the *Nyāyasudhā*’s position—which accords with the *Bhāṣya*—that "effort-ness" (*yatnatva*) is the delimiting factor of the potency.

Even if there were a potency in an operation that produces something else, since the various instances of "operation-ness" (*vyāpāratva*) differ according to the difference between each respective "other" and the difference between each respective producer, there would be no single delimiting factor for the potency; thus, the postulation of a single, all-encompassing potency is untenable. Furthermore, if one were to postulate separate potencies for each specific object, [the following would apply:]

Since this would result in the futility of the various injunctions regarding the specific procedures (*itikartavyatā*), and because accepting those injunctions as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) would entail the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating multiple powers (*śakti*), it is more appropriate to adopt the view that the power resides in effort (*yatna*) itself. This is supported by the fact that "effort-ness" (*yatnatva*) is established as the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of being produced by desire (*rāga*), and because effort is the denotatum of the verb *karoti*, as evidenced by its use in paraphrasing (*vivaraṇa*). Thus, it is proper to accept that the power belongs to effort alone.
The root *kṛ* does not denote action (*vyāpāra*) in its general sense;

for we observe the usage "I am not making a movement" even when Caitra is moving due to a wind-disease or similar cause—wherein a movement exists despite the absence of effort, and there is a conjunction of a distinct kind conducive to that movement—and thus it is understood that the meaning of the root is an action conducive [to the result].

Furthermore, although there is no difference in being produced by an action, we observe the linguistic distinction between "done" and "not done" regarding a cloth and a sprout based precisely on whether they are produced by effort or not.

Although usage is observed even in the case of non-conscious activity—such as "the chariot performs the act of going" (*rathaḥ gamanam karoti*) or "the cooking pot performs the act of cooking" (*sthālī pākam karoti*)—nevertheless, because the effort residing in the draught-horses and so forth is metaphorically attributed (*āropa*) to the chariot and the like, or else, because effort is grasped in its primary sense as power (*śakti*), its occurrence [in the case of the chariot] is justified through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as a favorable operation; therefore, it is not improper. For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "one should strive in such a manner."
In whatever manner it may be, he has demonstrated with effort that these are words denoting an entity (*bhāva-śabda*) by showing this explanation.

Likewise, in the section concerning those desiring specific qualities (*guṇakāmādhikaraṇa*), [it is stated]: "The capacity of the word *juhuyāt* (one should sacrifice) is this: that it expresses an effort characterized by the act of offering (*homa*).

For this very reason, intending that even the rule that an injunction (*vidhi*) impels a conscious agent is consistent, he presents the opinion of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* as his own preferred view.
"In [the sense of] being the basis, etc. means: in [the sense of] being the support and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), there is an inclusion of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding counter-positiveness (pratiyogitva) and so forth in expressions such as "the jar perishes" (ghaṭo naśyati).
(Reviving the view of Pārthasārathi by refuting [the arguments of] the authors of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra* regarding the rejection of effort (*yatna*) as the delimitor of denotability.
As for the refutation of the denotation of effort by the authors of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra* and others in order to support the view of Pārthasārathi:

namely, since even the property of being an operation (*vyāpāratva*) is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) and is thus equivalent to a universal (*jāti*), there is no obstacle to its being the delimitor of denotability.
Nor is there a lack of evidence for this;

for, in accordance with common usage—the fact that a sweet taste heard [by the ear] brings its own substratum within the range of people's desire—it follows that the operation (vyāpāra) consisting of inherence in that [substratum], the act of eating it, and so forth, must necessarily be postulated. Since such an operation cannot consist of being produced by that [taste] and so on, it follows that an indivisible adjunct (akhaṇḍopādhi) alone is appropriate.
Or rather, let it be that only that which is heavy possesses the status of being the delimiting factor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*).

For if that were the case, then just as from the word *pacati* ("he cooks") there arises the certainty regarding the effort of cooking, so too in cases such as *patati phalaṃ vṛkṣāt* ("the fruit falls from the tree"), gravity (*gurutva*) must necessarily be the object of certainty through the removal of doubt; likewise in *sravati jalaṃ gireḥ* ("water flows from the mountain"), velocity (*vega*); and in *kampante taroḥ patrāṇi* ("the leaves of the tree tremble"), contact with air (*vāyusaṃyoga*) must likewise be the object of certainty.

Since the co-occurrence (anvaya) of [grammatical] properties such as presentness with gravity and so forth cannot be established otherwise than through the suffixes expressing the result of the action (*phala*) or the operation (*vṛtti*), and since— just like effort (*yatna*)—

gravity and the rest could also be considered denotable meanings (*śakyārtha*) by virtue of their being universal classes (*jāti*) and thus capable of serving as the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), it would follow that these too possess denotative power (*śakti*).
Consequently, it would be impossible to determine that [denotative power] resides specifically in effort.

Therefore, rather than accepting a multiple relationship between denotatum and denoter by admitting multiple delimiters of denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) that are mutually independent, it is more appropriate to accept a single relationship between denotatum and denoter by admitting a single, albeit more complex, delimiter of denotative capacity.

For if the operation (*vyāpāra*), which consists of an adjunct (*upādhi*) formed by multiple word-meanings, were to serve as the delimiter, one would have to postulate that multiple entities possess its substratum-hood (*tadāśrayatva*); thus, complexity (*gaurava*) must be admitted.
However, the delimitorship of the substratum (*āśrayitva-avacchedakatva*) would have to be one and the same, pervading all [the individual instances].

Even if one were to accept multiple delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), such as "effort-ness" (*yatnatva*) and so on, the status of being the substratum would still have to be postulated in multiple locations, and there would also be the redundancy of having multiple relations. Thus, this too is cumbersome (*gaurava*).

For if activity in general (*vyāpāra-sāmānya*) were the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), then because a generality requires particulars, its connection with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) would be logical through the expectancy of "how" (*katham*). However, if the effort directed toward a specific object such as sacrifice (*yāga-viṣaya-viśeṣayatna*) were the productive operation, then because a particular does not require another particular, its connection [with a procedure] would likewise be difficult to establish.
Thus, in cases such as "the chariot goes," since there is no cognition such as "the chariot performs going," [the action] cannot be understood as being conducive to going.

Since "cultivation" (bhāvanā) is not recognized [as the meaning], it is the very operation of moving based on a chariot that is expressed by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) without even resorting to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā); thus, it does not incur the status of being figurative.
Nor, moreover, does the root *kṛ* have "effort" as its meaning.

Since we observe that just as "Caitra cooks" (caitraḥ pacati) is glossed as "he performs cooking" (pākaṃ karoti), so too "the pot supports" (sthālī bibharti) is glossed as "it performs supporting" (dhāraṇaṃ karoti), it is more appropriate [to maintain] that [the meaning of the verb root] is exclusively a general activity (vyāpārasāmānya), as this applies to both cases alike.
As for the distinction between what has been done and what has not been done (kṛtākṛtavyavasthā):

However, that [distinction] is untenable because we observe the usage of "agent" even in cases where no effort has been exerted—for instance, when there is no effort, one still uses the expression "cooking was done by fire," or "fire is the agent of cooking.

As for the designation of "done" or "not done" based on whether something is accomplished through effort or not, that occurs only between two things both of which are accomplished by effort; in such a case, just as there is the designation "not done" for that which requires less effort, so too here, although there is no difference in being accomplished through an operation (*vyāpāra*), the designation "not done" is logically possible due to a deficiency in effort, since it is accomplished by only a slight operation. Thus, there is no impossibility [of the distinction].

Just as, even though Caitra and the horse are equal in being the locus of effort, the distinction between the designations "agent" and "instrument" is established by their independence and dependence respectively— as in "Caitra goes by means of a horse," but never "the horse goes by means of Caitra"—

so too, although the root *kṛ* denotes activity and all case-factors (*kāraka*) are equal in being the locus of that activity, that same distinction is possible by virtue of those two [independence and dependence] alone.
And just as, despite the presence of an effort conducive to that action, there is the conventional usage of denying agency due to the absence of independence—
just as one says regarding a messenger, "He speaks the words of another; he is not the speaker here,
for another is his speaker"— so it is here.
Thus, even though the substratum of the activity conducive to that [result] exists, the conventional usage of negating agency is possible precisely through the intention (*vivakṣā*) to exclude it;
just as when something is broken by the wind or other forces, one says, "By whom was this broken? By this very thing, not by another.
Therefore, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) expressing the activity.

On the contrary, since the possession of an effort conducive to cooking is common to both Caitra and the Lord (Īśvara), there would arise the undesirable consequence that just as one says "Caitra cooks," one could also say "The Lord cooks. This constitutes an objection to the view that effort (*yatna*) is the denotation [of the verbal suffix].

Alternatively, it may be held that the delimitor of the denotability of the verbal suffix is indeed a specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*), which is subordinate to the universal of effort (*yatnatva*) and serves as the delimitor of the denotability of the suffix, being the very factor delimited by which [an action] is produced by desire (*icchā*).

Alternatively, the status of being a producer (janakatva) of the fruit denoted by the verb suffix—such as the act of cooking denoted by the verbal root—is established only through the mediation of effort (*ceṣṭā*) and so forth.

Or else, one may avoid the undesirable application of the expression "The Lord cooks" (*īśvaraḥ pacati*) by accepting that the relation [between the effort denoted by the verb suffix and its substratum] is that of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the effort denoted by the verb suffix within the referent of the nominative word, such as Caitra;
for the Lord does not possess produced effort (*janyakṛti*).
Nor can it be said that [the Lord's] causality is mediated by effort and the like, nor that He possesses a delimiting condition (*avacchedakatva*) in the production of an action just as Caitra does;
for if that were the case, there would be an inconsistency regarding the verbal forms found in the Vedas, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas that denote actions performed by the Lord as their agent.
If it is argued that there is no acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) by arriving at those [Vedic examples], we say no;

for it has been stated in the sūtra *śāstrasthāvā tannimittatvāt* (JS 1.3.9) that one must accept a linguistic usage that follows such words, according to the principles of the *trivṛt*, *caru*, and *aśvavāla* mantras. Furthermore, all efforts that produce a result are individually denotable by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).
Alternatively, one must state that entire collection [of causes] for which there is a rule regarding the production of the fruit.
In the first case, such a statement would not be employed with reference to someone possessing such effort nor to another possessing such a collection, as in:
"This person did not cook."
But it is only the other [type of effort],
because there is no difference in the presence of the effort that produces cooking in both cases.
In the second case, the property of being an effort (*yatnatva*) is not the delimitor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).
Because that [activity] resides in each individual [action] and does not reside in the aggregate,

whereas in our view, although "activity-ness" (*vyāpāratva*) is the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), it is only that activity which resides in the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*)— by virtue of the relation of being "conjoined with the result"— that is conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); and since this state of being conjoined with the result resides in the entire collection of activities, [the activity is thus established].

Since the conventional usage "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to the extended process beginning from the initial movement [of the agent] up until the attainment of the fruit, and since—when there is the inquiry "What is this activity?"—the connection is stated as "this is that activity" with respect to the collection of constituent parts (*padārtha*) starting from the placing of fuel (*anvādhāna*) and ending with the satiation of the Brahmins (*brāhmaṇatarpaṇa*), the usage is justified even for the aggregate; thus, the employment of a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is possible for that which possesses a collection of activities.
As for the objection regarding the impossibility of the rule that an injunction (*vidhi*) must impel a conscious being:

It is ineffective [to argue] that because the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) to be performed is denoted as being colored by a specific activity (*vyāpāra*), there would necessarily follow a restriction (*niyama*) to that alone;

for even in the *Bhāṣya* and other texts where the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is explained as "one should strive" (*yateta*), this is not contradictory, since effort (*yatna*) is indeed included within the activity that is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and while other activities are not fixed, effort itself is invariably present. Thus, the explanation is directed precisely toward that [effort].
Thus [it is said].

Having first refuted all the criticisms raised by the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*, and having first dispelled all the arguments established for the position that [the verbal root] expresses action (*vyāpāra*) in general, [the claim] that "effort-ness" (*yatnatva*) alone is the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is also set aside by this [following analysis].
To explain: as for what was said—that the usage "only when it is heard," etc., serves as proof for the fact that "action-ness" (*vyāpāratva*) is an impartite adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).

That is not so; for, since a favorable effort is generally impossible, even if one accepts that there is a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the operation (vyāpāra), it is precisely the experience having sweet flavor as its object that is accepted as the operation having sweet flavor as its object. And since the designation "operation" is justified by its being produced by the object itself, there is no evidence for accepting its indivisibility (akhaṇḍatva).
For indeed, even if the sweet taste has not been experienced, it cannot—merely by being heard—become an object of desire with respect to its own substrate;
therefore, the state of being the delimitor of the denotable (śakyatāvacchedakatva) remains fixed in the heaviness itself.
As for the argument that since gravity, fluidity, and so forth are also of the nature of universals (jāti), effort alone must be the delimitor of the denotable: [this is refuted as follows].

Even that [conception] is untenable for them, as it would not be understood from those [words]. For this very reason, in cases such as "the water flows" (*dravati jalam*), even though gravity, fluidity, and so forth are presented as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) based on such linguistic usage, they are conveyed by another word alone, and not by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).
For we do not observe a verbal suffix being explained by its weight (*gurutva*) and so forth, in the same way that "cooking" (*pāka*) is explained [by its root meaning].

Therefore, even in that case, when the primary meaning is sublated, the verbal suffix has *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) with respect to the substratum (*āśrayatva*). Thus, there is no contingency of postulating a linguistic capacity (*śakti*) for something never experienced. By this, the objection regarding the introduction of unnecessary complexity—arising from the assumption of multiple relations such as the multiplicity of substrata and the acceptance of multiple properties like "effort-ness" (*yatnatva*) as the delimiters of the denotable (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—is also refuted.

As for the objection that the connection with the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is untenable because the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) lacks an expectancy regarding its "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*), that too is incorrect; for when a result is being produced by an instrument generated by the *bhāvanā*, the very expectancy for an auxiliary (*anugrāhaka*) constitutes the nature of the *kathaṃbhāva*-expectancy. Thus, under the view that [the root] denotes the result, there is no obstacle to its connection with that [auxiliary] through such an expectancy.

Furthermore, as for the attempt in the *Nyāyaprakāśa* to justify the comprehension [of meaning] without resorting to *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) in expressions such as "the chariot goes"—where, in the case of insentient entities, there is an absence of *bhāvanā* (efficient force)—by taking the activity of motion residing in the chariot and so forth;

that too is untenable, because since such an activity is already understood through the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, there can be no claim that the general category of activity (*vyāpāra-sāmānya*) is the meaning of the suffix (*ākhyāta*), given that no activity other than that [root-meaning] remains to be the meaning of the suffix. Consequently, one would inevitably have to resort to *lakṣaṇā*.
Thus, in such a case, it is incorrect because it contradicts the definition of *bhāvanā* as something distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

Furthermore, as for the claim that even the root *kṛ* (to do) has the general sense of "activity" (*vyāpāra*) on the basis of the analysis of the sentence "the pot bears" (*sthālī bibharti*) as "it performs bearing" (*dhāraṇaṃ karoti*), that too is not correct. For it was previously established that in the case of an inanimate agent, as in the analysis "the chariot performs going" (*ratho gamanaṃ karoti*), there is an absence of being an object of universal experience; the same applies here to the analysis "the pot performs bearing" (*sthālī dhāraṇaṃ karoti*).
Furthermore, because its status as a technical term (*lākṣaṇika*) is established in both cases regarding the sentient being (*sattva*).

Otherwise, since the word "Ganges" would be common to both instances—"a hamlet on the Ganges" and "a fish in the Ganges"—it would follow that its primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides only in the region near the Ganges. By this same reasoning, usages such as "cooking was done by fire" or "fire is the agent of cooking" are also refuted as being impossible; they must be explained in some way through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, the justification for the conventional designation of "unaccomplished" (*akṛta*) with respect to that which is accomplished with little effort—despite there being no difference in its being accomplished through activity (*vyāpāra*)—is based precisely on the deficiency of effort; for it is accomplished by only a slight amount of activity due to the paucity of exertion.
This is according to the principle of designating something as "unaccomplished" when it is achieved with little effort. (The second sentence is a repetition of the first.)

Since the linguistic usage of "not being done" is never observed in the case of something accomplished with little effort, it is incorrect to claim that the mere absence of effort in general is what prompts the usage "the sprout was not made by me," for it is illogical for such slightness [of effort] to be the cause of that usage.

Furthermore, as for the attempt to justify the denial of agency in one who is moving due to the wind— even while possessing an activity conducive to that movement— on the grounds of a lack of independence,
that too must be intended to mean a lack of one's own exertion as an answer to the question, "Is the movement being performed by you?"

In the statement, "While [the action] has proceeded, I do not perform the movement," because it necessarily refers to the absence of one's own effort, it is not tenable [to claim] that it intends to express the absence of autonomy (*svātantrya*), since that is not established thereby. When a messenger speaks the words of another, even though effort exists, he is not the speaker of these words.

However, since the negation of [the child's] being the agent (*kartṛ*) is established simply by the absence of being the locus of an effort that resides in another person— the "other" being defined here in accordance with common usage as the instigator who conforms to the verbal expression— and because there is no purpose in intending to express a lack of independence (*svātantrya*), [the objection is untenable]. Furthermore, regarding the argument that if one were to accept "delimitingness" (*avacchedakatva*) as the relation [between the effort and the body] in order to avoid the undesirable consequence of the usage "The Lord cooks" (*īśvaraḥ pacati*), it would follow that words in the Veda and other texts denoting actions whose agent is the Lord would have to be considered figurative (*gauṇa*).

That too is incorrect, because for a bodiless Lord (*īśvara*), it is impossible anywhere to employ such expressions as "he reads" or "he speaks" by taking his agency in those respective actions [as a basis].

As for the usage "the fish spoke" (*mīna uvāca*) and so forth, which occurs due to his assuming a body such as that of a fish, that is indeed justified by postulating that his own action has that specific body as its delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*), based on the force of the cognition that "he reads this Veda" while in the fish-body.
Or, let us grant that there is some usage based on the agency of a bodiless God; even so, there is no harm if that [usage] is figurative (*gauṇa*).

Otherwise, in order to avoid contradicting the usage of the scripture "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), one would have to assume a single power for the word "sacrificer" that is common to both the figurative and the primary senses. This would apply even to words denoting actions whose agents are God according to your own view.

If [the locus of the action] were established merely as the substratum of a favorable operation (*anukūlavyāpāra*), then since such a substratum of operation exists eternally within the nature of the *vibhāva*, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one could say "The Lord cooks" (*īśvaraḥ pacati*) would be unavoidable.

Therefore, in such a usage, if there is an intention (*vivakṣā*) to express him as a common agent (*sādhāraṇakartṛtā*), it is accepted; otherwise, since the agency of the Lord is not admitted at all, [the expression does not apply].

Even if it is argued that there is no such thing as "that action" (tatkṛti) because of the reasoning set forth in the *Kaustubha* regarding the section on "other words" (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*), there is no contradiction in stating that [the agent] is not required.

Furthermore, as for what was said starting with "whatever... and ending with "the use of the verb," that is incorrect; for there is no contradiction in accepting that the efforts directed toward the result conducive to cooking are denotable individually.

For this very reason, when many agents are engaged in the act of cooking, the linguistic usage "This Caitra also cooks" is justified even in the absence of the fruit being present in some particular effort. For this same reason, it is the practice of the experts (*tāntrika*) to establish the connection with the present tense by taking any one effort included within the aggregate of efforts (*kṛtikūṭa*). Furthermore, although there is no difference between two [agents] in terms of the existence of effort, the usage "He did not cook" is indeed justified on the basis of the intention that the fruit is not being produced.

For you as well, it would be impossible to avoid the undesirable consequence that the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*) could not be used for one who possesses only a portion of the collection of activities.

Furthermore, if the property of being an operation (*vyāpāratva*)—which is an indivisible property (*akhaṇḍadharma*)—is held to reside in a collection [of actions], then in the performance of a rite according to one's capacity, when there is a deficiency in even a single constituent part, the collection ceases to exist.

Consequently, since there would be no cognition from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in the form of an operation residing in that [collection], how could the performance of the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) be justified?

Therefore, one must accept that the property of being an operation resides in each individual [action] alone; it is by means of those respective forms that only those [actions] which are possible [to perform] are [cognized].

Even if one assumes that verbal roots denote actions (*vyāpāra*) and accounts for the usage of forms such as *pacati* ("he cooks") and *yajate* ("he sacrifices") by taking only one of those actions, it is nonetheless necessary to provide a similar explanation for usages such as "this person did not sacrifice" (*ayam ayajat*) when all participants in a sacrificial session (*satra*) rise together.

Just so, in my view as well, there is the further disadvantage that since multiple actions would have to serve as the delimiters of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), there is the burden of postulating multiple powers (*śakti*).

It is not tenable to postulate a capacity (*śakti*) in the general sense of "activity" (*vyāpāra*), as this would result in the inconsistency of the *Bhāṣya* and other texts. Therefore, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), and because it is restricted in contrast to other possible means, the capacity resides in the effort (*yatna*) itself; when that is obstructed, there is only figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). All of this has been indicated by the Venerable Teacher (*Pūjyapāda*) through the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*).

Therefore it has been said by the masters of logic: "Through the distinction between what is done and what is not yet done, and by way of establishing the nature of the agent, effort alone is 'action' (kṛti) in all causal operations (bhāvanā) regarding both the preceding and the succeeding."

(Regarding the refutation of the view of the *Prakāśakāra* that it is more logical to postulate a power (*śakti*) everywhere based on the uniformity of the conditions [of cognition], and thus that [the suffix] has the general sense of "activity" [*vyāpāra*]:

Furthermore, as for what the *Prakāśakāra*s say—relying on the statement of Maṇḍana: "Even one who asserts that the activity (*vyāpāra*) is the self as its agent [asserts] the productive drive (*bhāvanā*);
even when there is another agent, it is not expressed by a verbal suffix, because it is a metaphorical application of the generality of [mental] cognition"—[they claim that] "the elephant goes."

It was argued that because the cognition "the chariot goes" (ratho gacchati) is not distinct [from the cognition "he goes"], if effort were the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), then no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would be possible in this case; however, that too is incorrect, because the lack of distinction in cognition is not a decisive factor, since figurative indication would otherwise fail to apply even in cases such as "Caitra is the sacrificer" (*yajamānaḥ caitraḥ*) or "The sacrificial grass-bundle is the sacrificer" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), where the cognitions are likewise not distinct. This is the general direction of the argument.

(An exposition of the rule regarding the transitivity and intransitivity of *bhāvanā*): Since it was previously stated that the status of the meaning of the verbal root as the instrument (*karaṇa*) within the *bhāvanā* is mediated by the object to be realized (*bhāvya*), [the author] now establishes the transitivity of the *bhāvanā*—which has been defined in order to justify its connection with the object through first raising the requirement for such an object—by stating: "And of effort alone... (*yatnasyaiva ca*).

The meaning is as follows: because it would result in the subversion of the injunction’s power to impel and to inform; because an impulsion directed toward a sentient being is untenable if its intended end (*bhāvya*) is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*);

and because, since sacrifices and the like are not themselves human goals, they cannot serve as the intended end, and some other thing must be required as the intended end, [the verb] necessarily possesses an object.
Furthermore, just like the root *kṛ*, it possesses a single object, since without the particle *ca*, such an expression as "he makes a jar and a cloth" (*ghaṭaṃ paṭaṃ karoti*) is not used.
For this very reason, even the conventional distinction between transitive (*sakarmaka*) and intransitive (*akarmaka*) verbs resides solely in the verbal root (*dhātu*),

and not in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, it should be understood that even when a root is intransitive— as in "one desiring health lies down" (*svāsthyakāmaḥ śayīte*)— health and the like are construed as the object to be produced (*bhāvya*) within the productive activity itself.
(Defining its status as *ārthabhāvanā* by virtue of being conducive to the realization of the fruit):

Regarding the term *ārthabhāvanātvam*—it is called *ārtha* because it is sought (*arthyate*) or prayed for (*prārthyate*) as something desired on all sides (*āsamantāt*), such as heaven (*svarga*) and so forth; and since it is an activity conducive to the realization (*bhāvanā*) of that [fruit], it possesses the nature of *ārthabhāvanā*.
Alternatively, that by which a fruit is sought—that is, desired—is the person; because it resides in him, "that" (the treatise) is called "ārtha," meaning pertaining to him.

(The demonstration that the bhāvanā conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the primary qualificand [is intended] for the purpose of establishing that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the instrument of the fruit-producing bhāvanā, and for the purpose of ensuring that the grammatical rule of word-meaning connection remains unrestricted—namely, that suffixes are connected only with the meaning of their own base).
