According to the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), if the meaning of the verbal root itself were the primary qualificand, then the stated fact that the meaning of the verbal root is the instrument of the fruit-producing bhāvanā would not be established; therefore, in order to prove that the meaning of the verbal root is the primary qualificand in relation to [the bhāvanā], [the author discusses] the meanings conveyed by the sentence...

By demonstrating the logical concomitance (*anvaya*) of certain [factors] through their respective modes, he shows that they possess the status of being the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*), as indicated by the phrase "And this...
and the reason "because it does not terminate."

In the sentence "He cooks rice with wood in a pot," when it is paraphrased as "He produces rice by means of cooking [performed] in a pot with wood," there is an incompleteness (*aparyavasāna*) of the meanings presented by those respective words because, in the absence of a connection with the meaning of the root *√kṛ* (to produce), the other words lack mutual expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*). Although this incompleteness is equally true for the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as well, in the absence of its connection with those respective meanings; [it is resolved by the root *√kṛ*].

Nevertheless, since the suffix conveys its own meaning as being already connected with the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), it is logical to assume that the connection occurs as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) precisely within that [action] which has presented itself as the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*) relative to the root-meaning. This is the meaning.

And thus, he restates what follows from this: that in all cases, the connection of all case-factors (*kāraka*) with that [action] as the primary qualificand is entailed, "in accordance with fitness" (*yogyatādyanusāreṇa*).

And so, in cases such as "having cooked the rice in the pot, he goes," the bhāvanā expressed by the suffix -ktvā is construed as a qualifier (prakāra) within the bhāvanā expressed by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta).
Consequently, although that [latter] bhāvanā is the primary qualificand (mukhyaviśeṣya), the factors of action (kārakas) such as the rice do not connect with it because of semantic incompatibility;
rather, they connect only with the preceding bhāvanā.

For this very reason, it has been stated that although a preceding *bhāvanā* may stand as a qualifier (*viśeṣya*) with respect to its various *kārakas*, the *bhāvanā* conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) alone is the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*). Therefore, the sense is that while other *bhāvanās* may serve as qualifiers with respect to their *kārakas*, that which is conveyed by the verbal suffix possesses the status of the primary qualificand as a matter of necessity.
He demonstrates that same fitness by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in another case as well: "nipāteti" [etc.].

(Regarding the establishment of the connection of deities such as Agni with the *bhāvanā* even in cases like "āgneya," by postulating a derivation distinct from the rule that [a word] is understood through elements other than particles (*nipāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and is [furthermore] governed by case-endings (*sup*) and so forth:

Here, in the section concerning the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*), by means of the sentence "That which belongs to Agni" (*yad āgneyaḥ*), there is an injunction of the substance consisting of eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) qualified by the deity Agni, with reference to the rites designated as the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices (*paurṇamāsī-amāvāsyā*) enjoined by the two "Informed" sentences (*vidvadvākya*). Thus, [the connection is established] for the rite enjoined by the "Informed" sentences...

Anticipating the objection that it possesses a specific form (*rūpavattva*), [the author] will later refute this by showing that since the connection between the eight-potsherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) and the deity Agni is not established from any other source, it would necessarily have to be enjoined here itself; thus, because enjoining multiple things— namely,

"that which is the eight-potsherd cake is for Agni" and "and that [cake] is on the full moon day"— would result in the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*), an injunction regarding the form is not possible.

For when the deities such as Agni, which function as the meaning of the base, are construed with the substance— which is the meaning of the suffix and is denoted by the *taddhita*— the resulting qualification is well-established; thus, by means of a direct scriptural injunction (*śruta-vidhi*) that enjoins the qualified whole, and subsequently by an inferred injunction of the qualifiers, once the specific relationship between the eight-pot-sherd (*aṣṭākapāla*) and the deities such as Agni is established, a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) is untenable because a repetition of the direct scriptural injunction is impossible.

Therefore, since a specific distinction must necessarily be stated regarding the scriptural injunction itself—and this is not possible without postulating another etymological derivation—he states another derivation: "taddhita... (beginning with the word *taddhita*).

Furthermore, when the meaning of the base, such as "fire" (agni), is construed with the meaning of the suffix—divinity (devatātva)—by way of the relation of being the locus (ādheyatā), divinity itself does not have a connection with the substance;

rather, because it is a *kāraka*, it is construed with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). Consequently, since it is impossible for the divinity residing in fire to possess a specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) with respect to the substance, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is justified.
This is the meaning of the phrase "therefore, distinct from that."

(An exposition of the *Kaustubha*’s established conclusion—that even the genitive relation (*ṣaṣṭhyartha-sambandha*) is construed with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) alone—by refuting the ancient view following the *Śāstradīpikā*, which held that the genitive relation is construed with the meaning of the subordinate word [the noun]).

In this regard, the ancients maintained that while factors other than those [like the agent] and time (*kāla*) etc. are construed with the efficient force, the genitive relation is construed with the meaning of the subordinate word.
For this very reason, in the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*, even those [actions] expressed by separate words [are connected] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Alternatively, because they are connected to the action [of the genitive] even before [the connection between the two nouns], they obtain a mutual relationship both verbally and substantially, even while disregarding the injunction;
thus it is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* that there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in such a case.
In reality, however, whether directly or through a succession, the status of being a locus is a relationship denoted by the genitive.

Relying on the statement in the Kaustubha that "it is logical for the positive concomitance (anvaya) to apply to the mere category of word-meanings alone, in accordance with the simplicity of the causal relationship within the process of meditation itself," the phrase "of the mere word-meaning" was stated.

(An explanation of how the rule that all factors are connected to the *bhāvanā* is not violated, by showing that even for recipients (*saṃpradāna*) and so forth—which are capable of being directly connected to the *bhāvanā*—the connection to the *bhāvanā* occurs through a mediated sequence.

By this, [it is shown that] there is no violation of the rule that all are connected to the *bhāvanā*, because those factors lying outside the three parts [of the *bhāvanā*], such as the status of being an unintended object (*aniṣṭakarma*), recipient (*saṃpradāna*), source (*apādāna*), or locus (*adhikaraṇa*), are not required;

and because, since the verbal root-meaning and the *bhāvanā* are related as *kārakas*, when direct connection with the verbal root-meaning is impossible, [the connection occurs] through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

The claim made by the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*—that there is a direct syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—is refuted; for even those [factors] that are unfit for a direct connection with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) obtain a connection with it initially through a mediated relation (*paramparā-sambandha*), such as being the producer of the root-meaning which itself is the determiner of that [urge]. Once this general connection with the *bhāvanā* has first occurred, and subsequently the understanding of its connection with the specific activity in the form of a sacrifice—which is obtained through subsequent syntactic connection—has arisen...
In reality, this is because its apprehension as the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is logically consistent.

Likewise, in the section concerning desires for qualities (*guṇakāmādhikaraṇa*), the status of being the object of the sense-organ (*indriyakarmatva*) is construed with the *bhāvanā* itself through the relation of being the generator of the locus of the connection with the quality that defines it.
However, in cases such as the section on time (*kālādhikaraṇa*), where it is impossible for [the action] to be defined by a result, [this does not apply].

The intended meaning is that it should be understood everywhere as follows: since time, locus, and so forth have arrived there [in the verbal root], by accepting their status as instruments (karaṇa), they are construed with that very [root] through another relation—namely, being directed toward the fruit produced by itself—just like other qualities.

(Regarding the synthesis of the status of the root-meaning as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, despite all [factors] being construed with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), this is established through the justification of linguistic conventions such as the transitivity of the root-meaning.

Now, one might object: if rice and the like are construed with the *bhāvanā* by way of being its object (*karman*), then because the root-meaning itself would lack the status of an object, the root could not be classified as transitive (*sakarmaka*).

Furthermore, since even in the *bhāvanā* of lying down and so forth, well-being (*svāsthya*) and the like are construed as the object of that *bhāvanā*, it would follow that these roots are transitive, and thus their status as intransitive (*akarmaka*) could not be maintained. To this, he says: "They are the constituents of the mode-of-apprehension (*prakāratāghaṭakāḥ*)."

The meaning is this: the status of being the object (*odana-karmatva*) first connects with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) by way of the relation of having as its instrument the meaning of the verbal root that defines itself;
the same applies to the status of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*) and so forth.
Even though this is the case, there remains an expectancy for the subsequent connection of the object of the verbal root's meaning.
Therefore, the transitivity of a verbal root [is determined by whether it possesses an object at that time];
for that which lacks such an object at that moment is established as intransitive.

Indeed, there is no expectancy for an object—such as "whose is the lying down?"—in the same way that there is an expectancy for an object in the case of "whose is the cooking? (i.e., "what is being cooked?").

Therefore, since the prescription of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) and other grammatical markers occurs precisely by taking the object of the verbal root (*dhātvartha-karma*) and so forth as the basis, there is no inconsistency.

Just as a subsequent cognition (*pārṣṭhika-bodha*), even though produced by the heard word (*śruta-śabda*), does not necessitate a different rule of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), so it should be understood from the *Kaustubha*; it is not stated here for fear of prolixity.

And thus, since *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is eternally transitive, when there is a requirement for an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), heaven and the like are connected as the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

Then, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), being connected through the requirement for an instrument (*karaṇākāṅkṣā*), is related as an instrument by way of the fruit (*phala*). Consequently, because the meaning of the root serves as the instrument toward the fruit, that same [root-meaning] is also related to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), which is postulated as the means of accomplishing it.
Because it is the means of accomplishment, the *apūrva* to be accomplished by it is one and the same; he concludes with "therefore" (*tasmāt*) in order to indicate this result.

(An exposition of his own view—that *soma* and so forth are grasped by the *prakaraṇa* because they are permeated by the operation as the *itikartavyatā*—and Pārthasārathi’s view—that they constitute subsidiaries through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means.

Now, [an objection is raised]: "If the meaning of the verbal root is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*), how can substances such as *soma*, deities, and rites such as the *prayāja* be construed? To this, he says: "But *soma* and so forth..."

When a fruit is being produced by means of a substance (*dravya*) or a deity (*devatā*) acting as an instrument (*karaṇa*), these two connect with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) through their requirement for an auxiliary (*anugrāhaka*), by way of an operation consisting in the accomplishment of that instrument.

For this very reason— even though substances, deities, and the like, when not yet permeated by an operation, are not grasped as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)— it will be explained in the section on Context (*prakaraṇādhikaraṇa*) that they are subsequently grasped as the procedure by virtue of Context (*prakaraṇa*) once they have become connected with an operation.
Since the prayājas and other such elements are also grasped precisely through that expectancy, there is no inconsistency.

In the view of Pārthasārathi, since substance, deity, and so forth cannot function as qualifiers with respect to the general nature of the activity (*vyāpāra-sāmānya*), they are not grasped through the requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*).

Rather, by means of scripture and other criteria, these [substances and deities] possess subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) precisely because they are made the objects of the activity through the mediation of the production and accomplishment [of the result] implied by the sense; thus, they are not to be grasped by context (*prakaraṇa*).
However, the *prayāja* offerings and the like are grasped in that manner [by context].
The meaning is that it has already been indicated previously that [the Lord] does not act as a benefactor.
Thus ends the second section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*).

(B1) (Section 3 / [A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 3]) "But the injunction is the commencement" (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.5). Since it has been established that the *apūrva* arises from the meaning of the verbal root itself, there arises the inquiry as to whether the *apūrva* actually exists or not. [The opponent argues: Since the momentary sacrifice can be logically established as the means to heaven even through the medium of the destruction of the performed sacrifice, there is no need to postulate an *apūrva*.
This would result in the undesirable consequence [of admitting that destruction is an effect].

Nor can it be argued that because destruction is eternal, the scriptural statements "Dharma perishes through recitation" and "Even very great sins are destroyed by expiation" would be untenable regarding its being destroyed by recitation and expiation; for this is not so, since we accept that recitation and the like act as obstacles to the arising of the fruit, rather than being destroyers of the destruction itself.

Alternatively, there is no fault whatsoever in postulating causality on the basis of the specific individuality of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice as qualified by the absolute non-existence of its recitation (*kīrtana*).

Therefore, since it is concluded that there is no evidence for anything called *apūrva* (the unseen potency), [the opponent objects]: "In your view, because the two verbs 'to flow away' (*kṣarati*) and 'to perish' (*naśyati*), which denote destruction, would have to be taken in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*), one must postulate an *apūrva* that is susceptible to destruction;
for this complexity (*gaurava*) is not a fault when it results in a desirable fruit."

Therefore, when the principal act produces its fruit, such as heaven, and the subsidiary act produces its own result within the context of the principal act, the *apūrva* (transcendental potency) serves as their intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).
And because it is an intermediate operation, that *apūrva* resides in the self (*ātmaniṣṭha*), as established by the force of the resulting fruit.
Furthermore, precisely because it is an intermediate operation, the sacrifice and other constituent acts are not rendered superfluous (*anyathāsiddhi*).

In that regard, where there is only a single primary act (*pradhāna*), since the *apūrva* arises from that [primary] together with its preceding and succeeding subsidiaries, there is one intermediate *utpattyapūrva* (origination-*apūrva*) immediately following the primary; and by means of that, at the conclusion of all the subsidiaries, there is another, the supreme *apūrva*.
Thus, even when there is a plurality of primaries, it should be understood that while there is a distinction of *utpattyapūrvas* for each primary, the supreme *apūrva* is one.

In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, however, from the two sentences— “One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day” and “One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day”— it is understood that the three sacrifices, which are independent of one another in terms of their temporal intervals, possess a state of conjunction (*sāhitya*). Since this conjunction is untenable without being defined by a single effect, there must be a distinct collective transcendental result (*samudāyāpūrva*) for each group, and by means of that...
Thus, the establishment of the *apūrva* is ninefold, namely the *paramāpūrva*.
In the same way, the postulation of an *apūrva* should be understood in other cases as well, such as the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and the Dvādaśāha.

However, regarding the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*), the *apūrvas* produced by the auxiliaries that provide immediate assistance (*sannipatyopakāraka*) serve the purpose of generating a fitness conducive to the production of the *utpattyapūrva* (origination-*apūrva*) within the primary rite (*pradhāna*) itself.
And destruction occurs through the capacity residing in the final principal act (*pradhāna*).

However, for those [acts] produced by remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), their utility lies in generating a capacity conducive to producing that immediate effect which resides in the *utpattyapūrva*.
And the immediate effect, when the collective *apūrva* (*samudāyāpūrva*) exists, is that very [collective *apūrva*] itself.
In its absence, it should be understood that either the supreme *apūrva* or heaven (*svarga*) and so forth [is the result];
furthermore, destruction occurs upon the production of the final capacity (*yogyatā*).
However, if one should suspect that there is no such evidence for the supreme *apūrva*, [the following applies].
Therefore, let that not be so.

However, for the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) which provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), since there is no "composite apūrva" (*samudāyāpūrva*), let their function be simply the production of a fitness conducive to the fruit within the very "originative apūrva" (*utpattyapūrva*).
In any case, the *apūrva* is established. // 3 //
Thus ends the third section concerning the apūrva.

(B2) [The author] sets forth the inquiry into the section (*adhikaraṇacintā*), demonstrating the "suggestive connection" (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) by stating: "From the meaning of the verbal root itself" (*dhātvarthādeva*). [This is because] it would be cumbersome to postulate that the *apūrva*—which exists in the form of a potency—is resident in the self, given that it does not perish when the sacrifice perishes; rather, one should simply postulate that the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) already established possesses the mere capacity to produce its own effect.

Just as in the case of the relationship between the sacrifice and heaven as goal and means, since perception and other means of knowledge do not operate with respect to the *apūrva*, it is impossible for them to function as valid cognizers; therefore, only presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) must be postulated as the means of knowledge.

However, that [presumption] is not possible because it would result in a contradiction with the meaning of the revealed scripture (*śruti*). To explain: if one were to postulate the *apūrva* on the grounds that its being the means to heaven, which occurs at a later time, would otherwise be inexplicable, then it would be impossible for that [postulated *apūrva*] to serve as the actual explicant of that [means-ness].

For it is not the case that the sacrifice’s status as the means to heaven is established through an *apūrva* (unseen potency) postulated by that [sacrifice] itself, since heaven is produced by that very [sacrifice]; thus, the sacrifice, being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) with respect to the production of the *apūrva*, cannot be the means to heaven. Nor should it be argued that—because the *apūrva* is of the nature of a power (*śakti*) and thus constitutes an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*)—there is no "otherwise establishment," just as wood and other materials are not otherwise established [as causes of ash] due to the flame;

for there is a rule that power and operation must reside in the same locus as that which possesses the power and operation, and therefore, once that [locus] has perished, their continued existence is untenable.

Nor is it reasonable to assume that the *apūrva* resides in the self—the substratum of the sacrifice—simply because of the necessity of postulating it on the strength of the result, even if its residence in the sacrifice itself is impossible; for since the incapacity [of the sacrifice] to be a means to that result is exhausted by [the fact that] it would be so without the postulation of a cumbersome *apūrva*, there is no evidence for such a postulation. With this in mind, he demonstrates the exhaustion of *arthāpatti* (presumption) with the words "kḷpta" etc.

The meaning is that since both the state of being produced by the sacrifice and existence are already established in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), only the mere capacity to produce the fruit needs to be postulated; thus, its status as an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) is easily attained.
In the case of the *apūrva*, however, since everything must be postulated, it is not so easily attained.
(An explanation of the justification for the statement "Dharma perishes through recitation," even though it involves the operation of destruction:

[Objection]) But surely—since dharma, being of the nature of an action, is momentary and thus perishes very quickly, whereas destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is eternal and therefore incapable of being destroyed, it is impossible for it to be destroyed by those respective recitations heard in the Smṛtis or by expiatory rites; therefore, it is necessary to postulate a different kind of *apūrva* suitable for that purpose. Thus it is argued.
Having died, he fears—"and not," [as stated in the following verse].
He avoids [the faults] such as reciting [the name], and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: since it has been determined that only the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) [of the act] can function as the mediating operation (*vyāpāra*), and since the various Smṛti texts can simply convey that acts such as *kīrtana* (recitation) act merely as obstacles to the production of the fruit— by means of the destruction they themselves produce— there is no evidence for postulating that they possess the power of destruction (*nāśakatva*).

(Regarding the view that the sacrifice possesses an operation consisting in its own destruction: the suspicion that another heaven might arise immediately after the production of [the first] heaven is refuted by postulating that the destruction of that heaven acts as an obstacle.
Furthermore, by postulating that the destruction of the fame of that sacrifice itself acts as the obstacle, other defects are also avoided.

For this very reason—since destruction is eternal—the contingency that another heaven would continue to arise even after the production of [the first] heaven is likewise avoided simply by postulating that the destruction of that heaven acts as an obstacle to it.
It must be rejected.

Nor does the assumption that the recollection (*kīrtana*) and so forth of [the sacrifice] acts as an obstacle entail the undesirable consequence of obstructing the production of the fruit from a subsequent performance;

for even in the view that [recollection] is a destroyer by virtue of the postulation of an *apūrva*, the capacity to destroy must necessarily be postulated for each specific instance of the sacrifice when it is recollected.

The point is that this undesirable consequence does not arise because one postulates that the destruction of the manifestation of that specific sacrifice acts as an obstacle to the fruit produced by that manifestation of the sacrifice.
(An exposition of the causality of sacrifice by way of its being characterized by the absolute non-existence of recitation, for the purpose of eliminating complexity):

He states another alternative—namely, "the absolute non-existence of recitation"—because postulating that the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of recitation and so forth acts as an obstacle would result in the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

The point is this: although in sentences concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, the causal status [of the act] exists only in the form of being a Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth, nevertheless, there is no obstacle to postulating a causal function in the form of being qualified by the absolute absence of recitation—this form being presented as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of the causal status that is itself defined by the effect-status delimited by a distinct type of heaven (vijātīya-svarga) as presented through the method of inference. Thus, there is no contradiction.

(Since only that which is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) can be an obstructer, the objection that the sacrifice would be an obstructer is refuted under the view that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is the operation; furthermore, this establishes the causality of a non-entity.

Nor does it follow that the sacrifice is an obstructer simply because it is the counter-positive of a non-existence that has become a cause; [for an obstructer must be the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence].

In other cases, although the absence of an obstacle (*pratibandhakābhāva*) may independently function as a cause such that its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) possesses the status of an obstacle, here [in the case of destruction], since destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is of the nature of an intermediate operation of the cause and lacks independent causality, it does not follow [that it is an obstacle] merely by being the counter-correlate of an absence.
Furthermore, where a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*) functions as a cause...

In that very case, there is an obstructive capacity (*pratibandhakatva*) toward its counter-positive; however, in the present instance, because destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) functions as a cause by virtue of being destruction, there is no such undesirable consequence.
Nor [should it be asked]: how can that which is of the nature of a non-existence (*abhāva*) produce an effect?

Thus, it should not be said [that there is a fault]; for just as the non-performance of the *sandhyāvandana* and other rites produces demerit (*pratyavāya*), and just as non-apprehension (*yogyānupalabdhi*), which is of the nature of an absence, produces the perception of an absence, so too here, there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*) against the assumption that it produces a result.
Therefore, it is indicated by this that there is no defect whatsoever.

Thus, since the requirements are fulfilled by the operation of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) alone with respect to both the subsidiaries and the principal acts, there is no need to postulate an *apūrva* (unseen potency). Therefore, he concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the investigation into the distinctions and non-distinctions of that *apūrva* is useless:
"Hence... (*ataḥ*).

(An exposition on the establishment of the *apūrva* [unseen potential] because it is untenable to assume that chanting (*kīrtana*) and so forth act as obstacles to the production of a result— due to the difficulty of establishing the specific individuality (*tadvyaktitva*) as the delimiting factor of the state of being obstructed (*pratibadhyatāvacchedaka*), and due to the resulting complexity— and because it is likewise untenable to postulate causality based on the qualification of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of chanting, and because it would entail resorting to figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*) for the terms "wastes away" (*kṣarati*) and "perishes" (*naśyati*). To begin with,

the acceptance that chanting and so forth act as obstacles to a specific instance of a result is improper precisely because the specific individuality of that instance is not established as the delimiting factor of the state of being obstructed.

If one were to accept that [the non-arising of the fruit] is obstructed by factors such as belonging to a different class (*vijātīya*) or being a heavenly realm (*svarga*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the fruit would not arise even in another performance [of the rite].

If, on the other hand, one were to postulate its causality based on its being qualified by the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of recitation (*kīrtana*), there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) regarding the delimiting condition of the causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), resulting in the necessity of postulating multiple causal relations.

Therefore, although there may be a multiplicity of causal relations if one were to postulate a relation between the destroyer and the destroyed based on [the cause] being "recitation-ness" (*kīrtanatva*) and [the effect] being the "unseen potency" (*apūrva*) produced by that specific instance [of recitation], [this is still preferable].

Even so, because there is no complexity (gaurava) in the delimiting condition of the causal capacity, and because it is established by scripture such as "Dharma perishes" (*dharmaḥ kṣarati*), it possesses scriptural authority (*prāmāṇikatva*).

Nevertheless, since there is no evidence for resorting to metaphorical usage (*lakṣaṇā*) for the roots *kṣarati* and *naśyati*, and having in mind that the apūrva capable of perishing must therefore be established as a last resort, he states the final conclusion: "It perishes" (*kṣarati*).

(An investigation into the necessity of the *apūrva* of subsidiaries, for the purpose of establishing the separate performance of subsidiaries in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) and for the purpose of establishing the distinction between subsidiary and principal acts:

If one were to accept that even in the case of subsidiaries (*aṅga*), destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) functions as the mediating operation (*vyāpāra*), then because that [destruction] is eternal and exists even at the time of the modified sacrifice, it would follow that the modified sacrifices could be performed by "extension" (*prasaṅga*)—just like the animal-sacrifice cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*)—since they would obtain the assistance produced by those [subsidiaries] despite a difference in ritual application (*prayoga*). Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of not performing the subsidiaries separately.
Because of the observation [in scripture] that "at each fore-offering (prayāja), one offers a kṛṣṇala," [the existence of an apūrva] would otherwise be untenable;
therefore, he says "and by means of the subsidiary" (aṅgena ca) to show that even in that case, the postulation of an apūrva is necessarily required.

In the phrase "in the primary [rite] and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the *apūrva* (unseen potential) produced by the primary rite. Since the primary rite is not itself produced by the *prayāja* and other subsidiary rites, it is impossible to conceive of the subsidiaries as being utilized within the primary rite. Furthermore, because even its destruction—which would serve as its intermediate operation—can occur even without the subsidiaries, such a conception is untenable. If one were to conceive of this [operation] with respect to the fruit, it would follow that the fruit itself is the primary rite; therefore, for the sake of establishing the distinction between subsidiary and primary rites, the *apūrva* must be postulated.
In our view, its utility is easily established by virtue of its necessity.
(An exposition establishing that all [objections] are resolved by postulating the *apūrva*—established by a Vedic statement inferred through *śrutārthāpatti*—which resides in the self of the enjoyer.
Nor is there a lack of evidence for this;
the meaning is that the very Vedic word inferred through *śrutārthāpatti*, namely "having produced the *apūrva* by means of sacrifice, one should produce heaven," serves as the proof.

And he dispels the doubt that it is impossible for the *apūrva*—whether in the form of a potency or in the form of an operation—to persist because of the destruction of its possessor (the potency) or its substrate (the operation), by stating: "And it... (*sa ca*).

Just as, even though the *apūrva* is produced by a sacrifice, one does not postulate a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) residing in the experience—as that would be a function of memory produced by experience—so too here, because of the force of the result, one does not postulate its residence in the sacrifice; rather, it is postulated as residing in the self, which accounts for its persistence.

For this very reason, in cases such as the *śrāddha* at Gayā, since both the father and the son are known from other scriptures to be enjoyers of the fruit, two distinct *apūrvas* residing in both are postulated, and these are destroyed respectively by the recitation of each individual's name.
Similarly, since both husband and wife are enjoyers of the fruit, there are two *apūrvas*, each of which is destroyed by the recitation of their respective names.

For this very reason, since even the grace of the deity has a result that resides in a different locus [from the agent], it cannot be postulated as an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*). And thus, in a case where the performance of the *darśa* and other sacrifices is undertaken solely for the sake of curing another's disease, although the agency (*kartṛtva*) may reside jointly (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) in both [the patient and the healer], because there is an absence of being the enjoyer of the fruit (*phalabhoktṛtva*), no separate transcendental potency (*apūrva*) residing therein need be postulated.
Moreover, since [the unseen potency] resides solely in the one who enjoys the fruit, the purificatory rites do not apply to the other.

Thus, even in the case of the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice and others, because the fruit is conceived as residing in the son alone, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) resides in him alone; however, the distinction is that in the case of the father, the *apūrva* generated by the non-performance [of the rite] is what causes the transgression (*pratyavāya*).
Therefore, [the results do not reside] in your father;
and because [the purificatory rites] produce a capacity for the locus of the result that resides in the agent.
The meaning is that even if one conceives of the self as being "not the son," there is no sublation [of the notion of self], and thus its persistence is logically established.
(Refutation of the alternative establishment of sacrifice):
He refutes the alternative establishment of sacrifice and so forth with the words "avāntara... (intermediate).
(An exposition of the unity and plurality of the *utpattyapūrva* based on the unity and plurality of the primary acts, and of the necessity of the *utpattyapūrva*):

Having thus established the *apūrva*, [the author] demonstrates its unity and plurality—arising from the distinction between a single primary act and multiple primary acts—as the general rule, stating: "In that case, here... (*tadatreti*).

Since it is stated that by means of the *prayoga-vidhi* (procedure for performance), the constituent parts (*aṅga*) constitute the causal complex for the fruit, and since the state of being complete with all parts (*sāṅgatā*) is possible only at the conclusion of the performance, the supreme *apūrva* (*paramāpūrva*) arising at that time cannot originate from the momentary principal acts (*pradhāna*). Therefore, there must be a single *utpattyapūrva* (origination-*apūrva*) which serves as the basis for that [supreme *apūrva*]; thus, there are two *apūrvas* in a single principal sacrifice. This is the case where there are multiple principal acts that accomplish a single fruit.
In that regard, the general rule is that there is one *utpattyapūrva* for each principal act, while the *paramāpūrva* is one; such is the meaning.

(Regarding the means for achieving the two collective apūrvas in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices) — he states an exception by postulating an additional apūrva in certain cases: "But in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]... etc.

Although, because each [element] possesses instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) individually in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is no single instrumentality here that exists by way of collective extension (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) over the three [elements]; nevertheless, it is necessary that the conjunction of the three instrumentals—understood through their inclusion in a single word (*ekapada*)—be intended as residing in the object to be accomplished (*upādeya*), insofar as it is defined by a single effect.
Otherwise, as in the case of the *Citrā* and *Saurya* sacrifices, the conventional usage of "conjunction" (*sāhitya*) would be untenable.
Therefore, in this context, "conjunction" (sāhitya) consists solely in the production of a single effect through collective action, and that is not defined in relation to the result;
for it is precisely the conjunction of the six instruments that constitutes its subordinate element (aṅga).
Therefore, it is neither defined by the supreme apūrva nor by the origination-apūrva (utpattyapūrva),

because the latter is produced by each individual instrument. Consequently, when there is a requirement for an effect regarding the conjunction of the three instruments within each respective sentence, the collective apūrva (samudāyāpūrva) is established.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is a repeated performance of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) in each of the two groups.

Thus, since it is necessary for the cause to be defined by each individual effect, even though the curd and milk offerings are performed together because they share a common deity— as understood from the injunction regarding their origin (*utpattivākya*) which specifies a single instrument—
the distinction between the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the origin remains.

Therefore, it should be understood that when one primary element is forgotten, only the other—whether it be the curd-sacrifice or the milk-sacrifice that was performed—is repeated, and not that which had already been performed. Thus it is to be seen.
(An extension of the principle of the New and Full Moon sacrifices [darśapūrṇamāsa] applies even to the Cāturmāsya and other rites.

By this very same principle, it is extended that wherever there is a collection of sacrifices, there the "unseen potency" (apūrva) of that collection is established— thus, "the same applies elsewhere."

In the case of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices as well—in passages such as "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva in the spring"—the establishment of a collective transcendental result (*samudāyāpūrva*) follows from the scriptural hearing that each respective seasonal juncture (*parvan*) serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
(An objection regarding the non-necessity of postulating a collective *apūrva* for the twelve-day sacrifice, and its refutation:

Even though in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) there exist distinct *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-apūrvas) because each specific *apūrva*— such as that of the *prāyaṇīya* and other rites— is established by its own originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) as an independent instrument (*karaṇa*), nevertheless, in the injunction of the fruit— "One desiring progeny should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite" (*dvādaśāhena prajākāmaṃ yājayet*)— the status of being an instrument as defined by the fruit would otherwise be untenable.
Since the postulation of the *paramāpūrva* (the ultimate transcendental result) alone suffices, there is no motive for postulating a collective *apūrva* (*samudāyāpūrva*).

Nevertheless, because the sentence "by means of the twelve-day [sacrifice]" (*dvādaśāhena*) uses a singular ending, it is understood that the collection as a whole functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Furthermore, since such instrumentality is untenable without being defined by some effect, and since the *paramāpūrva*—being produced by the individual members of the collection—cannot serve as its defining correlate, the establishment of a collective *apūrva* must be recognized.

"In the subsidiaries" (*aṅgeṣu*) [means]: by means of producing in the principal (*pradhāna*) the capacity for generating the *utpattyapūrva*—just as the *sannipatyopakārakas* [subsidiaries] function by producing that very capacity—the determination of the utility of the *ārādupakārakas* [subsidiaries] is explained through their production of a capacity conducive to generating that immediate effect residing in the *utpattyapūrva* of the principal. Furthermore, there is the demonstration that even in the absence of a collective *apūrva* (*samudāyāpūrva*), the extension of rules (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is logically consistent; and the determination that what lies outside the performance (*prayoga*) is utilized only for the generation of the fruit, and so forth.
"In the principal alone" (*pradhāna eva*) [is the meaning].
The meaning is "because of proximity.

Now, one might object: since even auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) that provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*) do not produce the essential nature of the primary sacrifice (*pradhānayāga*), the *utpattyapūrvas* produced by them also arise without any interval from the primary sacrifice; therefore, they too cannot have utility therein. To this, he says: "But as for those that provide remote assistance... [etc.]

Although it might be possible to state that the utility of the *ārādupakāraka* (remotely contributing) auxiliaries—just like the *sannipatyopakāraka* (directly contributing) ones—is solely in generating the fitness for the *utpattyapūrva* (origination-apūrva) residing in the principal act;

nevertheless, because of the parsimony (*lāghava*) involved in postulating their utility in only one place as delimited by the status of being *ārādupakāraka*, it is indicated that their utility lies specifically in the fitness residing in the *utpattyapūrva*. To this end, it was stated in general terms: "of the *ārādupakārakas*."

Now, one might object: since in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) serve to produce the fitness residing in the origination-apūrva (*utpattyapūrva*), which is conducive to the generation of the collective apūrva (*samudāyāpūrva*), how can there be an extension (*atideśa*) of them to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), where the collective apūrva is absent? To this, he says: "Immediately following that... (*tadavyavahita...*).

However, in cases where the Bṛhaspatisava—which is a subsidiary of the Vājapeya—is excluded from the performance [of the main rite], it has no utility there because its performance occurs after the production of the ultimate *apūrva* (transcendental result) generated by the performance of the Vājapeya together with all its subsidiaries.

In such instances, its utility lies solely in generating a fitness (*yogyatā*) residing in the ultimate *apūrva* that is conducive to the fruit. Likewise, this should be understood regarding the Vaimṛdha sacrifice in relation to the collective *apūrva*. To indicate this, the phrase "or indeed heaven and so forth" was stated, using "fruit" as a general indicator.
(An examination of the Kaustubha’s exposition regarding the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice being the establisher of the supreme apūrva):

In this context, the followers of the Mīmāṃsā-mūla [the author of the Kaustubha] should be seen to refute the view that the non-performance of the Bṛhaspatisava and other such rites causes the destruction of the supreme apūrva, and instead maintain that their performance establishes the supreme apūrva; furthermore, the utility of the subsidiary elements such as the *pratipatti* rites should also be understood from the Kaustubha.
And this will be established in the fourth [chapter].

(An exposition on the necessity of accepting the *paramāpūrva*, by resolving doubts regarding the lack of necessity for accepting it both for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary acts (*pradhāna*)):
Although it may be argued that wherever there is a collective *apūrva* (samudāyāpūrva),
the remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) can logically be employed in that very context [of the collective],...

Alternatively, even in that case, there is no evidence whatsoever for a *paramāpūrva* (ultimate transcendental result), because its utility can be established through the production of a fitness conducive to the fruit within the *utpattyapūrva* (the apūrva of origination) itself.
Furthermore, in cases where there are no auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) that provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), there is no basis at all for postulating such a [transcendental result].

Nevertheless, in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, since the fruit-statement (*phala-vākya*) reveals that the six sacrifices— qualified by their conjunction— are the instruments (*karaṇa*) that bring about the fruit, and since this [instrumentality] is untenable without an intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*), the *paramāpūrva* (the final transcendental result) is postulated in view of that requirement. For this very reason, the *utpattyapūrvas* (the individual originative results) or the *samudāyāpūrva* (the collective result) do not possess the status of an operation, because they are not produced as delimited by the conjunction of the six [sacrifices].

Although the instrumentality (*karaṇatā*) differs with each sacrifice, and the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) such as "belonging to Agni" (*āgneyatva*) and so forth also differ, nevertheless, there is a single property of being defined by the result (*phalanirūpakatā*) common to all these instrumentalities.
Because the fruit is a single entity, its delimitation consists in the conjunction of the six [auxiliaries].

Since it is not established that the origination-apūrvas (utpattyapūrva) and so forth are produced by those [auxiliaries], the postulation of the supreme apūrva (paramāpūrva) is for the purpose of establishing their causal operation.

Therefore, where the production of the apūrva of the aggregate and so forth is possible through the mediation of the instrumentality itself, there the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is established by intending the state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) without regard for an intermediate operation; thus, there is no requirement for an operation defined by a single effect.
However, in the present case, because the fruit occurs at a later time, its production cannot occur without mediation, and thus an operation is required—this is the distinction.

In this way, since it is understood through the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) that the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), only when combined with one another, produce the fruit consisting of assistance to the principal (*pradhāna*), and since that [assistance] does not arise without an interval [between the subsidiaries], there follows no [need for] another [assistance] in the form of an indivisible instrumental aid (*akhaṇḍakaraṇopakāra*) which would constitute its operation. This is likewise the case where there is only a single principal.

In that case as well, since the fruit occurs at a later time, there is a requirement for an operation; its establishment is achieved precisely by conforming to the fact that it arises subsequent to the principal rite together with its auxiliary parts.

(An examination of the desirability of not accepting a supreme apūrva: If it is considered that, although there is evidence for the existence of a supreme apūrva in both cases, there is no evidence for postulating that the operation (*vyāpāra*) belongs only to that which arises after the completion of the primary rite together with its subsidiaries; rather, it is more appropriate that the operation belongs to the established *utpattyapūrvas* themselves—then [the following is said]:

At that time, there would be no purpose whatsoever in accepting that [position]; thus, indicating this by means of the word "tathā" (so), he demonstrates the non-acceptance of it through the argument of an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), saying: "But if... (*yaditu*).

(Refutation, supported by the Vārttika, of the view of Prakāśa—who maintains that in the absence of a supreme apūrva, the subsequent subsidiaries must be held to exist for the sake of maintaining the *utpattyapūrva* until the production of the fruit—and of another view, regarding the occurrence of *prasaṅga* in the second and subsequent performances of the archetype and in the modified sacrifices [vikṛtis]).

By this [it is shown]: in the absence of a supreme apūrva, since it must be stated that the subsequent subsidiaries serve to maintain the *utpattyapūrva* until the production of the fruit, then for one who has performed the Darśa sacrifice once for the sake of heaven, during the second and subsequent performances of the archetype and in those modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*) whose fruits are to be experienced in this life—

Furthermore, the claim made by the *Prakāśakāra*—that there is no fault (*anāpatti*) regarding the performance of subsequent subsidiaries (*uttarāṅga*) because the result is established through the persistence of the assistance provided by previously performed subsidiaries—is refuted. This is because, since the purpose of the subsequent subsidiaries is accepted as being solely to instill the capacity conducive to the production of the fruit, when that final capacity is destroyed, the principle of "subsidiary application" (*prasaṅga*) does not apply. Consequently, there is no evidence for the view that their purpose is the maintenance of the "unseen potency" (*apūrva*) produced by those subsidiaries.

By this— namely, by the mention of each individual *utpattyapūrva* in the absence of a *paramāpūrva*, which leads to the consequence of its destruction and thus the impossibility of the production of the fruit— the argument of some who claim that "its postulation is necessary" is also refuted;
for in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*) even if the fruit is not produced, and thus such a postulation is untenable.

Therefore, in the Vārtika—having raised the objection: "Now, why is it that the individual *apūrvas* of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) do not themselves become the seeds of the fruit, while the distinct *apūrvas* of the primary rites (*pradhāna*) do not attain the status of being the seeds of the fruit?"—it is replied: "True; indeed, there is no fault here, for this is an accepted position (*iṣṭāpatti*). However, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), a single *apūrva* is first understood here; thereafter, for the sake of establishing that [single *apūrva*], there would be further valid cognition (*pramā*) of other *apūrvas*."

Because the principal acts are simultaneously enjoined with respect to their results, and the subsidiaries are simultaneously enjoined with respect to the principals, their connection is established through mutual dependence and by the postulation of a single *apūrva*; thus, there is no means of knowledge for postulating further *apūrvas*. Therefore, it is first determined that there is only one [apūrva]. Subsequently, since it is impossible to perform those many actions occurring in succession all at once, for the sake of accomplishing that [result],...

By the statement beginning with "there arises the postulation of an unprecedented [result] specific to each individual," the supreme *apūrva* (unprecedented result) is accepted merely on the grounds that it is impossible to abandon what has been relied upon.

(Conclusion following the refutation of the statement in the *Prakāśa* that the subsidiaries do not bring about the supreme *apūrva*): By this, the claim of the author of the *Prakāśa*— that one should not, in any way, accept the view written by Pārthasārathi that the subsidiaries bring about the supreme *apūrva* based on the *Anu-smṛti*— is refuted, because it contradicts the *Vārttika* and because of the reasoning already stated.
Furthermore, this point will be clarified specifically in the eleventh chapter;

however, with the intention that even if there is a dispute regarding the establishment of the supreme *apūrva*, there is no dispute whatsoever regarding the existence of the *apūrva* itself, he concludes: "In every respect."
Thus ends the third section concerning the apūrva.
(B1) (Section 4 / A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 4) These [actions] are twofold, being either subordinate or principal.
In such cases as "He threshes the rice," it is undisputed— just as in the previous instance— that threshing is the instrument for the production of the result.
And that result is not the rice grains themselves,
because they are not produced [by the act].
Nor is it the state of being dehusked,
because since its production is established by worldly convention, it is not something to be enjoined;
nor is there an injunction for the purpose of excluding threshing and the like, since those too are already implied by the sense of the context.
Because that [result] would also be fruitless,
and it does not have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*);
for if an invisible result must necessarily be postulated, it is more appropriate to postulate it from the very audible act of threshing itself.
Therefore, threshing has only an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha). Furthermore, that unseen result does not reside in the rice grains themselves,
because the self is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) with respect to that which is delimited by the [grains'] essence.

Therefore, as before, since rice grains alone are the objects of threshing, it follows that threshing qualified by rice is enjoined for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*). To this we reply: since an unseen result is improper when a visible result is possible, the removal of the husk (*vituṣībhāva*) alone is the fruit of threshing.
Nor is the injunction redundant on the grounds that the husking is already established through mere implication (*ākṣepa*); [for the injunction serves to restrict the means].

This is because the restriction (niyama), which has the result of excluding other means such as threshing with the teeth and so forth, is enjoined for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) based upon threshing.
For this very reason, in the *kṛṣṇala* sacrificial oblation, there is an omission of that [threshing] due to the absence of threshing.
In reality, however, it is the scripturally prescribed threshing itself that is enjoined for the purpose of dehusking, by virtue of its prior application through implication (*ākṣepa*).
Therefore, because of the exclusion [of other means] through the force of the restrictive injunction (*niyama*), the result is the exclusion of threshing and so forth.

As for the suspicion of futility—since the state of being dehusked (*vaituṣya*) can also be produced by threshing—it must be dispelled by postulating that an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the rice grains arises from threshing alone.
And regarding that unseen potency, only its status as something produced (*janyatva*) is to be postulated on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), not its status as a motivator (*prayojakatva*).
Because that [grinding] is conceptualized only with respect to the visible form, namely the state of being dehusked;
therefore, in the *kṛṣṇala* sacrifice, since the state of being dehusked is absent, that [grinding] is omitted.
Furthermore, because another implied injunction (*vidhyantara*) is postulated, there is no case of multiple intended objects (*anekoddeśyatā*).

Furthermore, since the fact that each respective unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resides specifically in the rice and other materials is understood through the very means of knowledge that apprehend those second and subsequent substrates, its status as an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is established precisely in that capacity, and not by virtue of being the Self.

Consequently, because threshing is enjoined with reference to the rice—which serves as a means to the *apūrva*—by way of both the removal of the husk (the visible result) and the production of the unseen merit, its character as a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*) is proven.

The practical implication (*prayojana*) is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), another variety of rice must be procured for the purpose of threshing, distinct from the rice intended for the sacrifice.
In the established conclusion (siddhānta), it is not so. // 4 //
Thus ends the fourth section concerning the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) of threshing.

(B2) [The establishment of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that rice grains serve the purpose of threshing, by means of the logic of the *prayāja* remnant, preceded by an investigation into the connection through objection (*ākṣepasaṅgati*) with the section on verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*): Since the very existence of the section on verbal roots depends upon the section on the *apūrva*, the section on the *apūrva* constitutes a supplementary part (*śeṣa*) to the section on verbal roots.

Since there is no purpose for its connection [to the word "barley"], he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by restating the established conclusion (siddhānta) of the section on the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvādhikaraṇa), in order to demonstrate the implied connection (ākṣepikī saṅgati) through that very section: "In cases such as 'one threshes the rice' (*vrīhīnavahanti*)," and so forth.
By the phrase "and so forth," examples such as "he grinds the rice" are included.

Even if threshing and other such acts have an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose, if that invisible result is admitted to reside in the rice and other materials, nevertheless the status of the rice as being for the sake of threshing is not established; it is for this reason that he says: "And that too... (tadapi ca).

Since [the result] arises in the self alone—just like the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the *prayāja* offerings—it is more appropriate to enjoin the substance such as rice for the threshing itself, which requires a substratum, rather than postulating rice and other substances as the substratum for something that does not require one.

Therefore, the meaning is that even if the accusative case is taken to indicate the instrumental sense according to the logic of the "remnant of the *prayāja*" (*prayājaśeṣa*), there is no fault, because this allows for the adoption of an injunction that fulfills a requirement.
(An introduction to the final conclusion [siddhānta] that threshing has rice as its purpose, preceded by an examination of the fourfold nature of action:
There is no rule that only that which possesses the quality of being produced is fit for connection as the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*).
Because the nature of an object (*karmatva*) is fourfold:
for some thing becomes an object precisely by virtue of being produced, as a lump [of dough] is by kneading;
and some [becomes an object] by virtue of being qualified by attainment, as milk is by milking.
One [type of action] is distinguished by producing a certain modification, as for example rice grains by threshing,
because it generates a modification known as the removal of the husks; and another is distinguished by producing a refinement, as for example rice grains by sprinkling.

Because it produces an unseen refinement of form (*adṛṣṭarūpasaṃskāra*), and because in the present case it is impossible for the rice grains to be the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*) in their own natural state, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the intention that— since it is possible for them to be the end to be achieved in the form of being characterized by the removal of the husks— it is not proper to assume an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*) when a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) is available.
"Arising from what is seen."
(An exposition according to the *Śāstradīpikā*’s established conclusion regarding the injunction of the rule based on threshing):

In this context, the *Śāstradīpikā*, in the concluding section of the relevant topic (*adhikaraṇa*), states that a single unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) is postulated from the rule of threshing which has a visible purpose; by means of indicating the avoidance of the futility of the injunction through this rule, it is declared that the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) of the object to be performed has an unseen purpose.
According to his view, he states the injunction of a restrictive rule based on the threshing that falls under the position that it serves the purpose of removing the husk: "dalana... (threshing).

Since that [threshing] which depends on threshing for the purpose of removing the husks is enjoined as having an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose, it therefore does not serve an invisible purpose due to the absence of its substratum (āśraya).
Thus he says "for this very reason" regarding the *kṛṣṇala* oblation: even though the rule [of threshing] would otherwise apply, there is indeed an omission.

(In the *Śāstradīpikā*’s own conclusion, since that [unseen result] is untenable because it would involve enjoining a restriction not heard in the text, there is instead the injunction of the directly stated threshing itself; furthermore, an imagined unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) cannot be the motive.

And regarding this position, dissatisfied because it involves abandoning the injunction of the directly stated verbal root-meaning and results in the imposition of an unheard restrictive injunction—which is further untenable as something unheard cannot produce an unseen result—the author states another position, beginning with "In reality, however" and "And of the state of being dehusked."
The phrase "without restriction" (niyamaṃ vinā) is a carry-over from the preceding [text].

Because it is produced by the restriction of threshing for the purpose of rice, he says "residing in the rice" (vrīhiniṣṭha) to indicate that, by the very means of proof that establishes the subject of the property (dharmigrāhakapramāṇa), it resides exclusively in the rice.

He states that even though an unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is postulated, it lacks the status of being a motivating cause (*prayojaka*) by virtue of its own independence, because it is merely a secondary consequence (*anuṣaṅgikatayā*) of what has been postulated: "And of that unseen force... and so forth.
Furthermore, the non-injunctionality of the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) consists in its non-performance when threshing is impossible,
and not in its performance even when threshing is possible— nor does it consist in the performance of alternatives such as pounding.

But that [removal of husks] does not occur even when the state of being free from husks is possible, because it would then follow that threshing and other such methods would also have to be performed.

Therefore, although it is produced by threshing, the reason for its designation as "unseen merit of restriction" (niyamādṛṣṭa) is that it arises from the necessity of avoiding futility, which results from the fact that the restrictive rule has the effect of excluding methods such as splitting [the grain]. This is the meaning.

(The resolution is as follows: Since there is no multiplicity of intended objects (*uddeśya*) in an injunction based on what is directly heard (*śruta*), and since the intended object is presented by a single accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) as qualified by both the visible (*dṛṣṭa*) and the invisible (*adṛṣṭa*), the syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by the multiplicity of intended objects is avoided.
He avoids the syntactical split resulting from the multiplicity of intended objects with the words "ārthiketi" (meaning "as an implied [object]").

When the injunction for threshing is prescribed with reference to rice grains (*vrīhi*) characterized by the removal of husks according to the explicit scriptural rule (*śrutavidhi*), there arises the cognition that such an injunction would otherwise be purposeless; subsequently, one postulates an implied further injunction (*arthikavidhyantara*) stating "one should produce an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) through threshing. Thus, there is no multiplicity of objects to be enjoined (*uddeśyānekatva*) within the explicit scriptural injunction.

Alternatively, there is no fault because the rice grains—which serve as the substrata for both the visible (*dṛṣṭa*) and the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) results—are expressed as the objective (*bhāvya*) by a single accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*). This is the meaning.
(An exposition on how both the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the status of being a means to the *apūrva* and the acceptance of the *niyamāpūrva* are necessary regarding the word *vrīhi*):

Just as here, since the futility [of the injunction] cannot be avoided even with respect to the husked state (*vituṣībhāva*)—just as it cannot be avoided with respect to the essential nature of the rice (*vrīhisvarūpa*)—the indication of the status of being a means to the *apūrva* is necessary; yet, because the injunction is justified by its being for the sake of the *utpattyapūrva* of the primary rite, the *niyamādṛṣṭa* is not the purpose.
This objection and its refutation are to be seen in the *Kaustubha*.

Therefore, since threshing does not have the rice grains as its purpose, there is no assumption of a separate transcendental result (*apūrva*) based on the status of being a motivator (*prayojaka*) with respect to the primary *apūrva*, as opposed to the threshing which serves as the purpose for the grains. Rather, the restrictive transcendental result (*niyamādṛṣṭa*) produced by the threshing for the sake of the rice grains is merely incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*). Thus, even though there is a difference in the meaning of the verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), there is no difference in the *apūrva*; demonstrating this through a negative inference (*vyatireka*), he concludes the established position (*siddhānta*): [The text ends here.]
And for this reason.

(Regarding the abandonment of the purpose of the inquiry as stated by the Bhāṣyakāra in the case of the *praiyaṅgava* oblation in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), and the statement of a different purpose— namely, that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) there would be other rice-grains for the purpose of threshing in the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself,

whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) they are only those grains intended for the sacrifice), as well as the reason for this and the manner in which the purpose is established: Here, the purpose of the inquiry regarding the *praiyaṅgava* oblation in the modified sacrifice has been shown by the Bhāṣyakāra and others.

Since there is no independent determination regarding the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) because it possesses the attainment of constituent elements dependent upon the original sacrifice (*prakṛti*), and since a determination must necessarily be made regarding the original sacrifice alone—where that [determination] is obtained—there is no purpose in running all the way to the modified sacrifice; therefore, setting that aside, he states the purpose regarding the original sacrifice itself: "the purpose."

In the injunction for threshing (*avaghāta*), since the rice grains (*vrīhi*) are not heard of as being a means (*sādhana*) by virtue of being employed for another purpose—as is the case with the sacrificial cake-pan (*puroḍāśakapāla*) and so forth—threshing, like the sacrifice itself, possesses independent *prayojaka* (motivating) status; consequently, they must be procured separately even for that purpose. However, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because those grains are objects of refinement (*saṃskārya*), and because it would result in futility (*ānarthakya*) if they were intended merely for their own material form (*svarūpa*), there arises a requirement for them to be a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*).

The meaning is that, since the word *vrīhi* functions as an indicator (*lakṣaka*) of those [rice grains], and since the context known as "subject matter" (*adhikārākhyaprakaraṇa*) serves to apprehend the intended purport (*tātparya*), it is logical to accept only those rice grains belonging to the sacrifice under discussion; thus, only the rice grains used in the ritual at hand are to be taken.
(Regarding the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa], where the threshing of only three handfuls of rice is performed only once;

and regarding the established conclusion [siddhānta], where the threshing of even the four-handful measure of barley continues until the production of the rice-grains—this is the author’s own demonstration of a different purpose:
Thus, according to the prima facie view, like the threshing of all herbs, the threshing of only three handfuls of rice is performed only once for an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha).

In the original ritual (*prakṛti*), because threshing is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *sānnāyya* and other sacrifices—just like the *prayāja* offerings—it is extended (*atideśa*) to their modifications (*vikāra*). Thus, even when using barley, there is threshing with three handfuls of rice.
However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), threshing is performed until the production of rice grains;
since it serves as a purification (*saṃskāra*) of the medicinal substance (*auṣadhadravya*) and is not an auxiliary to the *sānnāyya* and others, it is not extended to their modifications.

In the case of the *yava* (barley) alternative, the threshing applies to those very grains, because only those measured by four handfuls serve as the means for the sacrifice; thus, the threshing is performed on that many alone. This [statement] is also an indication of other purposes.
Thus ends the fourth section concerning the visible purpose of threshing.

(B1) (Section 5) (A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 5): But in the case of a mere property (*dharmamātra*), because the action does not cease [with its own result], as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings, [the second case ending] is used for the sake of instrumentality— just as it denotes the state of being an object (*sādhyatva*)— since, in instances such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) and "he cleanses the ladles" (*srucāḥ saṃmārṣṭi*), a visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakārakatva*) is impossible.

Furthermore, because we observe such usage as "he offers groats" (*saktūn juhoti*) and "make balbaja-grass into tufts" (*balvajān śikhaṇḍakān kuru*), it is simply an object of purpose (*arthakarman*), just like the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the preceding section.
For in the case of *balvajān*, since the verb *kṛ* would otherwise result in having two objects, they do not possess the status of being the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Therefore, the meaning of the accusative case is also instrumentality (*karaṇatva*).

Therefore, since it is argued that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) performed with rice (*vrīhi*) as its instrument is enjoined for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), [we reply: according to the grammatical rule "the accusative case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) and from common usage such as "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the meaning of the accusative is indeed the state of being an end to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), not the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*);
for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating multiple powers (*anekaśaktikalpana*).

And *karmatva* (the state of being an object), according to the rule "that which is most desired by the agent is the object" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*), consists precisely in the quality of being most desired; however, according to the rule "and likewise that which is connected [with the action] though not desired," it is simply the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), common to both the desired and the undesired.
How, this being so, the two rules are not redundant has been demonstrated in the *Kaustubha* itself.

And therefore, since the rice grains (*vrīhi*) are denoted as the object to be accomplished by the accusative case, and since they are understood to be subordinate to the sacrifice (*yāga*), they are perceived as being something desired; thus, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is enjoined with reference to them.
Even though a visible means (*dvāra*) is impossible, an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) means residing in the rice grains itself is postulated.
For this very reason, where no utility is established, [an unseen result is assumed].
Nor can it be so construed; for instance, as in the case of groats (*saktu*), where,
by accepting the instrumental sense indicated by the second case-ending, there is an injunction of the oblation itself— qualified by the groats— for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no definition of [the *saktūn*] as an instrument (*karaṇa*), because its connection [with the action] is established even as an unintended object (*anīpsita-karman*).

For if that were the case, since even something that provides indirect assistance (*adṛṣṭopakāraka*) would necessarily be connected to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) as an object, it would follow that [the sacrifice] possesses two objects (*dvikarmaka*), which would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by having multiple intended objects (*uddeśya*).

Therefore, although the oblation (*homa*) performed with groats (*saktu*) as its instrument is indirectly beneficial (*ārādupakāraka*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the like are indeed directly beneficial (*sannipatyopakāraka*).
The purpose is as before. // 4 //
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the sprinkling of rice-grains as part of the sweeping.

(B2) [Connection by way of counter-example with the preceding section, and the instrumental capacity of the second case: In the preceding section, it was established that an action is a subsidiary (*guṇakarman*) because it obtains a visible benefit; however, this is not the case where such a benefit is not obtained.

In this context, indicating the immediate connection by way of presenting a counter-example to the established conclusion—that the status of being a primary object (*pradhānakarmatva*) should obtain because it provides a visible benefit—the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), preceded by a demonstration of the subject matter:
"The rice-grains... (*vrīhīn iti*).

By the phrase "and so forth," there is an inclusion of such [injunctions] as "he cleanses the enclosing sticks" (*paridhiṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), "he cleanses the fire" (*agniṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), and "he carries fire around the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśaṃ paryagnikaroti*).

Since the ladle (*stru*) and other such items cannot be the *bhāvya* (the thing to be brought about) because they are not produced by the cleansing and other acts, and since— as in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*) and similar acts— they cannot be qualified by a visible benefit even on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of functional suitability, the cleansing and other acts as qualified by the ladle and other items are themselves [understood to be] remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*).
With the intention that its injunction is appropriate—just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and others—he says: "Because it provides a visible benefit."

[Objection: But surely, since the status of being a subordinate factor (guṇakarmatva) is impossible based on the mark (liṅga) consisting of semantic competency (yogyatā), that [status] is established by the very force of the heard accusative case-ending (dvitīyāśruti), as its meaning is thereby accomplished; to this, he says: "And of the accusative... (dvitīyāyāśca).

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because we observe its usage even in the absence of predominance (*prādhānya*). The last [alternative] is also not tenable; for an injunction that contradicts a usage upon which it depends cannot logically serve as its regulator. With this in mind, he says: "Even in the case of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*)."
The Vedic usage "make peacocks with balbaja-grass" [is used] in the sense of "with groats";
by the word "etcetera," it is indicated through a negative instance that even in the case of "with the remnant of the prayāja-offering," the clarified butter (*ājya*) possesses primacy.
Therefore, the meaning is that because of its more frequent usage, it possesses the capacity (*śakti*) for being an instrument (*karaṇa*).
(Regarding the doubt and its refutation concerning the connection with multiple objects in such cases as "Make tufts of *balbaja* grass" and "Offering groats into the fire"):

Now, one might object that just as properties such as redness (*āruṇya*), though first connected to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of purchase, subsequently undergo mutual connection (*pārṣṭhikaḥ parasparānvayaḥ*), so too here—in the sentence concerning *balbaja* grass—both [the *balbaja* grass and the *śikhaṇḍas*] might first be connected to the verb simply by way of being objects (*karmatvena*). To this, [the author replies] regarding the connection with multiple instruments (*anekakaraṇānvaye*): [the following applies].
