He refutes this by stating "balbajānāṃ hi," since it is impossible for multiple karmas to follow [from a single cause].

In this way, since it is impossible for even the barley meal (*saktu*) to be the object of the act of *juhoti*— which consists of the collection of the substance being offered and its casting with a deity as the intended recipient—
and since it is also impossible for it to be a partial object because it is not what is desired to be attained, he states that its purpose is to serve as an instrument:
"Therefore, it is also an instrument."

(An establishment that, when the second case [accusative] functions as either the object (*sādhya*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*), its power (*śakti*) resides in the instrument alone, or in the instrument only:
The meaning of that [suffix] is not exclusively the state of being an instrument in all instances;
for it is also employed in cases such as *ghaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a pot"), where it denotes the object (*sādhya*).
Therefore, according to the specific application, in some cases there is the status of being the object (*sādhyatva*), while in others there is also the status of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*).
And since the status of being an instrument is appropriate in the present context as well, there is no reason whatsoever for abandoning its primary object-status (*pradhānakarmatā*).

By this, it is also indicated that the effort expended by the ancients in their prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)—which accepts the meaning of "instrument" alone without admitting the meaning of "object"—is futile.

Alternatively, even though [the pot] is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the expression "he makes a pot," its meaning is not merely that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), but rather its status as an instrument; therefore, the particle *api* ("even/also") should be construed with the sense that its power resides precisely in its being an instrument. As for the usage where it is employed in the sense of something to be accomplished—as in "he makes a pot"—there too, just as a pot relates to cognition by way of the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*), its status as an instrument is logically possible in relation to the act of making (*kṛti*); thus, there is no contradiction.
This is the meaning.
And thus, there is no contradiction with what was stated regarding the Kaustubha gem in the sense that it serves as a mere instrument.
(The commencement of the established doctrine that [the root *gam*] has a quality as its object, due to the predominance of the grammatical instruction over usage:

Since the predominance of Smṛti over usage has been established, and because there is corroboration from certain usages in the form of practice (*ācāra*), it is proper to rely, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), on the very meaning taught by Smṛti as the power (*śakti*) of that [root];
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate multiple powers.

Therefore, since the predominance implied by the objecthood understood from that [verb] is untenable, he states the established conclusion—that it is indeed a subsidiary action (guṇakarman)—with the rule: "The second case ending is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2).
The meaning of the second case-ending is simply "the state of being the object" (*sādhyatvam*).

Even so, in the expression *agner māṇavakam* ("the boy [is heated] by fire"), two rules are necessary to prevent the fifth case-ending from arising after the word *māṇavaka*, because the properties such as "not being desired" (*anīpsitatva*) are obtainable through other means; thus, there is neither primary denotation (*śakti*) nor indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for them in that context.

Even if the meaning of the second case-ending were merely the state of being an object (*sādhyatva*), there would still be the general understanding of the predominance (*prādhānya*) of the rice and other materials; [this is] because, one might object, since the state of being an object (*karmatva*) is of many kinds—distinguished by whether it is desired (*īpsita*) or undesired (*anīpsita*)—the assumption of multiple powers remains unavoidable. To this, he says: "And the state of being an object... (*karmatvañca*).
It is precisely the state of being the probandum.

The term *sādhyatva* refers to being the locus of a result produced by four kinds of action— which is synonymous with *vyāpyatva* (pervadedness)— or else it refers to an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) co-extensive with that [pervadedness];
it does not, however, have the synonym of mere "being produced" (*janyatvamātra*).
By this, even the fourfold nature of *kāraka* is subsumed.

Thus, the meaning is that since the status of being desired (*īpsita*) or undesired (*anīpsita*) is obtainable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no expressive power (*śakti*) in the word itself for that purpose either.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then since the goal can be accomplished by the rule 'the object is that which is to be accomplished' (*sādhyaṃ karma*) alone, the formulation of two sūtras is redundant. To this, he says: "And as it is so... (*yathā caivam sati*).

Because the rule *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* prescribes the technical designation *apādāna* for that which is desired (*īpsita*) when used in conjunction with verbal roots meaning "to ward off," the word *māṇavaka* in the sentence *agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati* ("He wards off the boy from the fire") would—just like the word *agni*—be subject to the designation *apādāna* due to being something desired. Therefore, since it is necessary to prescribe the designation *karman* for it by virtue of its being the most desired (*īpsitatama*), the first rule [Pāṇini 1.4.29] is indispensable. Furthermore, the second rule [Pāṇini 1.4.30] is also indispensable for the purpose of including those who are objects of hatred (*dveṣya*) and so forth.

The meaning is that it has been demonstrated in the *Kaustubha*. By this, the view of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*— that because the two [other] sūtras would otherwise be rendered redundant, its expressive power (*śakti*) lies solely in the status of being an intended object (*īpsita-karman*) due to its being the first to present itself, while in cases such as the unintended object (*anīpsita-karman*) it functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)— is refuted.

The sense is that when a grammatical operation can be accomplished by a single power common to both [the agent and the object], it is improper to postulate that power for a portion obtainable through other means, as this would involve the assumption of a figurative (lākṣaṇika) application;
however, where such [a primary application] is obstructed,
there is no fault even in assuming a figurative application of the rule *akathita-*.

Now, one might object: "If the status of being the most desired (*īpsitatama*) is not understood through the accusative case, by what means would the *sruk* (ladle) and other such items be understood as such, whereby their primary status could be designated by the technical term 'object' (*karman*)? To this, he says: "And for this reason...

For an injunction (*vidhi*), which consists essentially in the impelling of a conscious agent, being unable to impel [the agent] toward a result that is not desired, makes known that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) has a desired objective (*bhāvya*). Thus, when there is a requirement for a desired objective, those things understood as the objective through the accusative case—[are established as such].

The meaning is that it is not unreasonable to apprehend the *strug* and other items as the most desired object (*īpsitatama*), since they are understood as subordinate members (*aṅga*) through injunctions such as "one offers with the *juhū*"; thus, the status of being the most desired is indeed cognized by the injunction itself.
[The opponent objects: "But surely... (nanu).
The meaning is that, because [the sacrifice] is already occupied by the Soma prescribed at the time of its origin, it is impossible to conceive of any other application [for the offering].
(The justification for the understanding of predominance by means of the accusative case-suffix:

Nor does it follow that the accusative and instrumental suffixes would be rendered purposeless simply because the status of a substance as subordinate or predominant with respect to an action is established through its being either purposeless or purposeful;

for in cases such as "with the *aindrī* [verse] one worships the *gārhapatya* [fire]," although both the *gārhapatya* fire and the *aindrī* verse are equally purposeful insofar as they are connected to the sacrifice, the understanding of predominance in the *gārhapatya* fire alone depends upon the accusative suffix.

Thus, although there is no difference between the *sūktavāka* and the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastara-praharaṇa*) in terms of their having a purpose, since the understanding of the *sūktavāka* as a means depends upon the third case-ending, its [the second case-ending’s] lack of purpose does not follow;

therefore, it should be understood from the *Kaustubha* that while the authority of the direct scriptural statement in the accusative case remains intact, the exception applies to the flour-meal (*saktu*) because it lacks a purpose.
And it is not so... [end of fragment].

(Regarding the passage "one offers the flour-meal" (*saktūn juhoti*), there is a doubt as to whether it intends [the meal] to be an unintended object (*aniṣṭita-karman*); the rebuttal stated therein in the *Tantraratna* and other works is that this is impossible because the root *hu* ("to offer") is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
However, since *hu* is also transitive (*sakarmaka*), there is another rebuttal offered by our own school.)

Regarding this, the authors of the *Tantraratna*, the *Nyāyasudhā*, and others have stated that while in cases such as "He gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa," it is possible for the Maitrāvaruṇa and others to be construed as unintended objects (*anīpsita-karman*) because the verb *dadāti* (to give) is transitive, here— because the verb *juhoti* (he offers) is intransitive— it is not possible for the groats (*saktūn*) to be construed as an unintended object; therefore, they maintain that [the term *saktu*] indicates the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Regarding the statement "that offering, having been offered, returned," since this is an application of the *niṣṭhā* suffix in the sense of an object (*karman*), and because the rule "the third case [is used] for the root *hu* in the Veda" prescribes the third case for the object of *hu*, one understands that this root is also transitive; therefore, [the objection] is irrelevant and should be disregarded. He provides another solution [to avoid this], beginning with "if that were the case."
"The purpose."
(An exposition here, as well, of the purpose of the prima facie and final conclusions of the preceding section):

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the number is intended to be significant because the ladles (*stru*) and other implements are things to be employed (*upādeya*), then according to the logic of the section on the *kapiñjala* birds, even when the number of ladles increases, the cleansing (*sammārga*) and other rites must be performed by only those [ladles] delimited by the number three;
and likewise, in the performance with barley, the preparation of rice (*vrīhi*) and other grains for the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) [would be required].

In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, [the rule] applies to all [grains], and since acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are performed upon those very grains even when barley is used, there is no need to procure rice; this is the meaning, as in the previous case.
As for the purpose stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* and others—
The refutation of that [view] is to be seen in the Kaustubha itself.
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the sprinkling of rice grains.
(B1) (The sixth section //)

(a.2 pā.1 adhi.6) "They praise with the *ājya* [verses]," "He recites the *prauga*," and so forth. Since these *stotras* and *śastras* reveal the deities and other elements of the sacrifice, they possess a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) just like other mantras; therefore, as in the case of *avaghāta* (threshing), they function as direct auxiliaries (*sannipatyopakāraka*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is replied: In common worldly usage, it is well-established that the term "praise" (*stuti*) denotes precisely an expression whose primary purport (*tātparya*) is upon a quality residing in a qualified substratum (*guṇin*). Consequently, an expression—whether accomplished by a chanted (*pragīta*) or unchanted (*apragīta*) mantra—whose primary purport is upon a quality residing in a qualified substratum [is what constitutes praise].

Furthermore, because they are designated by the terms *stotra* (hymn) and *śastra* (recitation), it is impossible for them to have the purpose of manifesting the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*); therefore, these mantras do not serve to manifest the possessor of qualities.

Rather, since the *stotras* and *śastras*, which consist in the manifestation of qualities, result in a transcendental effect (*adṛṣṭa*) residing within the self, they function as remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*).

Nor can it be argued that, following the logic of the *prayāja-śeṣābhighāraṇa* (sprinkling with the remnants of the *prayāja*), the mantra functions to reveal the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in order to conform to its visible purpose;
for since such a function is already established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) itself, the injunction would be redundant.
In this way, the praise addressed to Indra (*aindrī-stuti*) becomes appropriate in the proximity of the sacrifice to Mahendra (*māhendra-yāga*).
Otherwise, since the deity inherent in the word must be expressed in the *nigama* formulas by the very word occurring in the injunction, Mahendra could not be manifested by the word "Indra.
Therefore, in cases where Indra alone is the deity, there would be the consequence of displacement (*utkarṣa*).

Alternatively, due to the absence of any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishing a general relationship [between the two], there would be the consequence that Mahendra himself is manifested by the word "Indra" through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the case of the word "Agni" in the *manotā* mantra.
Therefore, the stotra and śastra are principal actions (pradhānakarman).

Thus ends the sixth section concerning the *stuti* (praise) and *śastra* (recitation). (B2) [Connection as an exception (*apavāda-saṃgati*]: Since the praise of deities serves to manifest frogs and so forth, the *stotras* and *śastras* have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*); thus, there is a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that they are subordinate acts (*guṇakarma*). Because an exception is made here to the status of being a subordinate act established in the preceding section, the connection as an exception is clear; therefore, without stating the doubt or the subject matter, he states the prima facie argument itself: The prima facie argument is stated as follows: [The *stotras* and *śastras* are subordinate acts. Why? Because they possess a visible purpose. For the praise of deities has the visible purpose of manifesting frogs and other such things. Furthermore, because they are recited by means of words, they are like the *mantras* used for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth. Therefore, they are subordinate acts. This is the prima facie view. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) will be stated later. Thus ends the sixth section. "With clarified butter," it is said.
The term *prauga* refers to a specific type of liturgical recitation (*śastra*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of such passages as "they praise with the *pṛṣṭha* [hymns]" and "he recites the *niṣkaivalya*.
A *stotra* (hymn of praise) is defined as the glorification of the relationship between a quality and its possessor, accomplished by means of chanted mantras.
That very [recitation] which is accomplished by means of non-chanted mantras is the *śastra*; this is the distinction between the two.

Although both the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) with respect to the *stotra* and *śastra*—which consist in the proclamation of a relationship through the relation of objective domain (*viṣayatā-sambandha*)—nevertheless, when their purpose is considered, since it is impossible for them to serve the purpose of proclaiming qualities not employed in the ritual action, they must instead serve the purpose of proclaiming the possessor of the quality who is employed in the ritual action.

Since it is improper to assume an unseen purpose when a visible purpose is possible— and because, like the *yājyā* and other mantras, it is appropriate that they serve the purpose of manifestation to obtain a visible purpose— he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the action] is indeed a subsidiary act (*guṇakarma*) because it effects a refinement of the qualified object (*guṇisaṃskārakatvāt*),
using the phrase "pertaining to the sacrifice" (*yāgīya*).
Nor should it be suspected: "In the absence of a direct statement (śruti) of the accusative case, how can there be the status of being a subordinate action (guṇakarma)?
For even in its absence, that status is established by a mere indicative mark (liṅga) that makes known its subordination to the primary substance (guṇin).

Therefore, the intention is that in the previously established siddhānta-sūtra—"Or, because of the equality of the direct statement, it should have the same characteristics as the others"—the mention of "direct statement" (śruti) is merely illustrative (upalakṣaṇa).

In the *āgnimāruta* and other sections, there are recitations such as "he recites the *akṣasūkta*" and "he recites the *maṇḍūkasūkta*. Since the dice (*akṣa*), frogs (*maṇḍūka*), and so forth mentioned therein lack the status of deities, it is impossible for them to reveal a deity. Furthermore, it is observed that these hymns merely reveal the praise of the dice and frogs as employed in the *rājasūya* and *agnicayana* sacrifices. Because this was raised here as a doubt by means of a *guṇasūtra*: "But the *stotra* and *śastra* are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*), like the *yājyā*, because they serve to designate the deity."

The inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "deity and so forth" (*devatādi*) is intended to indicate that the mention of the "deity" in the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra is merely an illustration for anything that is to be praised.

(An exposition on the fact that the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because if they were intended to reveal the qualities of the possessor of those qualities, it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication [*lakṣaṇā*]):

Intending that when the literal meaning of the scripture requires a purpose, it is proper to postulate a purpose that does not contradict that literal meaning, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "In the world... (*loke*).

The meaning is that, just as in expressions such as "Devadatta has curly hair-ends," a cognition of praise arises when the quality is denoted, this is not the case in expressions such as "Bring him who has curly hair-ends.

Now, one might object: just as in the case of the injunction "He sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings," where, for the sake of conforming to the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) of the remnant being disposed of (*pratipatti*), one resorts to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in both case-endings; [so too should it be here].

Anticipating the objection that even here the roots *stu* (to praise) and *śaṃs* (to recite) may have the sense of "manifesting" through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*).

Since, as in the case of the *yājyā* and other mantras, it is possible for the manifestation [of the deity] to be obtained through the very Vedic injunction (*śruti*) that enjoins the mantra based on its indicative power (*liṅga*),

there would result the futility of the injunction here, as it would lack the purpose of excluding other qualities (*guṇa-parisaṅkhyā*) and so forth. Furthermore, since the view that mantras have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*)— established by their effecting praise (*stuti*)— remains intact even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), and because postulating a visible purpose for the nature of the praise itself would lead to the sublation of that very nature of praise, one has no choice but to accept this.
The meaning is that the injunction is purposeful only when its referent is something not otherwise perceived; otherwise, it would be redundant.

Having thus presented the contradiction with direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) as a sublater of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), he also demonstrates the occurrence of a sublation regarding the connection with the sequence, by saying "and thus" (*evañca*).
(An explanation of how the *stotra* and *śastra* are indirect auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), even though their sequence and proximity are not sublated):
If it is accepted that the roots *stu* and *śaṃs* have the meaning of "manifesting a quality-possessor" (*guṇin*) and thus serve the purpose of recollecting the quality-possessor,

then [this applies] to the two [verses]— "Abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ"— which are prescribed as the means for the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* within the sequence of the performance (*abhyāsa*) of the *māhendra-graha-yāga*.

Regarding the two [verses] "natvā" and "avamanye," since these Ṛgvedic mantras have no [inherent] meaning [for this context], they cannot possibly manifest Mahendra by virtue of having Indra as their indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, because Indra is not an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, his manifestation would be useless. Consequently, just as with the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantra, these would have to be displaced (*utkarṣa*) to that very context where Indra is the deity.

Thus, following the sequence of the repetitions of the cup-sacrifices (*grahayāga*) prescribed in the Yajurveda, the verses recited in the *uttaragrantha* within the Sāmaveda must be applied according to their respective order.

Among those mantras whose status as subsidiaries is understood through direct textual statement (*pāṭha*), there would arise the contingency of subverting the sequence for their acceptance as subsidiaries and the *stotra* to be accomplished by them.

Furthermore, in order to effect the state of being *kakubh* for the two following [verses], there is the contingency of subverting the proximity to the *māhendra* cup, because the *pragrathana* (interlacing) prescribed in proximity to the *māhendra* cup by the rule "he begins the foot again," etc., is not accepted as a subsidiary to that [cup]. Therefore, since it is improper to subvert [the rules] when it is possible to do so without subverting the weaker *krama* and *sannidhi*, if they were intended to manifest a quality, then because Indra and Mahendra share a single quality...

The meaning is that, because it is established that they manifest the qualities of the functions of Mahendra, it is proper that the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns serve as remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) by means of favoring those two [the deities].

(Justification that Indra-mantras do not reveal Mahendra by establishing that Indra and Mahendra are distinct deities: Now, it may be argued that since Indra himself, following the slaying of Vṛtra, acquired greatness, there is a Smṛti stating: "Because Indra became great, that is the Mahendra-hood of Mahendra. Thus, in the absence of evidence for a collective denotative power (*samudāya-śakti*), [Mahendra] must be understood as qualified by the attribute of greatness.

To dispel the doubt that—since the manifestation of Indra is possible even through the repeated recitation of mantras dedicated to Mahendra—there is no necessity for the displacement [of the mantra], he says:
"Otherwise... (itarathā).
In the statement “He takes the *māhendra* cup,” because the deity-taddhita suffix produced from the word *mahendra* denotes a substance qualified by deityhood (*devatātva*),
and because deityhood— defined in the usage of the elders as the state of being the intended recipient of a substance being offered— is impossible in the case of an unuttered referent,
one must establish that [Indra] is "great" after the slaying of Vṛtra in order to effect the connection with the deityhood called "intendedness" denoted by the taddhita suffix.

Because it would otherwise entail the contingency of the Veda being non-eternal, and because the suffix requires the capacity [of the base] for its own increase, the nominal stem *mahendra*—which denotes a distinct meaning through a collective function (*samudāyavṛtti*) without regard for the meanings of its constituent parts, much like the word *aśvakarṇa*—prescribes the status of deity (*devatātva*) for that very [deity] by means of the suffix. Consequently, according to the rule of the tenth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra], the very word found in the injunction must be used in the ritual recitations (*nigama*). Thus, the employment of synonyms such as *Śakra* and so forth is untenable.

The meaning is that, since it is utterly impossible for there to be an application of the term "pure Indra," its manifestation [as such] is untenable; therefore, consequences such as the loss of excellence (utkarṣa) are unavoidable.
(An examination of how, although the word *agni* in the verse "tvam hy agne" indicates *manotā*, the word *indra* in the present context would likewise result in indicating *Mahendra*;
and an examination of the purpose [of this indication].
[This is shown in the section] beginning with "manotā-stha."

Even though Agni and Soma are the deities in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), just as there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of Soma—his constant companion—in the word "Agni" within the mantra "For you, O Agni, are the first thinker," so too here there would be the contingency of indicating Indra in the word "Indra.
However, that [indication] is not appropriate here; for in that case (the *paśu* sacrifice), there is no contradiction with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).

On the contrary, the meaning is that although one might resort to [the mantra] here based on the force of the injunction, "Recite for the *manotā* while the oblation is being cut," which—by virtue of its capacity—indicates that the purpose is the recollection of the deity of the oblation, such a resort is improper in this case. This is because, even though there exists a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) indicating a general connection with the Indra-sacrifice mentioned in the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is impossible for this [mantra] to find a place there due to being preempted by other mantras recited within the sub-context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*) of that sacrifice; therefore, it must be displaced (*utkṛṣṭa*) by finding a place in an Indra-sacrifice outside the context. It is for this reason that it was stated [in the commentary] either "with the intention of displacement" or "due to the absence of a means of knowledge indicating a general connection."
The detailed exposition should be consulted in the Kaustubha.
He concludes the established doctrine with the words: "Therefore..."

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: in the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice, by the statement "the cups (*graha*) belong to Agni," the character of being dedicated to Agni is prescribed for all the cups.

In that context, since according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) the hymns (*stotra*) and recitations (*śastra*)—which by their original nature (*prakṛti*) have various deities—are obtained [for the *agniṣṭut*], they must be modified (*ūhya*) according to the respective deity because they serve to consecrate the deity. However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because they serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there is no modification; thus, it will be stated in the fourth quarter of the tenth book by the very sūtra: "Since the hymn and the recitation are actions (*karman*), there should be no change when the deity is different. Therefore, it has not been mentioned here.
Thus ends the sixth section concerning the Stotra and Śastra.

(B1) (Section 7 / [A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 7]) Having examined the two types of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) that enjoin subsidiary actions (*guṇakarman*) and principal actions (*pradhānakarman*), a third type of verbal suffix, which expresses [an action] incidentally (*prasaṅgāt*), is now examined.
It is held that even those verbal suffixes occurring in *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas* which are co-occurrent with words such as *yat* possess injunctive force (*vidhāyakatva*).

And even when there is attainment through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the conclusion that there is a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*) due to repetition being reached, [it is replied]: in passages such as "with which he worships the gods" (*devāṃśca yābhiryajate*) and "if both his oblations should meet with ruin" (*yasyobhayaṃ havirārtimārcchet*), it is clear that the word *yat* (which), by indicating what is already attained, acts as an obstacle to an injunction (*vidhi*) whose nature consists in making known what was previously unknown regarding its own object.

Thus, in cases such as "O Agnīdh, distribute the fires" (*agnīd agnīn vihareti*), the vocative case—which refers solely to an addressee who is present—contradicts an injunction that applies equally to both those who are present and those who are not. Furthermore, the first-person pronoun in expressions such as "I give" (*dāmīti*) contradicts an injunction consisting of the instigation of another to act. Therefore, because they cannot function as injunctive, it should be understood that those [words] occurring in the *mantras* serve as reminders (*smāraka*), while those occurring in the *brāhmaṇas* indicate the occasion (*nimitta*) through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). // 7 //
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the expressive nature of mantras.

(B2) [The demonstration that the subject matter concerns the verbal suffixes occurring in the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas associated with words such as *yad*: He states the connection (*saṅgati*) for the subsequent discussion: "guṇakarma" (and so forth).
"Expressive" (abhidhāyaka) means "reiterative" (anuvādaka).
This refers to a mantra-word from the Sūtras, which is characterized as a mere verb-form (ākhyāta) associated with words such as "yat" (that which).
It is not for the purpose of asserting that being a mantra depends on non-prescriptiveness and being a Brāhmaṇa depends on prescriptiveness;
for in passages such as "For the spring, the kapiñjala birds," there is prescriptiveness despite being a mantra,
and in the passage "Of whom both [the fire and the soma]...," there is non-prescriptiveness despite being a Brāhmaṇa.
Intending this, he shows that those [words] occurring in the Brāhmaṇas are also examples, just like those occurring in the mantras, by stating: "of those occurring in the mantras."
By the phrase "the word 'yat' and so forth," the inclusion of words such as those in the vocative case and the first person pronoun is intended.
"And the gods by which... (the meaning of this mantra and its place of application):
"And the gods."

“They do not perish; no thief can harm them; no enemy or distress can overcome them. With those [cows] by which one sacrifices to the gods and gives gifts, the master of the herd (gopati) shall long enjoy their company. Although this is the full extent of the mantra, only the third quarter is cited here with the intention of highlighting its relevance to the present context. Those cows with which one sacrifices and those which one gives away—those cows do not perish, nor does a thief harm or steal them.

Neither does the affliction or calamity caused by a limbless enemy dare to overcome or oppress him; and the owner of the cow, together with them, for a long time—*jyok* meaning for a long duration—is joined with or endowed with the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*).
This is the meaning of the mantra for the purpose of praising the cow.

This [mantra] is employed as the *yājyā* (offering verse) in the *devī-haviḥ-yāga*, which is an oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) offered to the goddesses, following the animal cake-offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) belonging to the *ānubandhya* sacrifice, where the deity is the Cow.
(An exposition on how *yad* and other such particles obstruct the injunctive power):

Nor should it be argued that because the word *yat* indicates the established nature (*siddhatā*) of its own referent alone, an injunction is possible even when there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the cow's essential form, since that [form] serves as the means (*sādhana*).

This is because, in common usage—as seen in examples such as "He who cooks, he eats"—the word *tat* is observed to function as a restatement of what is already obtained by the preceding *yat*. Therefore, here too...

In the statement "those who give cows do not perish," because the word *yat* (which) is employed in conjunction with the word *tat* (that), it is understood as a reference to something already established; thus, since the sacrifice and the gift are perceived as being restatements of what is already accomplished, they cannot be the objects of an injunction (*vidheya*).

For this very reason, even in cases where [the agent] is mentioned in conjunction with the agent (*kartṛ*), since the status of being an agent—in the form of being the substratum of an action—is understood as already established, the action itself is also understood as established, and therefore it lacks the status of being an object of an injunction.

Even this being the case, if attainment were not possible even when examined in any way whatsoever, then— as in the case of "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (yad āgneyo ’ṣṭākapāla)— one would have to resort to the injunctive function of the injunction as a last resort, by accepting that it merely indicates the establishment of its own primary meaning;
but this is not the case.
The meaning is that [the performance] is already established through various methods such as the sacrifice of divine substances (godravyaka) and the giving of gifts (dāna).
Likewise, since the word "yadi" (if) also has the sense of indicating a causal condition (nimitta), it should be understood as signifying the attainment [of the action] co-occurring with itself.

Similarly, the injunction "agnīd" [addressed] by the speaker toward the listener is not possible in the Veda because of the absence of a speaker; therefore, the meaning is that it is merely a restatement (anuvādaka) of the Adhvaryu being the speaker.

For this very reason, even the *loṭ* suffix here does not signify an extraordinary injunction (*alaukika-vidhi*), but rather, as per the rule "the *kṛtya* suffixes [are used] for command (*praiṣa*), permission (*atisarga*), and the proper time (*prāptakāla*)," it should be understood as signifying a command (*praiṣa*) alone. It should be observed that where there is the use of the optative (*liṅ*) such as "I would give" (*ahaṃ dadyām*) even in the first person— wherein the instigation (*pravartanā*) resides in oneself— that should be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as having the sense of an instigation residing in oneself.
(An examination of the utility of words such as *yadā* which obstruct the force of an injunction:

Nor, in that case, are they purposeless; for those [words] occurring in connection with the Brāhmaṇas and so forth are useful insofar as they establish [the action] as a condition (*nimitta*) through syntactic unity with other finite verbs.

Regarding those [mantras] contained within the *mantra* category, however, since they lack utility as things to be performed (*vidheya*) or as providers of the objective referent (*uddeśya*), and since— by way of being mere praises (*stāvaka*)—

they stand at a distance such that there is no syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatā*) and thus no logical inconsistency, even if one were to assume a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of mere praise through the mode of word-meaning (*padārtha-vidhā*), there can be no utility because syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*) is also impossible due to the absence of completion in the cognition of their own literal meaning.

Nevertheless, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) and according to the principle of the section on mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*), he states that it is solely as a reminder (*smāraka*), saying: "Therefore... (*ataḥ*).
The purpose has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the expressive nature of mantras.

(B1) (Section 8 / [A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 8]) Regarding those [Vedic texts] that enjoin them, the term *mantra* is applied; following upon the discussion of mantras, the definition of a mantra is stated in order to determine the meaning of the word *mantra* as used in the Veda—such as in the passage, "O Ahibudhnya, guard my mantra"—[the definition being]: that in which there arises for those who are experts a presentation (*upasthiti*) characterized by being denotable by the word *mantra*, related [to the object] by the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*), is a *mantra*.
And as for the delimitor of the denotability [of the term "mantra"], it is either the universal *mantratva* or an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*); this is another matter. // 8 //
Thus ends the eighth section, concerning the characteristics of mantras.
(B2) (An examination of the incidental connection with the preceding section):

Since the word *mantra* was employed in the previous section even as a mere secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), the definition of the *mantra* now presented is introduced; thus he shows the incidental connection by stating, "on account of the occasion provided by the *mantra*."

(An exposition establishing that being the object of common usage as having the nature of a mantra is indeed the definition of a mantra, preceded by an investigation into the connection with the treatise):

Since it is declared at the outset of the treatise that an investigation into the meaning of Vedic words must be undertaken just like an investigation into the meaning of sentences, the term *ahirbudhnya* is stated here to indicate the connection with the treatise by demonstrating its status as a Vedic word, and thereby to suggest the undertaking of that [investigation].
"Ahirbudhnya is Rudra," say the authors of the Prakāśa;
others say it is the domestic fire (āvasathya).
By the word "that" (tat), one refers back to the designation mentioned in the preceding section, and that designation is the impeller (codaka) and the motivator (prayojaka).

Although the definition of a mantra as "that which reveals its meaning at the time of ritual application" (*arthaprakāśakatva*) appears in the Sūtra through the analysis of the *bahuvrīhi* compound *yeṣām*, it is nonetheless untenable as stated. For there is an under-extension (*avyāpti*) to those passages recited in the Mantra-Section, such as "One should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds for Spring," which, despite being mantras, lack the quality of revealing meaning because they function as injunctions. Furthermore, there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) since, in the fifth book [of the Mīmāṃsā], it is accepted that even a Brāhmaṇa passage may serve as a reminder (*smāraka*) in the absence of a mantra. Thus, the literal formulation is incorrect.
Setting aside that [definition], he states the definition otherwise, beginning with "where" (yatra).

(Conclusion by means of defining the delimitor of the denotability of the word "mantra," demonstrating that the stated definition of mantra is grounded in the Sūtras, and refuting definitions such as "extreme brevity" [atyantatva] and so forth):

Now, an objection is raised: if the delimitors of the denotability of the word "mantra" are not ascertained, it is impossible to have a certain cognition in which "being denotable" is the qualifier; therefore, the definition is not established.

For "mantratva" (the nature of being a mantra) is not a genus (*jāti*); for if it were so, there would result the confusion (*sāṅkarya*) of *mantratva* with other categories such as "being an injunction" (*vidhitva*), and because it is impossible for multiple individual phonemes to exist simultaneously, *mantratva* could never be manifested.
Nor is it a limiting adjunct (upādhi);
therefore, how can this be the definition? To this, he says: "and that which delimits the denotability" (vācyatāvacchedaka).

Since *mantratva* (the nature of being a mantra) is accepted as being of the nature of an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), just like *devatātva* (the nature of being a deity), and since it is determined that [the word "mantra"] denotes [the object] in that form, it is logically consistent for the state of being the object of a determinative cognition having that [adjunct] as its qualifier (*tatprakārakaniścayaviṣayatva*) to constitute the definition. Therefore, the intention is that the term "mantra" in the Sūtra refers precisely to the mantras themselves; thus, the designation "mantra" used in reference to those who prompt the recitation of mantras—that is, those who study the mantras—is based on the application of the word "mantra" to denote that which is denoted by the word "mantra. As for those definitions such as "ending in *as*" and so forth, which were formulated by the author of the Vṛtti—

These [definitions] are to be understood as being intended merely to state the essential nature [of the deity], and not as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); for they would fail to apply [as definitions]—as seen in the ancient treatises—because in the mantra "O steed, you are to be praised and worshipped," the term *asi* occurs in the middle, whereas in the mantra "For that I entreat you for the sake of Brahman," the term *tvām* occurs in the middle, and thus the definition would be over-narrow (*avyāpti*).
This and other such points are to be found in the works of the ancients.

Regarding the purpose (*prayojana*): according to the maxim of the experts—"In cases of objection, exception, attainment, and the function of a definition, the purpose need not be stated, as also that which one proceeds to do after having performed [something else]"—since the very nature of the knowledge of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) is already evident, it need not be stated separately; thus, it was not mentioned.
Thus ends the eighth section, concerning the characteristics of mantras.

(B1) (Section 9 / [A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 9]) “These five oblations are indeed the Brāhmaṇas. For the sake of fully understanding the meaning of the word *brāhmaṇa* as employed in the Veda, its definition is also provided here by way of incidental discussion. The nature of a *brāhmaṇa* is simply being that portion of the Veda which is distinct from the *mantras*. 9.
Thus ends the ninth section concerning the characteristics of a Brāhmaṇa.

(B2) [Demonstrating that the definition of *brāhmaṇa* consists in being a Vedic sentence other than a *mantra*, by first determining the connection with the treatise (*śāstra*), and establishing that even *arthavādas* and *upaniṣads* are included within injunctions (*vidhi*):
Just as before, by investigating Vedic categories, he demonstrates the connection with the treatise and the immediate topical connection (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*).

Although the definition of a *brāhmaṇa*—like the definition of a *mantra*—can indeed be stated as "that which is the object of the well-known usage of the term *brāhmaṇa* among experts," [he proceeds further...]

Otherwise, since a definition of mantra such as "that which is a Veda other than the Brāhmaṇas" is also possible, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*).
Nevertheless, following the maxim that "an independent seer cannot be constrained," he shows the very definition stated by the author of the Sūtras: "these are the Brāhmaṇas."

In reality, however, since the definition is established by the mere statement "the remainder is the Brāhmaṇa," the use of the term "word" (śabda) indicates that the previously stated definition is rooted in the usage of experts; thus, there is no lack of a decisive criterion—this is how it should be understood. [The phrase] "other than the mantras" [is used].

Since it is stated that the Veda consists of two groups—namely, the Brāhmaṇas and the Mantras—the inclusion of the Arthavādas, the injunctions (vidhis), and the Upaniṣads within the second group is indicated by the defining characteristic of being distinct from the Mantras. Furthermore, the definitions of these categories as stated by the author of the Vṛtti have already been refuted in the Bhāṣya and other works; they should be examined there.
Thus ends the ninth section concerning the characteristics of a Brāhmaṇa.
(B1) (10. Adhikaraṇa / A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 10) Although the *ūha*, *pravara*, and *nāmadheya* [terms] are to be uttered at the time of performance for the purpose of recalling their meaning,

and although they form a single syntactical unit with the mantra words, because they are not recited in their own form in the Veda and are not the object of the traditional knowledge of the learned (*abhiyukta*), [they are not considered mantras].
In the event of their failure, there is no expiation caused by the failure of the mantra; rather, it is only caused by the failure of the subsidiary element (aṅga). // 10 //
Thus ends the tenth section concerning the non-modifiability of mantras.

(B2) [Connection by way of exception with the preceding section; the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [certain passages] are mantras, preceded by a definition of the nature of *ūha*, *pravara*, and *nāman*:

Previously, when the twofold division of the Veda was stated, it was accepted that *ūha* and so forth are also Vedic because they are cognizable through inference and other means. In that case, since they lack the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*), they do not possess the status of *brāhmaṇa*; therefore, by elimination—or rather, due to a misconception regarding the previously stated definition consisting in the manifestation of meaning at the time of performance—[the following argument arises].
Or, since [the status of] being a mantra would have been established, this exception (*apavāda*) is now made.
And by implication, it is established that the two-fold division pertains to the subject matter of the Vedas.

Thus, without explicitly stating the connection as an exception because it is self-evident, he briefly indicates the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) after first demonstrating the scope of the subject, beginning with the word "it might be thought" (*ūha*).

"Modification (*ūha*) is declared to be the application in a modified ritual (*vikṛti*) of a different word-substitute for a primary word-position, by way of its function as a distinct entity. Thus, *ūha* refers to the employment of words such as "Sūrya" in place of words such as "Agni" within mantras during a modified ritual.
Furthermore, by virtue of injunctions such as "one should choose a lineage-ancestor (*ārṣeya*)," the lineage is proclaimed using names such as "Kāśyapa," "Vatsa," or "Naidhruva."
That is the *pravara*.

In the *subrahmaṇyā* recitation, where— according to the injunction that "the word denoting the sacrificer’s father and so forth, such as 'the son of Devadattaśarman sacrifices,' is used to take the name of the sacrificer"—
that name is employed.
And [this applies] when there is syntactic unity with the words of the mantra.

Otherwise, even those mantras that form a single syntactical unit with non-mantric [words] would lose their status as mantras—just like the syllables of a mantra that form a single syntactical unit with a verse (śloka); this is the meaning.
(The conclusion that *ūha* and other such modifications are not mantras, because being syntactically unified with a mantra or revealing meaning are not the defining criteria for being a mantra.
He states the established conclusion: "By its own nature... (*svarūpeṇa*).
The meaning is that because they have not been recited at the time of Vedic study (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*), there is an absence of established authority among those who are diligent in the tradition.
For this very reason, there is no fault even if these [mantras] lack a recitation preceded by the correct accents (*svara*). This is expressed by the phrase "not of these" (*naiṣām*).
Nor does it follow that those [syllables] which form a single syntactical unit with it lose their status as *mantras*;
for even when a single word is omitted, there is the perception of the non-destruction of the *mantra*, due to the very firm recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that same *mantra*.
For this very reason, even when the protracted pronunciation (*pluti*) occurs at the end of a *yājyā*, there is no loss of its status as a *mantra*.

However, in the case of the syllables of a mantra that have attained syntactic unity with a verse (*śloka*) or similar text, such [mantra-status] does not occur precisely because of the absence of established usage (*prasiddhi*).

And thus, even in the case of syntactic unity with a mantra—as in the phrase *iṣe tvā*, where the word *chinadmi* is supplied as an ellipsis—there is no status as a mantra due to the lack of syntactic unity with a [complete] mantra;
nor is there the quality of manifesting meaning, just as in the case of the mantra "upāvartadhvam," which takes the place of what was obtained by the original context.

The meaning is that even in the case of the "sound of the chariot" (rathaghoṣa) prescribed by the statement in the Mahāvrata ritual, "He begins the Māhendra hymn with the sound of the chariot," there is a deviation from the definition because of its existence [as sound] without being a mantra; therefore, they do not possess the nature of a mantra by that alone.

(The refutation of the status of *mantra* for the word *āpadaḥ* as recited in injunctive sentences, and for specific words in place of the word *asau*— such as "this sacrificer hopes for long life"— in the formula *āyur āśāste yajamāno 'sau*; and the determination of the purpose of the prima facie and final positions.)

And regarding this point in the *Vārttika*: it was stated that in the injunctive sentence, "one should sing having made the word *irā* into *aira*," the status of being a *mantra* certainly exists because it is recorded as being included within a *taddhita* derivative; however, since even that which is recorded in the *Brāhmaṇa* for the purpose of singing does not fall within the scope of the conventional usage of the term *mantra*, it cannot be considered a *mantra*.

Even if one were to somehow admit its recitation in the *Mantrakāṇḍa* under the heading of that injunction, because only the word *aira* is actually recited there, it is impossible for the word *irā* to be so recited; thus, [the statement] is made for the sake of emphasis.

Furthermore, regarding the mantra connected with a pronoun, such as "This sacrificer prays: *asau* [that one] has been pressed," although at the time of private recitation (*svādhyāya*) and so forth the form of the mantra is indeed *asau*, at the time of the ritual performance one must read the specific name such as "Devadatta" in place of that word; nevertheless, because the particulars are infinite and cannot be recited simultaneously, the essential form of the name exists in the manner of a pronoun within the recited text. Thus, since the position is not empty, it is indeed possible to determine the nature of the mantra.
It has been stated that whatever word is inserted here constitutes a mantra because it serves as a basis for chanting;
however, since those specific words are not recited in their own form, it is impossible for them to be the objects of established usage.

Furthermore, because the recitation of pronouns is neither redundant—given its utility during the time of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) or during formal recitations (*pārāyaṇa*) and the like—nor otherwise [meaningless].

In the *Kaustubha*, it is stated that [the mention of the *ṛṣis*] in the *subrahmaṇyā-nigada* during the selection of the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya-varaṇa*) must necessarily result in a specific application, as its general form would otherwise be untenable; furthermore, since the *pravara* and other elements are also enjoined by injunction, their status as *mantras* would be unavoidable.

For this very reason, in the *Vārtika*, having raised the objection that words used in the sense of a pronoun (*sarvanāmasthāna*) do not constitute *mantras*, the view of those who accept this as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*)—expressed by the phrase "some say it is so"—is also mentioned.

And for this reason, regarding the phrase "not for these," although the expiation for a failure of the mantra (*mantrabhreṣaprāyaścitta*) is the same in both views when there is a failure of the entire mantra composed of modified words (*ūhitapada*), in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the expiation occasioned by the failure of a mantra-word applies to the failure of the modified word alone. In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, even though it is included within the mantra, because it lacks the status of being a [standard] mantra-word, that expiation does not apply.
Rather, the meaning is that the expiation is for the cause of a deficiency in the constituent parts, whether known or unknown.
Thus ends the tenth section concerning the non-mantric nature of the *mūha* formulas.
(B1) (11th Adhikaraṇa / [A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 11]) Of them.

When the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*), such as being a mantra, has been defined, its subordinate properties (*avāntaradharma*)—such as being an *ṛc* and so forth—are defined by way of that very context for the purpose of fully understanding the referents of words like *ṛc* as employed in the Veda in the passage, "The *ṛcs*, the *sāmans*, and the *yajus*.
Just as there is a fixed structure of quarters (*pādavyavasthā*), so too is the nature of an *ṛc* defined as being a mantra. (11)
Thus ends the eleventh section concerning the definition of a Ṛc verse.

(B2) (The definition of the *ṛc*: Mantric status [is established] by means of the force of the context of the majority of readings, the purpose, and the meter, just as the division into quarters [of a verse] is determined; this is the determination of the definition of an *ṛc*.)

Although the definition was stated together with the inclusion of the reason "by virtue of the sense," nevertheless, with the intention that the definition is valid even without entering into that [reason] because it is faultless, he states the definition of *ṛc*: "that which possesses the arrangement of quarters."

By stating that [the definition] consists of being a mantra as indicated by the word "tat" (that) occurring in the Sūtra, the over-extension [of the definition] to verses such as the *Śloka* is shown to be excluded.

Furthermore, this division into quarters (*pādavyavasthā*) occurs in the case of "agnim īḷe purohitam," where, even though the meaning of the *ṛc* is not yet complete, it is established by the force of the sense (*arthavaśāt*) by taking the meaning of an intermediate sentence.

Similarly, for the other two quarters as well, there is semantic significance through the connection (*anuṣaṅga*) with the verbal form "īḷe. Thus, the phrase "by the force of the sense" (*arthavaśena*), although explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra, is also an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of other grounds such as the meter (*vṛtta*).
This has been stated in the *Prātiśākhya*: "The *prāya*, the meaning, and the *vṛtta*—these are the causes for the knowledge of the *pāda*.

The meaning of this is explained in its commentary (*bhāṣya*) as follows: *prāya* refers to the general context of recitation (*prāyapāṭha*), while *vṛtta* refers to the meter, such as in the rule: "Of these [two], in the *varṣiṣṭha* and *aniṣṭha* [metres], the penultimate syllable is light."
Regarding the other two [types of feet], the *Prātiśākhya* states: "The wise know that in those [feet] the same rule applies to the meters.
Among these feet, in the longest and shortest—namely, those with twelve and eight syllables respectively—the penultimate syllable is light (*laghu*).

For example, in the twelve-syllable foot "pradevam acchā madhumanta indavaḥ," the letter *da*, being the penultimate, is light; thus, it should be understood that the foot ends with its final syllable.

For example, in the verse "agnim īle," the penultimate syllable is light (*laghu*), and the foot consists of the syllables ending with that one. However, in the other two cases—those consisting of ten and eleven syllables—the penultimate syllable is heavy (*guru*), and the foot consists of that very final syllable.
For instance, in the ten-syllable foot "śrudhī havam vipipānasyādreḥ," the syllable *syā* is heavy.

For example, in the verse "pibā somam abhi yam ugratarda," within the eleven-syllable foot, because the syllable *da* exists as a conjunct consonant (*saṃyuktākṣara*), the preceding syllable is heavy, and thus the syllable *ta* becomes heavy.
The meaning is that those two feet should be understood as ending with their final syllables.
As for the illustrative example from the *prāyapāṭha*, in the *traiṣṭubha* foot of the verse "gornaparvaviradātiraśce," an eleven-syllable count is required.
However, let there be a ten-syllable structure in this *traiṣṭubha* hymn; for in this hymn, the preceding and following words possess eleven syllables.
The reason for this is simply the reading of the majority (*prāyapāṭha*).
As for the illustrative example of the meaning, it has already been stated.
Furthermore, for one who is disgusted [by a deficiency], water is offered to the deity;

this applies even when there is a shortage of one syllable in a *triṣṭubh* foot due to the requirements of the sense, as in the case of the phrase “*tam u trā indraṃ na rejāmānam*” (*Ṛgveda* 10.99.4), where despite the slight discrepancy, the word *na* is treated as the end of the foot.
Likewise: “*evā devān indro vivye nṝn praścyautnena maghavā satyarādhāḥ*. (*Ṛgveda* 6.25.8)

In the verse "viśvettā te harivo śacīvobhiturāsaḥ svayaśo gṛṇanti," the two feet in the second half-verse (*uttarārdharca*) consist of ten syllables each. However, in the first half-verse (*pūrvārdharca*), the end of the foot occurs at the word *nṝn* due to the requirements of the sense (*arthavaśena*). This is because, although the penultimate syllable of *nṝn* would be heavy according to the rules of meter (*vṛtta*), the sense (*artha*) takes precedence over the meter in this instance.

When the rule regarding the word *nṛn* at the end of a quarter-verse (*pāda*) is encountered, the quarter-verse ending in *pre* is determined by the fact that it is read in proximity to two ten-syllable quarters occurring in the second half of the verse; this is because the context of meaning is more powerful [than mere position].
As it is stated in the *Prātiśākhya*: "But when there is a conjunction of specific [rules], the preceding [rule] takes precedence over the following."
Thus, the meaning is that when there is a conflict between the *prāya* (preponderance) and the *vṛtta* (metre), each preceding factor is stronger and each succeeding one is weaker.

By this, that which was stated in the Vārttika regarding the passage "Agni by the ancient seers," namely that because no verb is supplied there, the determination [of the meaning] occurs by force of the metre since the sense remains incomplete—that too has been explained.

As for the explanation offered by the author of the Nyāyasudhā and others, who interpret the word *vṛtta* in the Vārttika as being due to the balance of light and heavy syllables by force of the metre: [this is refuted by the above].
That is incorrect,
because the word *vṛtta* occurring in the Vārttika can be reasonably understood as having the meaning of *vṛtta* (metre) as stated in the Prātiśākhya shown previously;
for there is no evidence to support an interpretation that takes it to mean a "syllable" (*vṛtta*) characterized by being light or heavy.

For this very reason, although the end of the quarter [of the verse] would have been reached at "iḍya" by virtue of the force of the meaning—which is stronger than the metrical form—the determination of the quarter's boundary is properly established by the reading of the eight syllables beginning with "agnim īle," which are stronger than the mere force of the meaning.

In the Vārttika, the mention of the metrical form is not intended to exclude the end of the quarter at "iḍya," but rather to address the expectation: "The end of the quarter does not occur at 'ṛṣibhiḥ' due to the force of the meaning; by what, then, does it occur?"
This [discussion] is intended merely as a supporting argument.

This being the case, it should be understood that in examples such as *agnim īle*, even when there is a combination of the causes for the establishment of metrical feet—namely, the meaning of the verse (*vṛtta*), the number of syllables (*akṣara-saṅkhyā*), and the definitions of meter (*chandas*)—there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, although this was not required by the root text, it has been explained here incidentally for the purpose of correcting the examples shown in the Kaustubha.
Thus ends the eleventh section concerning the definition of a *ṛc*.

(B1) (Section 12 / [A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 12]) "In songs, that is the designation" (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.36). The state of being a *sāman* is the quality of being sung, which stands in a relationship of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the state of being a mantra. 12.
Thus ends the twelfth section concerning the definition of Sāman.

(B2) (The definition of *sāman*—namely, that the word *sāman* refers to chanting—and the demonstration that there is no tautology between this [seventh book] and the two preceding sections, the section on *sāptamika-adhikaraṇa* and the section on *ākṛti*:

here too, in this sūtra, by the recurrence of the word "of them" (*teṣām*), the status of being contained within a mantra is obtained; thus, he states the definition of *sāman*, which is based on the well-known usage of experts and supported by reasoning, as follows: "In the state of being a mantra... (*mantratve...*) .
Therefore, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to worldly songs (*laukikagīti*).
Although experts employ the term for a *ṛc* verse qualified by melody, nevertheless: "Where a thing is understood as qualified by a single, indivisible word..."

By the principle stated in the Vārttika— "In all such cases, the denotability of the qualifier arises"— and by the maxim that "that which is not grasped as a qualifier [cannot be grasped as the qualified]," since the manifestation of the *ṛc* verses can be established even through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth— just as their individual instances (*vyakti*) are manifested— the author of the Sūtras has here adopted the position that the word denotes the melody (*gīti*) acting as a qualifier, which was to be established in the seventh book with greater parsimony (*lāghava*), following the maxim of looking ahead to what is yet to come (*anāgatāvekṣaṇanyāya*).
Therefore, there is no tautology with that [previous argument].
For there is no purpose in establishing here that [the word "sāman"] denotes merely the melody (*gīti*);
for even by its denoting a *ṛc* verse qualified by melody, the distinction from the *ṛk* and so forth is established.

However, in the seventh [book], regarding the injunction "he sings the Rathantara on the Kavatī verses" with respect to the verse beginning "kayā naścitra," if the word *rathantara* were taken as denoting the entire Ṛg-verse, it would be impossible for the Ṛg-verse to serve as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the singing. Therefore, for fear that this would necessitate assuming a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the effect in the word *kavatī*, it is established that the word denotes the melody alone; this is employed for the purpose of establishing the extension (*atideśa*) of the Rathantara melody produced in the Abhīvartī [verse].

It should be noted that there is no redundancy with the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (the section on generic form), because what was established there is stated here as an accepted premise (*siddhavatkāra*), and because the seventh book's section also serves the purpose of explaining the utility of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*.
Although it has been established that words such as *rathantara* denote the melody (*gīti*), this was not established for the word *sāman*;

nevertheless, once it is established that specific denoting words denote the melody, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the general term *sāman* in expressions such as "the *rathantara* is a *sāman*" becomes possible only by virtue of the word *sāman* denoting the general category of melody. It is with this intention that there is no contradiction in stating that [this point] is established in the seventh [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra].
Thus ends the twelfth section concerning the definition of the Sāman.
(B1) (13th Topic /) (a.2 pā.1 adhi.13) Regarding "roṣe": the term *yajus* refers to the state of being a *yajus*, which is the nature of a mantra distinct from *ṛk* and *sāman*.
Since this nature exists even in the *stobha* syllables, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). // 13 //
Thus ends the thirteenth section concerning the definition of the Yajus-mantras.
(B2) (The definition of a Yajus mantra): By employing the term "mantra-ness," he excludes the Brāhmaṇa and states the definition of a Yajus as follows: "The Ṛk and the Sāman... etc.
Regarding the definition stated by the Easterners, he avoids the consequence of over-extension to the *stobha* syllables by accepting it as a desired outcome, stating: "The *stobha*... etc.

Since there is no need for exclusion even though "close-reading" (*praśliṣṭapaṭhitatva*) has been included in the root texts, and since it lacks metrical foot-binding (*pādabandha*), it serves merely to describe the essential nature of a mantra as being composed of syllables;
thus ends the thirteenth section concerning the definition of a Yajus-mantra.

(B1) (14th Adhikaraṇa / [A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 14]) The Nigada should indeed be a fourth [class], because of its distinct property; for there is a difference from the Yajus-mantras due to the distinction of names—
since the rule "the Yajus is whispered, the Nigada is loud" establishes a difference in contradictory properties— and because of the difference in properties.

This being the position reached—since the Veda mentions only these three distinct types of mantras in the passage, “The Ṛcs, the Sāmans, and the Yajuses,” and because of the indicative mark (liṅga) stating, “This indeed is a mantra that has become a *nigada*; therefore it is a *yajus*”—the *nigadas* are nothing other than *yajus*. As for their specific designation (*saṃjñā*), it is justified even though there is no difference [in essence], according to the maxim of the “Brahmin mendicants” (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka*).
Furthermore, the state of being a *nigada* is a subordinate property (*avāntaradharma*) of the *yajus*, and not simply the state of being recited in a voice other than the *upāṃśu* (whispered) tone;
for this would result in the fallacy of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding those *nigadas* such as "namaḥ pravaktre," which are recited in the *upāṃśu* tone.
Nor does a difference [in classification] follow from a difference in properties.
Because the loudness specifically prescribed [for the *nigada*] leads to the conclusion that the general prescription of low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) is intended for another purpose;

and because, according to your own view, a restriction is necessary since it will be stated later that the rule "the *yajus* is to be recited low-voiced" prescribes low-voiced recitation for all rites enjoined in the Yajurveda in accordance with the introductory statement regarding the Veda—

therefore, just as the word *yajus* would have to be taken as indicating the Veda by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) due to the force of the introduction, so too would the word *nigada* result in indicating the Yajurveda, leading to the undesirable consequence of an option between two conflicting ritual properties (*dharma*) within a single rite.

Because the opening statement, "The Yajurveda [arose] from Vāyu," functions as an indicator of the intended meaning (tātparya) through a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) applied specifically to the word *yajus*;
otherwise, why would he not have said, "The Nigada-veda [arose] from Vāyu"?

Therefore, the rule prescribing loudness—stated independently as "one should recite the Nigadas loudly"—is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding loudness, directed toward those Nigadas that are distinct from those for which specific rules have already been prescribed.

For in those cases, although the cessation of whispering (*upāṃśutva*) occurs by virtue of the purpose consisting in the communication of others, and although various pitches such as *mandra* and so forth would otherwise apply, the restriction to the high pitch (*uccaiṣṭva*) is not untenable.

Therefore, in the event of a failure (*bhreṣa*) regarding the *nigada*, the expiation for a failure of a *yajus* applies; or else, in the case of the *āśvina* cup and others, there is the recitation of the *pāriplava* narrative. // 13 //
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning the consecration by means of the Nigada-formula.
(B2) [The connection by way of objection (*ākṣepasaṅgati*): the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the *nigadas* constitute a distinct class of *yajus* due to the difference in designation.

Since the previous sūtra—“In the remainder, they are called *yajus*” (Jaimini 2.1.37)—established the division of *yajus* as being distinct from *ṛk* and *sāman*, thereby declaring the threefold nature of mantras, the present section introduces its prima facie view by means of an objection against that. Therefore, because this connection by way of objection is self-evident, it is not explicitly stated here.
Regarding those [mantras] designated as *nigada*:
And these [nigadas], such as "O Agnidh, spread the fires," are generally for the purpose of addressing others;

or rather, the nigada should be the fourth [type of Vedic text] because of its specific characteristics (dharmaviśeṣāt). This is stated in the sūtra of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.38, where by the word *dharmaviśeṣāt*, the difference in characteristics such as loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*) is presented as the primary reason for the prima facie view.

And because of the designation (*vyapadeśāt*), as stated in the second sūtra (Jaimini 2.1.39), although the difference in names is indicated there as being the cause [of the distinction between the Vedas], in the third section on sentences (*tārtīyavākyādhikaraṇa*)— specifically in the sūtra "Or rather, it is the Veda, because of the observation of the majority" (*vedo vā prāyadarśanāt*)— the status of qualities such as *upāṃśutva* (whispering) as belonging to the respective mantras is rejected, and instead their status as qualities of the rites prescribed in those respective Vedas is established.

Since that [reason] which is contrary to what is about to be stated—the reason for the difference in the nature of the mantra—is presented as the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position regarding that very topic, it is understood to be a secondary supporting reason; whereas the latter reason alone is primary.
To indicate this, [the author], setting aside the order of the Sūtra, presents the second reason first because of its primacy: "Because of the difference in name" (saṃjñābhedāt).

The meaning is that there is a distinction [of the mantras] because they are treated with distinct designations such as "these are *nigadas*, these are *yajūṃṣi*," just like [the distinction between] *jyotis* and so forth.
[The term] "contradictory" (*vipratiṣiddha*)... [is used].

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by refuting the following possible justifications for the rule "with loud recitation" (*uccair-nigadena*): namely, that it overrides general injunctions, that it serves the purpose of communicating to others, or that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of loudness which would otherwise not apply. For, if the *nigadas* were merely *yajus* formulas, the rule prescribing loudness would be untenable because it would conflict with the requirement of whispering (*upāṃśutva*) that applies to all *yajus*. Even though an override (*bādha*) is possible through a specific injunction, it is improper to accept an override of the general statement in the form of a restrictive limitation (*saṃkoca-lakṣaṇa-bādha*), when the matter can be resolved by postulating a distinction in the application (*vṛtti-bheda*) within its own domain.
It is logical that the conceptualization of difference occurs by way of their very own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

Nor is it the case that—on the grounds that the injunction regarding *upāṃśu* (whispering) is restricted solely in accordance with the purpose of communicating to another, and that the rule "loudly with recitation" (*uccair nigadena*) is therefore a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) and thus does not subvert that difference—the sentence belonging to the Brāhmaṇa portion could also be restricted in accordance with the purpose of communicating to another as established by the authority of the mantra; for such a restriction of the sentence is untenable.

The meaning is that since there is no purpose for [passages] such as "Homage to the speaker" or "Kindled by the gods, kindled by the mind," which are intended merely to inform others, the word *uccais* must necessarily be an injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, since its status as an injunction is established even through the cognition of a distinction [between loud and low], it is not proper to restrict the sentence concerning *upāṃśu* (whispering).

"According to the maxim of the Brahmin and the wandering mendicant, since a difference in designation does not establish a difference [in the object], it is established as a settled doctrine that [the mantra] is indeed the mantra itself."

Regarding this, they say: "The Subrahmaṇyā is a Ṛc, Yajus, and Sāman"—this is indeed a mantra consisting of a question and answer. Because it is of the nature of a *nigada*, it is therefore a *yajus*. By means of the reason of the commonality of the term *nigada* in the Veda, the status of being a *yajus*—defined as a mantra distinct from *ṛc* and *sāman*—is established for the *Subrahmaṇyā-nigada*.

Consequently, since the nature of being a mantra is perceived even in other *nigadas* apart from that [specific one], without abandoning their status as *yajus*, the meaning is that they possess the very nature of *yajus*.

As for the difference in designation that was mentioned, it is possible even when Brahminhood exists—just as there is the distinct designation of "wandering mendicant"—and it is also established through the connection with the quality of being recited in prose even while Yajus-status exists; therefore, it does not conclusively prove a difference.
Thus he says: "Because it is a designation... and so forth.
(Refutation of the etymological derivation established by the ancients regarding the word *nigada*,

and the establishment of its conventional meaning): The ancients, because the root *gad* signifies "a collection of words not bound by metrical feet," and because the prefix *ni-* signifying excellence leads to the determination that it signifies "a collection of words bound by metrical feet being uttered loudly and without interruption," derived the name from the etymological sense of the parts— namely, "those which are thoroughly spoken (*nitarāṃ gadyante*)"— on account of the function of communicating to others.

Refuting that [objection], he establishes the designation by accepting it as a conventional term (*rūḍhi*), like the designations "horse-ear" (*aśvakarṇa*) and so forth, stating: "and the state of being a *nigada*."

And thus, by virtue of the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), the application of both designations to a single entity is justified; furthermore, the establishment of the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for the word *nigada* prior to the injunction regarding loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*) is easily accomplished—this is the meaning.
(The refutation of the suspicion that *yajus* is a distinct category from *nigada*, due to the fear of restricting the injunction "with the *yajus* in a whisper"):

For even in the view of one who asserts a distinction between *yajus* and [other mantras] on the grounds that it would result in the restriction or sublation of the injunction for whispering (*upāṃśutva*), there is likewise a rejection of whispering and other such qualities as being attributes of *yajus* alone; rather, they are established as attributes of all mantras prescribed in the *Yajurveda* that serve as auxiliaries to ritual acts.

Since it must be accepted according to the manner previously stated, even for *nigadas*, which are mantras that are auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of those rituals, they necessarily sublate the *upāṃśutva* (whispering) obtained by default; this must indeed be accepted even though the injunction "one should recite loudly with the *nigada*" (*uccair nigadena*) constitutes a separate rule. Therefore, it is not proper to assume a difference [between the two rules] out of fear of that [conflict]; rather, there is only a relationship of the sublated and the sublater (*bādhyabādhakatā*) based on the relation of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*). Thus he says: "Whisperingly with the *yajus*. (*upāṃśu yajuṣā*)

(An examination of the sublation of the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*), though established by syntactical connection (*vākya*), by the indicative power (*liṅga*) of loudness): In reality, however, because the low-voiced recitation is sublated by the indicative power itself— namely, the necessity of the effect consisting in communicating to another— the injunction for loudness does not incur the possibility of being that sublater,
even if one were to suspect that the purpose of communicating to another, as understood through indicative power, might be sublated by the low-voiced recitation understood from the Brāhmaṇa sentence.
