Nevertheless, there is no fault, because even though the inferential [recitation] is for the purpose of communicating with others and is thus primary, its sublation by the subordinate quality of low-voiced recitation is impossible; this is according to the principle that, between the relative strength of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the relative strength of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the latter is more authoritative.

Furthermore, the injunction for low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) does not apply at all to such a case. Even if a restriction of low-voiced recitation were made regarding a matter where an indefinite tone had been obtained, since loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*) itself is necessarily obtained in the case of a *nigada* due to the requirements of the ritual action, there is an absence of the condition of "obtaining what was previously indefinite. This and other points should be seen in the Kaustubha.

Regarding the phrase "with loud recitation" (*uccair-nigadena*), the ancient view—that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of loudness already established by necessity, and that "in a low voice with the *yajus*" (*upāṃśu-yajuṣā*) serves as its commendatory supplement (*arthavāda*)—is rejected. Instead, its status as an injunction (*vidhi*) is accepted, along with its purpose and the purposes of the preceding and following alternatives. As for the point that the ancients held loudness to be obtained solely through functional necessity (*kāryavaśāt*), such that "with loud recitation" is a restatement intended to praise the injunction "in a low voice with the *yajus*," even though loudness applies to *nigadas* in the form of *yajus* due to necessity, it does not apply to *yajus* in general.

Having stated that "being whispered (upāṃśutva) alone is appropriate," he refutes that [view] by means of the phrase "ataśca" (and therefore), because the necessity of it being an injunction is unavoidable.

In order to indicate that [the mantra] beginning with "namaḥ pravaktre" is not the subject of a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi), the phrase "other than what is specifically prescribed" (viśeṣavihitātirikta) was stated.
Its meaning is "other than the accents specifically prescribed for it.
[This refers to] the various [accents] such as *mandra* and so forth.

Since low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) would also optionally apply to *nigadas* that lack the purpose of communicating to others, it would be impossible to treat its mention as a mandatory restatement; therefore, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes those cases where low-voiced recitation is to be excluded, such as the *āśvina* cup and others.

The meaning is that the purpose [of the discussion] is as follows: according to the injunction, "One recites all the Ṛg-verses, all the Yajus-formulas, and all the Sāman-chants as the *pāriplava* in the *Vācastoma*," in the final position (*siddhānta*), the recitation of the *pāriplava* occurs within the *āśvinādi-śastra* of the *Vācastoma* sacrifice because it is included among the Yajus; whereas in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because it is not included therein, that recitation does not take place. This is the practical application.
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning the status of the *nigada* as a *yajus*.

(B1) (Section 15 / [A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 15]) The quality of being a *yajus* is present in as many words as suffice for syntactic unity (*vākyatva*), and not in a collection of sentences; for the latter is unfit for ritual application (*viniyoga*).
And the status of being a sentence (*vākyatva*) resides in as many [words] as there is unity of meaning (*arthaikatva*) and mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) when analyzed.
Unity of meaning, moreover, is the absence of more than one principal predicate (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) that would be the object of distinct cognitions; for anything else is difficult to define.
And this is because, in such cases as "Bring the cow," there is oneness of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) which serves as the primary qualificand;

and because, even though there are multiple productive urges in sentences concerning the *daśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *āmanahoma*, and so forth, they do not constitute objects of distinct cognitions;

and because, in the case of the *vrīhi* and *yava* injunctions, as well as in "May Bhaga divide you two," and so forth, although there is indeed a difference in the objects of cognition, [the productive urges remain one].
Because the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), which is the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*), is one, there is unity of meaning (*arthaikatva*).

Therefore, in that context, to exclude [the application of] the term "single sentence" (*ekavākyatva*) where it does not apply, the second qualification is added: that the two word-meanings being construed must possess a state of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) due to their non-construction [with anything else]. In the case of "I make a pleasant seat for thee; sit upon it," although there is expectancy due to non-construction [of the two parts with each other], they constitute separate sentences; therefore, the first qualification [unity of meaning] is required. // 1.5 //
Thus ends the fifteenth section, concerning the unity of the sentence.

(B2) (The demonstration, preceded by the refutation of the objection that this section is intended to determine the extent of *yajus* mantras recited in a continuous sequence— setting aside the mutual distinction between *ṛc* and *sāman*, which is well known through the tradition of teachers—

by means of the following argument: Since the internal distinctions among *ṛc*, *sāman*, and *yajus* have been established in connection with the introduction of mantras, and since a distinction is perceived from the Vedic text stating "the *ṛcs*, the *sāmans*, and the *yajus*" where these are spoken of in the plural, their mutual distinction must be determined as a consequence of that context.

In the case of the *ṛk* and *sāman*, because their distinction is easily understood from the instructions and recitations of teachers and students—such as "the *ṛk* here is of such length" and "the *sāman* here is of such length"—one may overlook the determination of their difference.

However, since the *yajus* are recited in a continuous (praśliṣṭa) manner, their distinction is difficult to discern; therefore, that which makes their difference known must necessarily be stated here.

Even though the distinction between *yajus* formulas is evident from the application of distinct introductory portions (*pratīka*), such as "With 'iṣe tvā' he cuts the branch," and "With 'ūrje tvā' he wipes it," and also from the rule stating that "the beginning of the subsequent [formula] marks the end of the preceding one," [the following is said].

Nevertheless, O Brāhmaṇa, since all such applications (viniyoga) are recorded [in the scriptures], and because an application stated in a Sūtra is rooted in the perception of a distinction [between parts], it cannot function as a defining characteristic independently of that [scriptural basis]; likewise, because the "Uttara" and so forth lack the status of being Veda, they cannot possess independent authority; and because a collection of words based on a single meaning constitutes a single sentence, this is the statement of the author of the Sūtras.
Intending to show that because it is rooted in reasoning, the nature of that reasoning must necessarily be stated, he says: "The state of being a Yajus."

(The definition of a single sentence is provided for the purpose of the final conclusion: "In as many words as there is sententiality, in that many there is the nature of a *yajus*")—this refers to the word "tasya" (of that).

The word "remainder" (*śeṣaḥ*) precedes the phrase "because of the inability to be employed [in ritual], due to the absence of the capacity to illuminate a single meaning" (*ekārthaprakāśakatvābhāvena*).

Thus, since the term *yajus* is derived from the root *yaj* with the suffix *usi*, and because this suffix belongs to the *uṇādi* class and is characterized by its irregularity (*bāhulakatvāt*), [the derivation is established].

Intending to show that the mention of "sentence-ness" (*vākyatva*) in the Sūtra is for the purpose of establishing the distinction between different *yajus* mantras—since a specific mantra used as a means of sacrifice is understood either through etymological derivation (*yoga*) from the word *yajus*, which denotes an instrument according to its application, or through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), and since such a mantra can only be employed when it constitutes a single sentence—he says:
"And sentence-ness... [referring to] "in those many... (*tāvatsu*).

And therefore, that which lacks such sentential character is a different sentence from the preceding one; the meaning is that such a Yajus, being of the nature of a sentence, should be understood as distinct from the preceding one.
(The difficulty of explaining the unity of meaning otherwise, and the validity of defining it through distinct cognitions, etc.
Now, what is this "unity of meaning"?

First of all, there is no unity of word-meanings, because those meanings are multiple within a sentence, since the sentence consists of their mutual relations and thus differs with each pair of word-meanings. Nor is there unity of purpose.

If, on the other hand, the unity of purpose consists in the unity of the remaining form (the *śeṣin*), then in cases such as "a sacrificial pap for Sūrya" (*sauryaṃ carum*), there would be a lack of unity of purpose because of multiplicity— namely, the sacrifice with respect to the substance and the deity, and the fruit with respect to that sacrifice. Similarly, in cases such as "for all [desires]" (*sarvebhyaḥ*), there would be that same lack of unity due to multiplicity.
Nor is it the unity of the purpose in the form of the principal qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*);

for in such cases as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," there would follow [the undesired consequence] because the principal qualificands—the various productive operations (*bhāvanā*) of the Āgneya and other rites—are distinct.
Nor is it the unity of the word that expresses the principal qualificand; [for that too is not the case].

Since the sentences concerning rice and barley, as well as those such as "May Bhaga divide for you two," do not result in a single meaning simply because of the difference in the words expressing them, it is necessary to include the qualification "having expectancy when being divided.
Therefore, since a single meaning is difficult to define, [the author] asks how this definition [of a sentence] is possible and says: "And 'single meaning'..."
Because there is an absence of being objects of distinct cognitions.
The meaning is that the definition is consistent because of the absence of the qualified [subject], which is itself occasioned by the absence of the qualifier.
(The significance of the qualification "being expectant of a word that is being analyzed"):
"Because of oneness."

The meaning is as follows: in passages such as “May life be perfected by the sacrifice; may breath be perfected by the sacrifice,” there is a multiplicity inherent in the *kḷptis* (perfections) mentioned in the injunction “He causes the sacrificer to recite the *kḷptis*,” which serves as an indicator for a plurality of *kḷptis*.

However, in the present case, since that [multiplicity] is absent regarding a plurality of divisions (*vibhāga*), and because the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of division is singular, [the action remains one].

In passages such as "syonaṃ te" (pleasant for thee), in order to exclude the state of having a single referent, [the definition of a sentence] is specified as "the absence of multiple primary subjects that are objects of distinct cognitions"; this is the determination of the syntactic connection (*saṃsamanvaya*).
Thus, it is called a "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*).

For in the case of the phrase "May Bhaga divide for you two," there is no expectancy toward the connection with "Aryaman for you two," because the requirement for completion is satisfied by the connection with "divides" (vibhajatu) which is contained within its own sentence.
Therefore, the meaning is that this [phrase] serves to exclude that [connection].
"Non-concomitance" (ananvaya) means:

The meaning is as follows: because the word "in that" (*tasmin*) depends on a previously mentioned referent, there is no syntactic connection with the first half-verse; furthermore, although the two [actions]—the making of the seat (*sadanakaraṇa*) and the establishing (*pratiṣṭhāpana*)—are expectant [of one another], they do not constitute a single object of cognition because they are not expressed by a single word.

Moreover, since the word "that" can be justified even as referring to the "seat" (*sadana*) mentioned in a separate sentence, it is impossible for the direct indicative power (*liṅga*) to be sublated by the sentence; thus, there is an absence of unity of purpose (*arthakatva*).

(An examination of the following: the pervasiveness of the status of being a *yajus* in its parts as well as in the whole; the refutation of the etymological definition of the word *yajus* as favored by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*; and the determination that the status of being a *veda* is pervasive only in the collection as a whole.)
And here, the nature of being a *yajus* is neither merely the state of being a means for a sacrifice,
nor is it a determinate attribute (*sakhaṇḍopādhi*) consisting in being a means for a sacrifice by way of manifesting its meaning; for otherwise, the same would apply to the *ṛc* as well.
Moreover, it consists of an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), just like the nature of being a mantra.
For this very reason, the word *yajus* is indeed a conventional term (*rūḍha*).

And although its occurrence is conceived as being distributed across all mantras—just as the status of being a Veda is—there is no contradiction in its subsistence even in a single part, because it serves as an illuminator through the application (*viniyoga*) of that very portion of the *yajus*.

Therefore, this very mantra indeed becomes a *nigada* (a loud recitation), and for that reason it is called a *yajus*. Consequently, the designation of *yajus* is also appropriate for a sentence in the form of a *subrahmaṇyā-nigada*.

By this [it is shown that]—since the word *yajus* is etymological (*yaugika*) in the sense of being a means to a sacrifice, just like the *sūktavāka*—even if no distinction is admitted at the time of private study (*svādhyāya*), a distinction is understood at the time of the ritual performance due to the difference in application (*viniyoga*); thus, it must be employed as distinct [from other mantras].

The claim by the author of the Nyāyasudhā that [the term *yajuṣ*] is etymological is refuted; furthermore, [if it were so], the status of being a *yajus* would not apply to the means of recitation such as *japa*.
Likewise, the nature of being a *mantra* is also fully established in a sentence alone.

Because of the employment of the word "mantra," its status as a Veda, however, does not apply to a single sentence; rather, due to the absence of the conventional usage "the Veda has been studied" when only one sentence is studied, it exists only as a collective whole (vyāsajyavṛtti).

Just as the prohibition against Śūdras hearing the Veda applies even upon hearing a single portion of the Veda, so too will be demonstrated in the Kaustubha under the section concerning the commencement of the Veda (vedopakramādhikaraṇa).

Therefore, the sense is that since the status of being a *yajus* resides solely in the sentence as a whole, a distinction [between types of *yajus*] is appropriate based on the distinctions between those sentences.
Thus ends the fifteenth section, concerning the unity of purpose.

(B1) (16th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.2 Pā.1 Adhi.16) "In the case of equal [independent] elements, there would be a split of the sentence" (Jaimini 2.1.47). However, where there is not that aforementioned state of having a requirement when divided— as in the case of these two [mantras], "ime tvā" and "ūrje tvā"— [there is no split].

Or, as in the case of "May life be perfected by the sacrifice; may breath be perfected by the sacrifice," and so forth—wherein, despite the unity of meaning, there is a division of mantras as in the case of "bhago vām" and other such formulas—how much more so when, according to their application (*viniyoga*), a difference in meaning is itself supported by authoritative evidence? In that case, there is simply no basis for the unity of the mantra.

For here, because of the difference in application (*viniyoga*)—namely, “He cuts the branch with ‘For sap, thee! and “He wipes it with ‘For strength, thee!’”—the primary substantive is indeed distinct, through the supply of the verbal action-pads “I cut thee for sap” and “I wipe thee for strength. Likewise, in the case of “He causes [the sacrificer] to recite the *kḷptis*,” there is a difference of meaning due to the comprehension of a plurality of *kḷptis* from the plural suffix.
Therefore, in this case, the distinction between *yajus* formulas is merely a counter-example to what was stated previously. // 16 //
Thus ends the sixteenth section, concerning the division of sentences (*vākyabheda*).

(B2) (Connection by way of counter-example with the preceding section, and summary of the subject sentence: Since the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established here in the form of a counter-example to what was stated previously, the author states the conclusion itself—preceded by the presentation of the subject matter—by way of connection through a counter-example, beginning with the words: "But where... (*yatratu*).

In the phrase "and so forth," the word "etcetera" includes everything up to the end of the passage: "May the apāna be perfected by the sacrifice; may the mind be perfected by the sacrifice; may speech be perfected by the sacrifice; may the self be perfected by the sacrifice; may the sacrifice be perfected by the sacrifice."

(i) [The manner of the prima facie argument of the ancients regarding the lack of distinct meaning and the absence of being *karaṇa-mantras* due to having a single unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), along with its refutation]: Here, the ancients [asserted] that the four-word phrase "iṣe tvorje tvā" as well as the collection of sentences beginning with "āyuryajñena kalpatām" [are not distinct mantras].

And although [the mantra] does not illuminate a meaning that is to be performed—just like the sound of a chariot—it is nonetheless logical for it to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, accepting its purpose as *adṛṣṭa* (unseen/transcendental), and by the parsimony of postulating a single *adṛṣṭa*, since all [mantras] can be construed with that purpose consisting of a single *adṛṣṭa* through mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) by virtue of having a single purpose and being mutually expectant when divided.

For this very reason, in cases such as "O winds, stay! (*vāyavaḥ stha*), where the sense "be swift-moving like the wind" is understood as serving the purpose of driving away the calves, there [occurs] the word *iṣe tvā* ending in the singular...

Because a connection with the name is impossible, the portion preceding "vāyavaḥ stha" alone possesses the status of a *yajus*. Although the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was established that there is a distinct *yajus* in the phrase "vāyavaḥ stha," nevertheless, because words such as "iṣe tvā" require an action, and because we observe their application [to specific rites] through expressions such as "he cuts" and "he wipes," [the entire sequence must be considered a single unit].

Since the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "chinadmi" (I cut) is necessary, and since the mantra is understood to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) there by means of the particle *iti*, and since that [instrumentality] is untenable without denotation, it is understood to reveal the act of cutting; thus, because an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*) is impossible in the first four words, and likewise, because even the mantras for longevity (*āyuḥ*) and so forth have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) by way of encouragement (*protsāhana*), an invisible purpose is impossible for them as well— therefore, that [objection] is not raised due to its utter triviality.
Therefore, it will be indicated by the word "mere" (*mātra*) in the concluding section of the discussion that this is merely a counter-example;
[this applies] even when there is unity of meaning.
(Regarding the rejection of the status of a single sentence for "iṣe tvā" and "ūrje tvā" on the grounds that they lack expectancy when divided, while assuming their unity of meaning):

Here, although there is an expectancy for an action, one might somehow intend to establish the aforementioned unity of meaning by supplying the single word "chinadmi" at the end of each of the four words;
however, this is merely stated as a counter-example based solely on the absence of expectancy when divided.
Thus, having granted that there is a single purpose, he has established the absence of syntactic unity (ekavākyatva) merely on the grounds of the absence of a subsequent member;
now he says "how much more so" (kimuta) to show that even that [single purpose] does not exist in the present case.
(Regarding the determination of the distinctness of the mantra and the determination of the purpose of the prima facie and final positions even in cases such as *āyuryajñena kalpatām*:
in the word *kḷptīḥ*, the term *kḷpti* does not refer to the word *kalpatām*, nor does it refer to the mantra containing that word.)
Because it would result in [the fault of] secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [the word *kalpaya*] rather refers to the action of fashioning (*kḷpti*) as its primary meaning.

And since, in that context, the plural number is heard, a plurality of the objects of fashioning is established; for the mere generality is not intended to be expressed, the words must express distinct actions of fashioning characterized by specific qualifiers such as "long life" (*āyus*) and so forth, in their particularized forms.
It has commenced.

Since the Adhvaryu’s activity is enjoined by the sense of the statement, "The Adhvaryu causes the sacrificer to recite," it is established that the plural number is prescribed for the purpose of the *kḷpti* (mental assignment) performed by the sacrificer as its agent.

Thus, even though they lack the status of being auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) in their own form, they are designated merely by way of being the objects of reference (*uddeśyatva*), and therefore [the deities] are [established].

Since it is possible for [the mantra] to be a constituent part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*) by virtue of its illuminating that [action], and since one gains a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) by assuming that passages such as "May life be perfected through sacrifice" illuminate the perfection characterized by life and so forth, there is indeed a difference of mantras even in that case, due to the difference in the specific objects being illuminated—namely, the specific forms qualified by life and so forth.
With this intention, he says: "In this way."
The purpose in the first example is that, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is a single simultaneous application of the four words.
In the Siddhānta, however, it concerns only two words.

Regarding the *kḷpti* mantra, in the case of an error in a single mantra, according to the Siddhānta there is a repetition of only that much, whereas according to the Pūrvapakṣa there is the recitation of the whole; this has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the sixteenth section concerning the division of sentences.
(B1) (Section 17 / [A.2 Pāda 1 Adhikaraṇa 17]) Where a supplementary portion (*śeṣa*) is recited immediately after the first of many [verses] that require a supplement—
as, for example, the supplement beginning with "tanūr varṣiṣṭhā" is recited immediately after "yā te agne ayāśayā"— [that former verse is the *prakaraṇa*].
The two subsequent mantras are: "O Agni, that [form] of yours which dwells in the dust," and "O Agni, that [form] of yours which dwells in the flame.
In this regard, for these two [mantras] which require a supplement, this very supplement is to be supplied.
But a worldly [meaning] is not supplied by ellipsis, because it has not been established [by the text];
nor is it the case that something fixed in one place cannot be brought over to another.
This is because it is recorded as being for the sake of all [the subsequent mantras].
Nor should one suspect that its recording is for the sake of the first mantra alone, since it is recited in a position where it is required immediately after that first mantra;
for there is no difference between the two cases regarding expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and semantic fitness (*yogyatā*).
Furthermore, proximity (*āsatti*), which consists in the absence of intervention by unrelated words, is indistinguishable in all cases.
Indeed, mere contiguity (*ānantarya*) alone is not the cause of syntactic relation;
for even in its absence, verbal cognition is experienced provided there is no intervention by unrelated words.

Since it is impossible to recite everything without interruption all at once, and since the understanding that [the mantra] applies to all [verses] is established by the triad of expectancy and so forth alone, it is impossible to effect either a repeated recitation or a recitation extending to the end of all [verses]. Furthermore, because the recitation in the required location can be known through indicative power (liṅga) itself, the textual tradition (āmnāna) is understood to apply to all; thus, there is indeed *anupaṅga* (syntactic connection).
Nor does it follow that, if non-interruption were not a cause [of syntactic connection], the sacrifice itself could not be established as the instrument by the direct hearing of the word;
for even if it is not a cause, we accept its status merely as a regulator in cases of doubt.

In the present case, however, since the fact of being for the sake of all [the sacrifices] is understood through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, there is an absence of the expectancy that would require a regulator; therefore, ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) alone is appropriate.
And for this reason, even when that [Sāman] fails, the expiation for the failure of a Yajus is to be performed.

Thus, where a supplementary element (*śeṣa*) that requires a complement is recited at the end of many principal elements (*śeṣin*) that themselves have no further expectancy—as in "May the Lord of Thought purify you; may the Lord of Speech purify you; may the god Savitṛ purify you with an unbroken strainer"—there too, because proximity (*saṃnidhi*) and syntactic fitness (*yogyatva*) are present without distinction, the supplementary element is to be supplied (*anuṣaṅga*) everywhere.
Nor can proximity (*ānantarya*) be established as a restrictive factor on the grounds that the requirement [of expectancy] is satisfied by a single relationship alone without being aroused;

for even if expectancy is aroused by the expectancy for a subordinate element (*śeṣa*), since the primary elements (*śeṣin*) are predominant, all of them would be understood as recipients of the subordinate element due to the absence of any specific criterion for selection (*vinigamanāviraha*).
Therefore, the *upahoma*s (subsidiary offerings) recited in proximity to various modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) involving multiple oblations (*havir*) pertain to all of them.

And for this reason, in these mantras intended for the purification of the mouth, the navel, and the ankles, the remainder is supplied [to each] according to the principle of repetition for each primary element. // 17 //
Thus ends the seventeenth section concerning incidental application (anuṣaṅga).

(B2) (The connection [of the topic], including the indication of the context for the subject-sentence, etc. And here, since in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) it will be proven that the recitation (*āmnāna*) serves all purposes under the view of "supplementation" (*anuṣaṅga*), and because it is logical that what is supplemented possesses the status of a *yajus*— just like a mantra— by virtue of being recited, the connection with the present topic consists in the nature of the deliberation regarding the transformation of the *yajus*, as in the preceding case.
Omitting [the definition] because it is self-evident, he states the subject matter: "where... (yatra).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, during the second, third, and fourth days, the three Upasad rites in the form of sacrifices are enjoined by the passage: "Agni is the point, Soma is the barb, Viṣṇu is the shaft. These three sacrifices, when practiced on a single day through the divisions of forenoon and afternoon, constitute each individual Upasad.
In that sequence, these three mantras are recited respectively as subordinate offerings (upahoma) belonging to those constituent parts.
In this context, the meaning is that "it is investigated," and so forth.
The summary is given by the opening words of the mantra: “*gahvareṣṭhograṃ vaco apāvadhīntveṣaṃ vaco apāvadhīṃ svāhā*.

O Agni, that body of yours which, abiding in iron (*ayaḥ-sthitā*), most excellent (*varṣiṣṭhā*) and most ancient (*jīrṇā*), dwells in a deep cave (*gahvare*) within a sharp substance—that fierce word (*ugraṃ vacaḥ*) [I have driven away].
Hunger and thirst;

likewise, the meaning of the first mantra is: "I have destroyed (apāvadhīm), that is, I have slain, this speech—both the minor offenses (upapātaka) such as the killing of a hero, and the great sins (mahāpātaka).
Similarly, *rajāśayā* means "situated in silver," and *harāśayā* means "situated in gold."
And it is said in the Brāhmaṇa: "Hunger and thirst, indeed, are the fierce word; sin and the slaying of a learned Brahmin are the terrible word.
Therefore, the first mantra does not require the remaining ones.
The two subsequent [formulas] have a remaining expectancy;

the question here is whether the status of being a *yajus* belongs to what is merely recited according to its textual order, or to those two [formulas] whose expectancy has been satisfied through syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*). Thus, the meaning is that this deliberation is for the purpose of determining the extent of a *yajus*.

(The prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] is as follows: Regarding the two subsequent mantras that have a requirement for a supplement, the fulfillment of that requirement occurs through a worldly word supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*); even though there is a necessity for filling the requirement with a Vedic word, there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by a lapse in the mantra.
In this regard, because the two subsequent mantras contain the relative pronoun *yat* and a feminine gender indication, they necessarily require a word denoting a female.

Since it is impossible to assert that the Vedic portion is taught for all purposes— given that one must assume some part capable of fulfilling the requirement, and because that very [Vedic] portion is understood from the first mantra due to its being recited there and its being read in the required location, and because there is no lack of a discernible distinction [between it and other parts]— and since the subsequent expectancy can be satisfied even by taking secular supplements that are fixed [in context], as in the case of the secular fire in the passage "Having placed the fire, one should praise," so too here.
It is logical to supply [the word] from the worldly context itself.
Even if, because the worldly is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*), it were to be attached to the present topic by way of the *āgneyī* principle;
nevertheless, since even the application elsewhere of the *āgneyī*—though already applied elsewhere—is based on the scriptural statement "kuśa grass, ladle, and so forth," [it is justified].

Even though its status as a mantra is not lost through its entire application, since it is illogical for a portion of this mantra to retain the status of a mantra when taken elsewhere, and because even if the original context were maintained, the status of being a *mantra* and a *yajus* would be absent [in that displaced portion], the doubt that there should be no expiation for an error in that [portion] caused by an error in a *yajus*—being considered easily refuted under the guise of dispelling such an objection—the author states the final conclusion itself: "In that case, regarding the latter two... and so forth.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the two subsequent [sentences] are indeed to be supplied (*anuṣaṅga*) according to the three factors beginning with expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*);
and the purpose (*prayojana*) is because of their being experienced (*ānubhāvikatva*).

In such cases as "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot," it is established by experience that the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs even when the word *devadatta* lacks immediate proximity to the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), provided there is merely an absence of intervention by a word incapable of connecting with the meaning of the suffix. Consequently, since there is no distinction between the two subsequent [words]— namely, the *yogyatā* (semantic competency), which consists in the capacity to satisfy the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) directed toward the qualificand, and the *āsatti* (contiguity), which consists in non-intervention by unrelated words—

the fact that a word already connected with a second [word] may also be connected with a third is possible, because the second word serves as a related term (*saṃbandhipada*) and thus contiguity is maintained.
The meaning is that the preceding remainder alone is connected.
This being the case, he states "all" [in the verse], implying that for a single [element], immediate sequence and the required order of recitation and so forth are of no consequence.

And for this reason, just as the *prayāja* offerings and others—despite being separated from the *āgneyī* verse—pertain to all [offerings] because the triad of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth is common to the *agnīṣomīya* and the rest, so too here, since an immediate sequence must necessarily occur somewhere in the text, it is recited for the sake of all; such is the meaning of "attachment" (*anuṣaṅga*).
This refers to the doubt.

For in that case, since there is no fixed rule as to whether the sacrifice (*yāga*) or the *soma* and so forth is what defines the fruit, the proximity of the word (*padapratyāsatti*) serves merely as a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*).

However, in the present context (*prakṛte*), because a restriction is already established everywhere without doubt, it does not function as a restrictive factor; thus he says: "But in the present case... (*prakṛtetu*).
He states the purpose [of the following]: "And for this reason" (ataśca).

(The prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] is as follows): Since the subordinate element (*śeṣa*), which requires a principal element (*śeṣin*), becomes free of expectancy through its connection with the *ekaśeṣa* (the single remainder), there is no connection between "with the unbroken [sieve]" (*acchidreṇa*) and so forth, and "may the Lord of the Mind purify you" (*citpatistvā punātu*) and so forth; thus, there is no *anuṣaṅga* (supplying an ellipsis).
[The author] introduces another interpretation (*varṇaka*) presented in the Bhāṣya for the sake of comprehensive coverage of the subject matter, beginning with "In this way" (*evam*).

Considering the doubt that there might be a distinction—namely, that when many remain requiring [an auxiliary], even if one has been rendered free of expectancy through connection with a single auxiliary, it is proper for the others to undergo *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) to achieve their own lack of expectancy; whereas once an auxiliary has achieved lack of expectancy through connection with one principal (*śeṣin*), it is not proper for it to undergo *anuṣaṅga* for connection with another principal—he shows the scope [of the rule] by saying "where...
and "with the purifier" (*pavitreṇa*).
By the use of the word "iti," there is a summary of the passage ending with "with the rays of the sun, the Vasu.

In that context, considering that the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) could be easily refuted by means of dispelling the very doubt hinted at within its own specific objection, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta) itself with the words: "In that case also... (tatrāpi).

(Regarding "citpatistva" and so forth, the word "acchidreṇa" is also to be supplied [as an anuṣaṅga]; the position that there is an option between the three aforementioned mantras is the one favored by the author of the Vārttika, as well as its refutation.)
"Even when there is the arising of a desire."
The phrase "of the principal elements (śeṣin) which have previously become independent" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

Here, in the Vārttika, because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of both the word and its meaning in the purifying action (*pāvana-kriyā*) enjoined by the injunction "he purifies the sacrificer," even though Citpati and the others—like Bhaga and the rest—are mentioned for the sake of praise, their difference is not established; rather, due to their unity, that [action] is performed by all three, just as in the case of the distribution (*vibhāga*).
Because the *karaṇa-mantras* serve the purpose of manifesting the single purificatory act— which has become a means to the *apūrva*— through its manifestation as being free from defects and so forth,

the two preceding mantras must also be employed just like the final mantra. For this very reason, since there is no distinction between the *apūrvas* here as there is in the case of the *apūrvas* resulting from the repetition of each individual cup (*graha*), the preceding mantras do not have the status of being for the sake of the prior [acts] merely through the repetition of the final purificatory act.

In that regard, it has been stated that there is an option (*vikalpa*) among the mantras because they serve the purpose of manifesting a single purificatory act (*pāvanakriyā*). However, since the statement made by Pārthasārathi—“He purifies the sacrificer with three”—is consistent with the principle of number, and because the combination (*samuccaya*) of mantras is established by the very words “her with four,” an option is untenable. Even though the action is one, this is determined upon a careful examination of the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of Bodhāyana and others.

Since it is understood from the threefold repetition at the mouth, the navel, and the region of the ankles—even for the *pāvana*—that each mantra is to be repeated once, the subsequent qualification [of the mantras] as "without flaw" (*acchidra*) and so forth must be construed as a single syntactical unit with the word indicating the practice of the *pāvana* rite for the sake of purification at the region of the ankles; therefore, it is logical that they serve as subsidiaries to the practice of the *pāvana* rite which produces a heterogeneous *apūrva*. For, just as the boiling with milk prescribed by the rule "he boils the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk" applies only to that specific instance and not to other repetitions, here too, since it is impossible for the practice to apply to other instances of repetition, a fixed restriction (*vyavasthā*) alone is obtained.

For this very reason—intending that [the rule] is for the sake of excellence (*atiśaya*), since otherwise there would be no possibility of option (*vikalpa*) in the absence of such a statement—he establishes the connection of the remainder (*śeṣa*) everywhere precisely because there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*), stating: "Because of its primacy (*pradhānatvāt*)," and "of the immediate sequence (*ānantaryasya*)."

Since it was previously stated that [the mantra] serves as a determiner when there would otherwise be no fixed rule regarding immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), the meaning here is that even in this case, it lacks determinative power in the absence of such immediate sequence.

He concludes by indicating, through the phrase "ataśca" ("and therefore"), that the purpose of the mantras is the practice of their respective ritual actions, as established by a careful examination of the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of Bodhāyana and others.
By presenting the reason "according to the principle of repetition for each principal element" (*pratipradhānāvṛttinyāyāt*), the refutation of what was stated in the Vārttika is indicated.
As for the purpose—consisting in whether or not there is an expiation for an error in the *yajus* formula used in the remaining [ritual] applications—it has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the seventeenth section concerning the application by connection (anuṣaṅga).
(B1) (Section 18 / [a.2 pā.1 adhi.18]) Because of intervention.

But where there is an intervention by unrelated words—as in "May the breath go with the wind; may the limbs [go] with the sacrificial objects; may the lord of the sacrifice [go] for the sake of the blessing"—here, the word *gacchatām* ("may they go") does not have *anuṣaṅga* (syntactic connection) with *āśiṣe* ("for the sake of the blessing").

In the phrase "aṅgāni," since there is no syntactic connection with the singular form, it is necessary to supply the plural form "gacchantām. In reality, however, because the plural must be supplied, this is merely an illustration of the non-attachment (*pratyudāharaṇa*) of the singular verb root *gam*. Thus, it is the singular that is not attached here. // 18 //
Thus ends the eighteenth section, concerning the supplying of ellipses (adhyāhāra).
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Bhāṭṭadīpikā composed by the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.

(B2) (The determination of the absence of *anuṣaṅga* due to the absence of proximity): He shows an example where *anuṣaṅga* is impossible and where there is an intervention in the middle, as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to *anuṣaṅga*, by saying "for example" (*yathā*).

And these three mantras are applied in sequence for the anointing of the head, the two shoulders, and the right hip of the animal with the remainder of the clarified butter from the northern half [of the vessel].

In that regard, in the first sentence, the prefix *sam-*—which is declared to be grammatically correct even when separated by another word according to the rule *chandasi vyavahitāśca*—is construed with the word *gacchatām*.
This is because here it is the life-force (*āyuḥ*) and breath (*prāṇa*) of the animal itself that should unite with the external air.
"The meaning of the three mantras is: 'May the lord of the sacrifice and you be united with the blessing, that is, with the fruit.

He says [this] regarding the word 'may they go' from the first mantra: even though expectancy and semantic fitness exist, there is no *anuṣaṅga* (supplying a word) because of the absence of proximity."
Because there is a necessity for supplying ellipsis (adhyāhāra).

(The traditional view is that the word *gacchatām* is to be supplied [as an ellipsis] after *saṃyajñapatirāśiṣā*). Consequently, since it is necessary to supply the word *gacchantām* after *saṃyajatrairaṅgāni*, because of the intervention by that [word], one must likewise supply the word *gacchatām* after *saṃyajñapatirāśiṣā* in order to establish its status as an explicit verbal expression (*śābdatva*).

The meaning is as follows: since even the conceptualized word (*kalpya-pada*) functions as the instrument of expression (*abhidhāna-karaṇa*), it is impossible for it to function as such without the activity of an agent; and because, as in the case of other mantras, there is no activity of an agent directed toward the sound itself beyond its mere utterance, one must assume that utterance alone constitutes [the word]. Thus, the status of being something to be uttered (*uccāryatva*) is established.
(One's own established position is that there is merely the supply of a case-ending.

Having thus justified the supply of the word "gacchantām" (let them go) as stated by the ancients, he states the specific distinction therein: "In reality, however..."—namely, that it is indeed an *anuṣaṅga* (an elliptical extension).
In the case of "saṃ yajatraiḥ," since the ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) is possible from its original context (*prakṛti*), even if only the plural ending is supplied,

then because the ellipsis can also occur from its original context without interruption in the phrase "saṃ yajñapatiḥ," the singular ending found in the first mantra does not undergo ellipsis due to being interrupted in the middle by the plural ending.
However, the meaning is that it is more appropriate to treat this merely as a counter-example for the singular number, on the grounds that ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) must indeed be supplied.

(The refutation of the view of the author of the *Prakāśa* that [the word] must indeed be supplied, along with its purpose: As for the objection raised by the authors of the *Prakāśa*, the response is as follows: it is the word-meaning itself that is required, not merely a part of it.

Because of its verbal nature (*śābdatva*), it is the word itself that is required, not a part thereof; thus, there is *anusaṅga* (supplying) or *adhyāhāra* (insertion) of the entire word, and not of a mere part such as the suffix alone or the stem alone. For just as the insertion of a mere suffix is accepted as being based on Vedic authority (*ārṣatva*), so too here the supplying of the stem is logically established as being based on Vedic authority. Otherwise—

In that case as well, since it would follow that the entire word must be supplied, and because there is no obstacle to supplying only the suffix, [the objection] is incorrect; this is made clear in the Kaustubha.

And thus, the expiation for the corruption of a Yajus applies only to the corruption of the base (prakṛti), whereas in the case of the corruption of the suffix (pratyaya), it does not apply; this further purpose has not been stated here because it is obvious.
Thus ends the eighteenth section, concerning the supplying of ellipses (adhyāhāra).
